entry.title: New $48 million Westlake elementary school stays on track despite heavy rain, flooding
entry.summary: A new elementary school in Westlake is quickly taking shape, with project leaders saying construction remains on time and on budget despite recent heavy rain and flooding. WPTV reporter Christy Waite first toured the construction site in August , when much of the school was still a concrete slab. She returned to the site on Friday and found a much different scene, with the building now taking shape. WATCH REPORT BELOW: PROGRESS ON WESTLAKES NEW SCHOOL Site Superintendent Brad Stapleton said recent weather created challenges for crews, with parts of the construction site underwater. 'We joked that we should have brought kayaks and canoes to work to get from our trailer and parking to the building because a lot of this area that we are standing in now was underwater,' Stapleton said. Despite those conditions, Stapleton said construction has stayed on track. 'We are looking great for meeting the August turnover for the next school year,' he said. Principal Darline Winewski has watched the school rise from the ground up and said seeing the individual spaces inside the building is making the project feel more real. 'To actually see the walls come up and really be able to see the individual spaces, I'm just so excited,' Winewski said. As Westlake continues to grow, the $48 million school will have room for 972 students in pre-K through fifth grade. Winewski said the new school will fill a need for families whose children currently attend two different schools. 'We really have a need for this school in our community. Our families deserve that. Our kids deserve that. They are going to two different schools right now,' Winewski said. Waite also connected with parent Krystal Lexima, whose daughter is looking forward to the new school opening. 'She's so excited to walk the halls for the first time,' Lexima said. Another milestone is coming soon. The school's official name, mascot and colors are expected to be revealed next month. 'We submitted our names to the board and we will find out soon enough and start identifying ourselves officially,' Winewski said.

entry.title: Día de Muertos celebration to be held in West Palm Beach after Lake Worth Beach festival canceled
entry.summary: A longtime organizer of Lake Worth Beachs Da de Muertos festival is bringing the celebration to West Palm Beach this weekend after this year's Lake Worth Beach event was canceled. Local artist and educator Jose R. Mendez will host Da de Muertos at The Peach on Saturday from 3 p.m. to 9 p.m. at The Peach arts collective, 3950 Georgia Ave. Admission is free, and the event is open to the public. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Da de Muertos tradition continues in West Palm Beach Mendez co-founded the original Da de Muertos celebration in Lake Worth Beach in 2016 and helped develop and coordinate the festival for years. He said he organized Saturdays independent event because he did not want the local tradition to disappear. 'I do not want to see a tradition that I helped create, that has become so meaningful to our community, come to an end,' Mendez said. This year's celebration also carries a personal significance for Mendez. His father, Juan J. Mendez, recently died in Guatemala. 'Part of the reason I moved forward with this was to honor my dad, who passed away a couple of weeks ago,' Mendez said. 'He was big on culture.' What to expect Saturdays celebration will feature traditional Da de Muertos ofrendas, or altars, along with local artisan vendors, face painting, outdoor art installations and a childrens activity zone presented by Raices Creative Arts Academy. The entertainment lineup includes Mariachi De Mi Tierra Internacional, vocalist Emmanuel Gonzalez, a Selena tribute by Liz Ramirez and a performance by Latinos A Bailar, a dance group from John I. Leonard High School. Catrin and Catrina costume contests will also be held for adults, children and pets. Food and drinks will be available from El Segundo, the restaurant located at The Peach. Organizers say this years event will be smaller than previous celebrations in Lake Worth Beach, which attracted as many as 6,000 people. 'I'm not the kind of guy that likes to scale back,' Mendez said. 'But I believe bringing even one-quarter of our audience to a new location would be a significant step toward keeping this tradition alive.' Mendez helped coordinate Lake Worth Beachs Da de Muertos celebrations from 2016 through 2024. His work has focused on public art, cultural research and creating opportunities for people of different ages to participate in the arts. Organizers said the goal of Saturday's event remains the same despite the new location: creating a place where families can celebrate and share cultural tradition

entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.article_text: Votes are still being counted in Mississippi, in the tight senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.Part of the delay in counting is because thousands of voters cast their ballots by affidavit rather than a traditional ballot. Many voters said they were caught by surprise when they learned they would have to vote by affidavit because their registration was marked inactive. “It was very disheartening to be labeled inactive,” voter Kevin Green, a Mississippi voter, told Scripps News this week. “And there was no real rationale behind it.”Green said he has voted consistently since moving back to his home state of Mississippi in 2020. He said he received a notice from the NAACP telling him to look up his registration status in the days before the election. When he did, he was shocked to see his status was inactive. After speaking to the county clerk, he learned he would have to vote by affidavit because he had not responded to a mailer seeking to verify his address. After successfully voting on Election Day by affidavit, Green posted about his experience on social media. “We know there was some shady business going on there,” Green told Scripps News, pointing to the state’s history of disenfranchising Black voters. “It's really not a good look for our state when we've come so far, and the fact that this election is now so close speaks volumes about where we've come.”Ralph Sandidge said he was disappointed to find out he had been purged from the voter rolls when he arrived to cast his ballot this year.“I said, ‘Well, who did that? Under what authority?’” Sandidge said. Sandidge said he was told he was no longer registered to vote because he had not voted in several elections. Election experts told Scripps News the large number of inactive voters this election in Mississippi may be due in part to the state’s reliance on consumer data provided by Experian to maintain its voter rolls. The state used the data to check voter addresses, but experts said the data may have contained errors affecting thousands of voters. “Everything we've heard from the Secretary of State's office is that this was a good faith effort to keep the voter rolls accurate,” said Daniel Griffith, the senior director of policy at Secure Democracy. “Because it wasn't based on the best practices, and because the credit agency data is not reliable, it has had an unfortunate outcome for a lot of individuals.”Thomas Minor said he encountered such an error when he attempted to vote in the primary election earlier this year. He told Scripps News the clerk told him his registration was inactivated because Experian data said he lived in another city. However, he told Scripps News, he has not moved for a decade. He was able to fix the error and vote normally during the general election on Tuesday but was dismayed to see so many other voters encounter the same problem he had months ago. “It feels like somebody’s trying to pull strings somewhere and mess things up,” Minor said. “We have no evidence that there is something sinister (happening), and election officials are very, very careful and very committed to protect elections and not disenfranchise voters,” said Thessalia Merivaki, a distinguished professor of government at Washington State University. “Sometimes your data are bad, and this is what happens.”An Experian spokesperson said its company has not provided services to the state since 2025.“The solution provided at that time consisted of supplemental address information and was not designed or intended to validate voter records,” said Scott Anderson, vice president of corporate communications for Experian, in a statement sent Friday to Scripps News. “Decisions regarding voter registration policies, procedures and record updates are made solely by election officials in accordance with applicable local, state and federal laws.”The Mississippi Secretary of State’s Office did not respond to multiple voice messages and emails from Scripps News.RELATED STORY | Democrat clings to razor-thin lead in Mississippi Senate raceIn a Friday interview with Democracy Docket, Colom criticized the state for its use of Experian data and said voters experiencing ballot problems should contact his campaign for help. Merivaki said she expects the Secretary of State’s office will investigate what went wrong. In the meantime, election clerks across Mississippi are counting affidavit ballots to determine the winners of Tuesday’s election. Voters who provided identification and voted by affidavit do not need to take any further action for their votes to be counted. Those who did not have ID with them have until Tuesday to rectify their affidavits. The Secretary of State’s office posted a tracker online for voters who voted absentee or by affidavit to ensure their ballot is being counted.Kevin Green said he’s happy to know his vote will count, but wants the process to change going forward. “Obviously there are some gaps there, and we need to revisit that and ensure that we have effective policies that are in place,” he said.

entry.title: $1,000 grants offered to Greenacres residents displaced by deadly Learjet crash
entry.summary: Nearly a week after a Learjet crash killed nine people in Greenacres and forced hundreds from their homes, some residents are still waiting for an answer to the question that has consumed their lives since the crash. For those who haven't been allowed to return, the cost of being displaced is adding up. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Organizations mobilize to help residents displaced from jet crash 'When are they going to let us back home?' Joseph Santana Quiroz asked WPTV. He hasn't been allowed home all week. He told WPTV he has also had to miss work without pay. 'If you can't work, they can't pay you?' WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked. 'Exactly,' Santana Quiroz said. But even without a paycheck, the bills don't stop. 'We can't tell the bank we can't pay because this happened,' Santana Quiroz said. He is one of 31 people still sheltering at the Greenacres Community Center as the investigation continues. 'We actually are ready and prepared to start taking in grant applications at this time,' said Josselyn Hodges, director of the People First Fund Initiative at Emergency Assistance Foundation. entry.article_text: Nearly a week after a Learjet crash killed nine people in Greenacres and forced hundreds from their homes, some residents are still waiting for an answer to the question that has consumed their lives since the crash.For those who haven't been allowed to return, the cost of being displaced is adding up.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "When are they going to let us back home?" Joseph Santana Quiroz asked WPTV.He hasn't been allowed home all week.He told WPTV he has also had to miss work without pay."If you can't work, they can't pay you?" WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked."Exactly," Santana Quiroz said.But even without a paycheck, the bills don't stop."We can't tell the bank we can't pay because this happened," Santana Quiroz said.He is one of 31 people still sheltering at the Greenacres Community Center as the investigation continues.Now, organizations are stepping in to help with everything from those immediate financial pressures to the challenges residents could face when they are finally allowed back home.The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched the People First Fund for Green Acres Mobile Home Community Learjet Crash to provide direct financial assistance to eligible residents impacted by the crash."We actually are ready and prepared to start taking in grant applications at this time," said Josselyn Hodges, director of the People First Fund Initiative at Emergency Assistance Foundation.She told WPTV the organization normally responds to disasters and hardships around the world, but this time the need is close to home."We are a global public charity that does financial assistance to impacted individuals after disasters around the world. However, we're headquartered here in West Palm Beach, so we felt compelled to help our neighbors," Hodges said.The organization plans to provide $1,000 cash grants to eligible individuals, allowing residents to decide where that money is needed most."Our goal is to be able to provide that financial assistance so people can take care of their most urgent self-assessed needs," Hodges said. "We understand that when people get displaced from their homes, you know, they experience financial hardship in seeking temporary housing, in seeking food and other personal hardships."Hodges said the cash assistance is intended to complement the food, shelter and other services being provided by different organizations."While there may be other organizations that support with food or housing, you know, this financial assistance and cash assistance that will be, you know, landing directly into the hands of individuals is meant to be able to help those individuals, you know, take, you know, buy supplies or take care of whatever items are, you know, heaviest in their mind at this time," Hodges said.Through donations from community foundations and individual donors, Hodges said the fund currently has enough money to provide $1,000 grants to 18 people.But the organization wants to go further."We understand that there are about 68 impacted individuals from the mobile home community, the Green Acres mobile home community, so we are calling on to the community to come together and be able to, you know, turn that compassion into tangible support and help us reach every single one of these members," Hodges said.Hodges said the goal is to raise enough money to provide a grant to all 68 individuals the organization has identified.Residents looking for assistance won't simply have to navigate the process on their own. Hodges said EAF is working with members of the Emergency Operations Center to identify people with the greatest needs and provide them with a direct link to apply.For residents who don't know when they'll be able to return home, Hodges said the goal is to provide some immediate relief while other assistance is still coming together."We believe in the power of community. We know that people wanna come together and help community members in the wake of hardships and disasters, so we have a way to be able to provide that immediate impact now while other resources are still mobilizing," Hodges said. "That is our goal, to be able to support people in the very first critical days of their recovery process."Preparing for what happens when residents return homeThe financial fallout may not end when people are finally able to return.State Rep. Debra Tendrich is working through her organization, Eat Better Live Better, to prepare for another expense some families could face: replacing spoiled food."If you look at what's happening with their electricity being cut off and the power grid shut down, you're looking at people returning to their homes and having to throw out their entire refrigerator full of food that they might have just purchased or or that they need to fill now," Tendrich said.For families already dealing with displacement and lost income, Tendrich wants to make replacing those groceries one less thing they have to worry about."I'm really working right now to make sure that we are able to help fill those refrigerators," Tendrich said.Tendrich's nonprofit operates an affordable farmers market-style food pantry with fresh and healthy items.She said her organization was already seeing an increased demand for grocery assistance before the crash."We, we've been seeing an increased need as is. My organization has received between 25 and 100 new applications every week needing grocery assistance," Tendrich said. "So to pile that up with having to now, have your entire refrigerator needs to be thrown out and then also replenish that just doubles down on how hard times are right now for my community."For Tendrich, it's about helping families move toward some sense of normalcy after days of uncertainty."The last thing that you want to worry about is how are you going to feed yourself, your family and your children after a tragedy like this," Tendrich said.Tendrich said displaced families are also dealing with needs that can easily be overlooked during a prolonged evacuation, including getting to doctor's appointments and accessing medications."Families with their children are trying to get to doctor's appointments, get their medications that they need, uh, we're really trying to make sure that people are accessing everything they need at this moment to get through this while they're displaced from their homes," Tendrich said. "We're doing everything we can between the county, the police, the fire and my office. We're working hard to make sure not only while you're, you're displaced, but once you get back home, we're trying to make sure that you're supported as much as possible during this, this tough time."While groups are getting to work countywide, help continues while families wait as other organizations are addressing needs at the shelter itself.Many other organizations like the Red Cross, and community members have dropped off supplies this week.Dare to Care has been providing mobile showers and laundry services at the Greenacres Community Center."They called us on Monday and said, ‘Can you come out?’ We've been here ever since," said Timothy Murphy, with the organization Dare to Care. "My message to residents is that there are people who care. We're here for those in need no matter what," he said. "When crisis happen it just complies, so we're here to relieve some of the loss."It remains unclear how long all of the impacted residents will be displaced.Click here if you'd like to help make monetary donations.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Boynton Beach police seek driver who ran over, killed 6-month-old puppy
entry.summary: Police are asking for the public's help identifying a driver after a 6-month-old dog was found dead in a Boynton Beach parking lot earlier this week. Shortly after 2:30 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3, Boynton Beach Police received a report of a dead dog in a parking space at the back of a parking lot at 1500 Southwest 8th Street. WATCH VIDEO BELOW: Police seek driver after puppy found dead in Boynton Beach An animal cruelty officer responded and found a small white dog that appeared to have been run over, according to police. Investigators described the dog as a female Jack Russell Terrier, approximately 6 months old, with white fur and light tan or brown spots. Detectives obtained surveillance video that police said shows a dark-colored sedan, believed to possibly be a Tesla, entering the parking lot at about 1:35 p.m. According to police, the driver parked and got out before walking around the back of the vehicle toward the passenger side. The dog was then seen walking from the passenger side toward the front of the vehicle while the driver walked back around the car and returned to the driver's seat. entry.article_text: Floodwaters are receding in Indian River County, but some areas remain affected by standing water as crews and officials work to address the aftermath of this week’s severe downpours. Law enforcement officials said County Roads 510 and 512 were reduced to one lane at one point due to flooding. Crews installed an emergency pipe under the roadway Thursday night to help drain the area. Dave Kubacki, a resident of Sebastian, shared cellphone video of the flooding outside his home. "Holy smoke, I can't believe how much water was out there, and I can't believe how fast it disappeared," Kubacki said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates He said he was surprised by the flooding, noting that the only time it had been this bad was during a hurricane. "The hurricanes were bad, but I've never seen rain come down like this for such a long period of time and so heavy," Kubacki said. Officials shared video of flooded roads taken just after the severe downpours, along with body camera footage showing deputies responding to incidents caused by the high water. Deputies were called to a residential driveway to secure an alligator that had been pushed out of its usual habitat by the flooding. The alligator was safely relocated to another area within the county. County leaders said assessment teams were out Friday surveying the damage, and results are still pending. Schools in Indian River County were closed Friday but are expected to reopen Monday. Kubacki said he shared the news with his granddaughter. "I said, 'Are you mad that schools are closed?' and she said, 'Oh no!' I said, 'What about your friends?' She said, 'That's OK, I'll see them on Monday,'" Kubacki said. Officials are reminding residents to avoid flooded roads as cleanup efforts continue. entry.title: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall    WPBF
entry.article_text: Five days after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still dealing with several feet of standing water inside their homes, with little indication of when it will recede. The street remains accessible only by boat or kayak, with floodwaters reaching mailboxes and entering most homes along the road. For longtime resident Linda Weisbecker, the flooding has left decades of memories and belongings underwater. “Sixty years of your life is gone. We raised our kids, our grandkids, our great-grandkids. It’s all gone,” Weisbecker said. Weisbecker said her home still has several feet of water inside, preventing her from beginning the cleanup process. “Our main goal is to get this water off so we can get in and start getting things done. If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said. Just down the road, Lisa French is dealing with similar conditions. French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. However, as water continued to accumulate in the neighborhood, it eventually entered her home two days later. Now, she is concerned about mold growth and how much of her home may need to be torn out and replaced. We’re a single-family income. I stay at home with my kids. So it’s, you know, we don’t even know where to start. And we can’t start because the water is still here,” French said. The affected neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. Martin County officials told WPBF 25 News that crews will be working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. entry.title: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary seeks help after historic flooding
entry.summary: Save the Chimps, a 150-acre chimpanzee sanctuary in Fort Pierce, is asking the community for help after historic flooding left parts of its property underwater, damaged equipment and disrupted normal operations. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary seeks help after historic flooding The sanctuary's more than 200 chimpanzees are safe and continue to receive food, medication, enrichment and other daily care, according to Mark Yohannan, the organization's director of facilities. But Yohannan told WPTV the sanctuary faces a long recovery after receiving 19 inches of rain. 'We've got a long way to go,' Yohannan said. He said it is the worst flooding the sanctuary has experienced in its 25 years in Fort Pierce. 'We're absolutely shut down until we get the water gone,' Yohannan said. Staff adapts to care for chimpanzees Since Tuesday, Save the Chimps staff members have had to find new ways to reach parts of the flooded sanctuary. Workers have used tractors and trailers to navigate the property and deliver supplies. Video shared with WPTV shows staff using a drone to drop food to a chimpanzee during the flooding. Despite the difficult conditions, Yohannan said the chimpanzees have continued receiving their normal care. 'They're doing great. The care staff have been on their game,' Yohannan said. 'They're getting everything they would get normally: enrichment, all their food, all their medication, blankets. They haven't missed a beat.' Yohannan said some staff members have been unable to get to work because of the flooding, but those who can reach the sanctuary have come together to keep operations moving. 'It's heavy, but it's good heavy,' Yohannan said. 'Everyone's come together.' Flooding damages vehicles and equipment The flooding has also taken a toll on equipment used for everyday operations. Yohannan said nearly 15 golf carts used to transport food, supplies and staff around the 150-acre property have broken down. 'We'd seen the water and we figured, well, no big deal, we'll drive through it, and that became impossible immediately,' he said. Yohannan said the sanctuary is looking for taller four-wheel-drive vehicles that can safely move people and supplies through the property while floodwaters remain. 'We need four-wheel-drive vehicles that are taller that can move supplies and people,' Yohannan said. He said the vehicles could be rented or donated for a short period. entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said. Just down the road, Lisa French is dealing with similar conditions. French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. However, as water continued to accumulate in the neighborhood, it eventually entered her home two days later. Now, she is concerned about mold growth and how much of her home may need to be torn out and replaced. We’re a single-family income. I stay at home with my kids. So it’s, you know, we don’t even know where to start. And we can’t start because the water is still here,” French said. The affected neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. Martin County officials told WPBF 25 News that crews will be working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. entry.article_text: Nearly a week after a Learjet crash killed nine people in Greenacres and forced hundreds from their homes, some residents are still waiting for an answer to the question that has consumed their lives since the crash.For those who haven't been allowed to return, the cost of being displaced is adding up.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "When are they going to let us back home?" Joseph Santana Quiroz asked WPTV.He hasn't been allowed home all week.He told WPTV he has also had to miss work without pay."If you can't work, they can't pay you?" WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked."Exactly," Santana Quiroz said.But even without a paycheck, the bills don't stop."We can't tell the bank we can't pay because this happened," Santana Quiroz said.He is one of 31 people still sheltering at the Greenacres Community Center as the investigation continues.Now, organizations are stepping in to help with everything from those immediate financial pressures to the challenges residents could face when they are finally allowed back home.The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched the People First Fund for Green Acres Mobile Home Community Learjet Crash to provide direct financial assistance to eligible residents impacted by the crash."We actually are ready and prepared to start taking in grant applications at this time," said Josselyn Hodges, director of the People First Fund Initiative at Emergency Assistance Foundation.She told WPTV the organization normally responds to disasters and hardships around the world, but this time the need is close to home."We are a global public charity that does financial assistance to impacted individuals after disasters around the world. However, we're headquartered here in West Palm Beach, so we felt compelled to help our neighbors," Hodges said.The organization plans to provide $1,000 cash grants to eligible individuals, allowing residents to decide where that money is needed most."Our goal is to be able to provide that financial assistance so people can take care of their most urgent self-assessed needs," Hodges said. "We understand that when people get displaced from their homes, they experience financial hardship in seeking temporary housing, in seeking food and other personal hardships."Hodges said the cash assistance is intended to complement the food, shelter and other services being provided by different organizations."While there may be other organizations that support with food or housing, this financial assistance and cash assistance that will be, landing directly into the hands of individuals is meant to be able to help those individuals, take, buy supplies or take care of whatever items are, heaviest in their mind at this time," Hodges said.Through donations from community foundations and individual donors, Hodges said the fund currently has enough money to provide $1,000 grants to 18 people.But the organization wants to go further."We understand that there are about 68 impacted individuals from the mobile home community, the Green Acres mobile home community, so we are calling on to the community to come together and be able to, turn that compassion into tangible support and help us reach every single one of these members," Hodges said.Hodges said the goal is to raise enough money to provide a grant to all 68 individuals the organization has identified.Residents looking for assistance won't simply have to navigate the process on their own. Hodges said EAF is working with members of the Emergency Operations Center to identify people with the greatest needs and provide them with a direct link to apply.For residents who don't know when they'll be able to return home, Hodges said the goal is to provide some immediate relief while other assistance is still coming together."We believe in the power of community. We know that people wanna come together and help community members in the wake of hardships and disasters, so we have a way to be able to provide that immediate impact now while other resources are still mobilizing," Hodges said. "That is our goal, to be able to support people in the very first critical days of their recovery process."Preparing for what happens when residents return homeThe financial fallout may not end when people are finally able to return.State Rep. Debra Tendrich is working through her organization, Eat Better Live Better, to prepare for another expense some families could face: replacing spoiled food."If you look at what's happening with their electricity being cut off and the power grid shut down, you're looking at people returning to their homes and having to throw out their entire refrigerator full of food that they might have just purchased or or that they need to fill now," Tendrich said.For families already dealing with displacement and lost income, Tendrich wants to make replacing those groceries one less thing they have to worry about."I'm really working right now to make sure that we are able to help fill those refrigerators," Tendrich said.Tendrich's nonprofit operates an affordable farmers market-style food pantry with fresh and healthy items.She said her organization was already seeing an increased demand for grocery assistance before the crash."We, we've been seeing an increased need as is. My organization has received between 25 and 100 new applications every week needing grocery assistance," Tendrich said. "So to pile that up with having to now, have your entire refrigerator needs to be thrown out and then also replenish that just doubles down on how hard times are right now for my community."For Tendrich, it's about helping families move toward some sense of normalcy after days of uncertainty."The last thing that you want to worry about is how are you going to feed yourself, your family and your children after a tragedy like this," Tendrich said.Tendrich said displaced families are also dealing with needs that can easily be overlooked during a prolonged evacuation, including getting to doctor's appointments and accessing medications."Families with their children are trying to get to doctor's appointments, get their medications that they need, uh, we're really trying to make sure that people are accessing everything they need at this moment to get through this while they're displaced from their homes," Tendrich said. "We're doing everything we can between the county, the police, the fire and my office. We're working hard to make sure not only while you're, you're displaced, but once you get back home, we're trying to make sure that you're supported as much as possible during this, this tough time."While groups are getting to work countywide, help continues while families wait as other organizations are addressing needs at the shelter itself.Many other organizations like the Red Cross, and community members have dropped off supplies this week.Dare to Care has been providing mobile showers and laundry services at the Greenacres Community Center."They called us on Monday and said, ‘Can you come out?’ We've been here ever since," said Timothy Murphy, with the organization Dare to Care. "My message to residents is that there are people who care. We're here for those in need no matter what," he said. "When crisis happen it just complies, so we're here to relieve some of the loss."It remains unclear how long all of the impacted residents will be displaced.Click here if you'd like to help make monetary donations.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

entry.title: Pinewood Elementary's Richard Acosta named Martin County Teacher of Year - WPBF
entry.summary: Pinewood Elementary's Richard Acosta named Martin County Teacher of Year    WPBF
entry.article_text: Richard Acosta of Pinewood Elementary School has been named the 2026-2027 Martin County Teacher of the Year, the Martin County School District and the Education Foundation of Martin County announced. Acosta was selected from 24 educators representing schools throughout the district. He was earlier named the Elementary Teacher of the Year. The announcement was made during the Education Foundation of Martin County’s Teacher of the Year Awards Celebration on Friday at the MIDFLORIDA Credit Union Event Center in Port St. About 800 people attended the event. It was the 42nd year of the Teacher of the Year Award. “The Teacher of the Year celebration is a special tradition that allows us to pause and celebrate the educators who give so much to their students, colleagues and school communities,” Superintendent Michael Maine said. “We are incredibly proud of all of our school-level honorees and especially proud to recognize Richard Acosta as the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year. Thank you to the Education Foundation of Martin County and our sponsors for helping make this evening such a meaningful celebration of our teachers.” “On behalf of the Education Foundation of Martin County, I am thrilled to congratulate Richard Acosta on being named the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year,” Kelley Decowski, president of the Education Foundation of Martin County, said. “We are fortunate to have so many exceptional educators who inspire and empower students every day. Selecting just one to represent Martin County's public schools is no easy task. Acosta exemplifies the passion and dedication that make our teachers so extraordinary.” An educator since 1991, Acosta joined the Martin County School District in 2019 and serves at Pinewood Elementary School as the Related Arts-Science teacher. Acosta brings a hands-on approach to learning that connects classroom instruction to real-world discovery, including helping students tackle challenging concepts or encouraging them to explore the world through scientific inquiry. “After I teach a lesson, I’m always thinking of as I teach that lesson, how can I make it better," Acosta said. "And I’m never tired of it because I teach science. And I’m always one-upping the lesson, and I’m always striving to be better than I was the day before.” At Pinewood, Acosta has helped lead schoolwide STEAM initiatives, chaired the STEAM School Improvement Team, and secured two Martin County Education Foundation grants to support innovative science projects. He also developed a Birds of the Everglades curriculum in partnership with Friends of the Everglades and Inwater Research Group, scheduled to be piloted at Pinewood in fall 2026. His efforts have helped strengthen science instruction and contributed to an increase in fifth-grade science proficiency by 12 percentage points. Acosta exemplifies what it means to be a passionate educator. His love for teaching is evident in every learning experience he creates,” former Principal Susanna Deutsch shared. “His ability to make complex concepts accessible, engaging and meaningful has fostered authentic excitement for learning, with students eagerly sharing their discoveries and newfound knowledge throughout the school.” Miriam Hernandez, an intensive reading teacher at Indiantown Middle School, was named Middle School Teacher of the Year. Hernandez’s career with the Martin County School District began in 2006 as a paraprofessional before she became a teacher in 2012. Since joining Indiantown Middle School in 2018, she has served students in a variety of roles, including Spanish and Intensive Reading, building a reputation as a trusted educator who believes deeply in every student’s ability to grow. “In every role, she has approached her work with professionalism, compassion, and an unwavering belief that every student is capable of growth and success,” Assistant Principal Kellie Siters shared. “She meets students where they are, builds meaningful relationships with them, and works tirelessly to ensure they receive the support they need to thrive both academically and personally.” Marc Turull, an International Baccalaureate physics and chemistry teacher at South Fork High School, was named High School Teacher of the Year. An educator since 2007, Mr. Marc Turull has served students at South Fork High School since 2011. He brings science to life through real-world applications, career exploration and hands-on learning. Outside the classroom, he has been involved in the Engineering Club, First Priority Club and Architecture, Construction and Engineering Mentorship Program, as well as annual STEM experiences that connect students with opportunities and careers in their community. “Marc is widely admired for his ability to foster a positive, inclusive, and engaging learning environment,” South Fork High School Principal Jaime Thompson shared. “He believes that every student can achieve at high levels when provided with meaningful, challenging, and supportive instruction – and he brings that belief to life daily in his classroom.” Felix A. Williams Elementary School earned the Spirit Award for the team that displays the most school spirit. The event’s presenting sponsors were Audi Stuart and Infiniti Stuart, along with Cigna Healthcare, Publix Super Markets Charities, and Keiser University. The nominees are listed on the Education Foundation of Martin County website. The A-rated Martin County School District serves approximately 16,000 students with opportunities. entry.summary: Two men accused of stealing light poles during St. Lucie County flooding emergency    WPEC
entry.article_text: Two South Florida men were arrested Friday after deputies said they stole 34 aluminum light poles from a Fort Pierce property while St. Lucie County was under a state of emergency due to flooding. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies and the South Florida Criminal Apprehension Team investigated suspicious activity Friday night at a property in the 3500 block of Eleven Mile Road. With help from the Fort Pierce Police Department , investigators used a drone to confirm two people were removing property and loading it into a truck, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies tracked the truck as it left the area and stopped it on Okeechobee Road. See also: Woman accused of inventing newborn baby to scam two West Palm Beach adoption agencies The suspects, identified as Pablo Rojas Castro, 33, of Pembroke Pines, and Alberto Guia Hernandez, 35, of Miami, were taken into custody without incident, according to the sheriff’s office. Investigators said about 34 aluminum light poles, valued at $6,800, were stolen. Castro and Hernandez were booked into the St. They face charges of burglary of an unoccupied dwelling during a state of emergency, traveling across county lines to commit burglary, grand theft during a state of emergency and possession of burglary tools. Lucie County remains under a state of emergency following this week’s historic flooding.

For some, Dolphins fandom is a lifelong commitment. For others, its a brand-new experience. Suzanne Hobbs attended her first Dolphins game last year and quickly found herself hooked. Im going to learn everything I can about football. Im so excited, Hobbs said. This year, Hobbs and Ringe became Dolphins season ticket holders, stocked up on new team gear and plan to attend every home game. For them, Dolphins football has become about more than wins and losses. Its about tradition, friendship and being part of a community that keeps showing up.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

entry.title: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall    WPBF
entry.article_text: Five days after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still dealing with several feet of standing water inside their homes, with little indication of when it will recede. The street remains accessible only by boat or kayak, with floodwaters reaching mailboxes and entering most homes along the road. For longtime resident Linda Weisbecker, the flooding has left decades of memories and belongings underwater. “Sixty years of your life is gone. We raised our kids, our grandkids, our great-grandkids. It’s all gone,” Weisbecker said. Weisbecker said her home still has several feet of water inside, preventing her from beginning the cleanup process. “Our main goal is to get this water off so we can get in and start getting things done. If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said. Just down the road, Lisa French is dealing with similar conditions. French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. However, as water continued to accumulate in the neighborhood, it eventually entered her home two days later. Now, she is concerned about mold growth and how much of her home may need to be torn out and replaced. We’re a single-family income. I stay at home with my kids. So it’s, you know, we don’t even know where to start. And we can’t start because the water is still here,” French said. The affected neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. Martin County officials told WPBF 25 News that crews will be working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. entry.title: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage through online survey - WFLX
entry.summary: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage through online survey    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. WATCH REPORT BELOW: County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts. The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems. People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this week County officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. Instead, the information will be used to help officials better understand the scope of the damage. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about impacts to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property. Residents should only report conditions they have already observed. Officials are warning people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment in order to assess damage. Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

entry.title: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue    WPBF
entry.article_text: Floodwaters are receding in Indian River County, but some areas remain affected by standing water as crews and officials work to address the aftermath of this week’s severe downpours. Law enforcement officials said County Roads 510 and 512 were reduced to one lane at one point due to flooding. Crews installed an emergency pipe under the roadway Thursday night to help drain the area. Dave Kubacki, a resident of Sebastian, shared cellphone video of the flooding outside his home. "Holy smoke, I can't believe how much water was out there, and I can't believe how fast it disappeared," Kubacki said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates He said he was surprised by the flooding, noting that the only time it had been this bad was during a hurricane. "The hurricanes were bad, but I've never seen rain come down like this for such a long period of time and so heavy," Kubacki said. Officials shared video of flooded roads taken just after the severe downpours, along with body camera footage showing deputies responding to incidents caused by the high water. Deputies were called to a residential driveway to secure an alligator that had been pushed out of its usual habitat by the flooding. The alligator was safely relocated to another area within the county. County leaders said assessment teams were out Friday surveying the damage, and results are still pending. Schools in Indian River County were closed Friday but are expected to reopen Monday. Kubacki said he shared the news with his granddaughter. "I said, 'Are you mad that schools are closed?' and she said, 'Oh no!' I said, 'What about your friends?' She said, 'That's OK, I'll see them on Monday,'" Kubacki said. Officials are reminding residents to avoid flooded roads as cleanup efforts continue. entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - cw34.com
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.article_text: Two South Florida men were arrested Friday after deputies said they stole 34 aluminum light poles from a Fort Pierce property while St. Lucie County was under a state of emergency due to flooding. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies and the South Florida Criminal Apprehension Team investigated suspicious activity Friday night at a property in the 3500 block of Eleven Mile Road. With help from the Fort Pierce Police Department , investigators used a drone to confirm two people were removing property and loading it into a truck, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies tracked the truck as it left the area and stopped it on Okeechobee Road. See also: Woman accused of inventing newborn baby to scam two West Palm Beach adoption agencies The suspects, identified as Pablo Rojas Castro, 33, of Pembroke Pines, and Alberto Guia Hernandez, 35, of Miami, were taken into custody without incident, according to the sheriff’s office. Investigators said about 34 aluminum light poles, valued at $6,800, were stolen. Castro and Hernandez were booked into the St. They face charges of burglary of an unoccupied dwelling during a state of emergency, traveling across county lines to commit burglary, grand theft during a state of emergency and possession of burglary tools. Lucie County remains under a state of emergency following this week’s historic flooding.

entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - cw34.com
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.title: Okeechobee family forced to rebuild after historic flooding destroys home
entry.summary: A family in Okeechobee is facing a long road to recovery after historic flooding sent more than two feet of water into their home, destroying much of what they spent years building. Jennifer McArthur says her family never expected to experience flooding like this, especially because their home is not in a designated flood zone. Ring camera video captured the frightening moments when the family rushed out of their home with backpacks on their shoulders as floodwaters quickly overtook the property. 'We really didn't have a warning, we knew it was going to rain but that was it. Within an hour everything was under water,' McArthur said. One week later, McArthur took WPTV reporter Brooke Chau inside the home, showing the damage left behind. 'For six years I worked so hard to give my family a beautiful home,' she said. Now, the family is left trying to figure out how to rebuild. 'We never thought we'd have to go through something like this and watch everything that we built and worked for be literally washed away,' McArthur said. The home is currently unlivable, and the family does not know when they will be able to return. McArthur's husband, Richard Maraj, also hopes the flooding will bring attention to drainage concerns in the area. 'This area especially we'd really like to improve the drainage; it's something that as taxpayers we'd really like to see an improvement,' Maraj said. For now, the family is focused on picking up the pieces and rebuilding their lives after losing the home they worked so hard to create. A friend of the family has also set up a GoFundMe to help Jennifer and her family cover home repairs and other essential needs as they navigate the difficult road ahead. Those who wish to help can find the fundraiser here .

entry.title: Cape Coral man arrested for threats against Martin County community - WPBF
entry.summary: Cape Coral man arrested for threats against Martin County community    WPBF
entry.article_text: Video above: News and weather for Sunday, November 8, 2026 A southwest Florida resident is in jail on allegations of making threats. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office announced on Sunday, Nov. 8, that 51-year-old Michael G. Davis, from Cape Coral, was arrested on Saturday night in Cape Coral. According to the Lee County Sheriff’s Office, Davis is facing a charge of resisting officers without violence along with an out-of-county warrant from Martin County. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it was contacted by a concerned citizen on Friday, Nov. 6, about a video that a man, later identified as Davis, posted on the social media platform TikTok threatening the lives of a local student, members of the community and Martin County law enforcement. Investigators reviewed the threats that targeted a school and were able to identify Davis, who posted the video. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said its criminal investigations division and warrants unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Service and the Cape Coral Police Department to arrest Davis. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office added that at first, Davis refused to surrender to law enforcement outside his home but was eventually taken into law enforcement custody. “If you threaten any of our students, our schools, anyone in our community or any of our law enforcement officers, we will use every investigative resource available to identify you, find you and lock you up,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said in a statement on Sunday morning. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office noted it is undetermined why Davis targeted Martin County or the specific people he threatened. The following statement by Felix A. Williams Elementary School Principal Sarah Tuthill was posted to the school’s Facebook page on Sunday morning: FAWE Families, This is Principal Tuthill writing to make you aware of a law enforcement investigation involving threatening statements posted on social media that included a reference to our school. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office has been investigating an individual who made multiple threats on social media, including one that referenced a specific student, as well as vague threats against the school. Law enforcement has confirmed that the individual was arrested last night in Cape Coral and is currently in custody. We understand that information of this nature can be concerning for families, particularly when it involves the safety of our students. We also recognize the importance of providing you with accurate information directly rather than leaving families to rely on social media speculation or secondhand accounts. Here is what we want our families to know: -The threatening statements were brought to the attention of law enforcement, which has been actively investigating the matter. -The individual responsible for the statements has been arrested and is currently in custody. -School and District officials are coordinating with the Martin County Sheriff’s Office and will continue to follow law enforcement’s guidance regarding any necessary safety measures. -To protect the privacy of the student referenced in the statements, we will not be sharing identifying information or discussing the student’s circumstances. We anticipate that the Sheriff’s Office will release additional information about this investigation. Because this remains a law enforcement matter, we encourage families to rely on official communications from MCSO for details rather than information circulating on social media. Please know that we remain committed to maintaining a safe, secure, and supportive learning environment for every child and adult on our campus. We appreciate the work of our law enforcement partners and thank you for your continued trust and support. Williams Elementary is located in Stuart. Davis is being held in the Lee County Jail on $100,000 bail for the Martin County arrest warrant.

entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.article_text: Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. WATCH REPORT BELOW: County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts. The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems. People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this week County officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. Instead, the information will be used to help officials better understand the scope of the damage. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about impacts to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property. Residents should only report conditions they have already observed. Officials are warning people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment in order to assess damage. Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

entry.title: Cape Coral man arrested after threats against Martin County community - WPBF
entry.summary: Cape Coral man arrested after threats against Martin County community    WPBF
entry.article_text: A southwest Florida resident is in jail on allegations of making threats. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office announced on Sunday, Nov. 8, that 51-year-old Michael G. Davis, from Cape Coral, was arrested on Saturday night in Cape Coral. According to the Lee County Sheriff’s Office, Davis is facing a charge of resisting officers without violence along with an out-of-county warrant from Martin County. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it was contacted by a concerned citizen on Friday, Nov. 6, about a video that a man, later identified as Davis, posted on the social media platform TikTok threatening the lives of a local student, members of the community and Martin County law enforcement. Investigators reviewed the threats that targeted a school and were able to identify Davis, who posted the video. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said its criminal investigations division and warrants unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Service and the Cape Coral Police Department to arrest Davis. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office added that at first, Davis refused to surrender to law enforcement outside his home but was eventually taken into law enforcement custody. “If you threaten any of our students, our schools, anyone in our community or any of our law enforcement officers, we will use every investigative resource available to identify you, find you and lock you up,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said in a statement on Sunday morning. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office noted it is undetermined why Davis targeted Martin County or the specific people he threatened. The following statement by Felix A. Williams Elementary School Principal Sarah Tuthill was posted to the school’s Facebook page on Sunday morning: FAWE Families, This is Principal Tuthill writing to make you aware of a law enforcement investigation involving threatening statements posted on social media that included a reference to our school. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office has been investigating an individual who made multiple threats on social media, including one that referenced a specific student, as well as vague threats against the school. Law enforcement has confirmed that the individual was arrested last night in Cape Coral and is currently in custody. We understand that information of this nature can be concerning for families, particularly when it involves the safety of our students. We also recognize the importance of providing you with accurate information directly rather than leaving families to rely on social media speculation or secondhand accounts. Here is what we want our families to know: -The threatening statements were brought to the attention of law enforcement, which has been actively investigating the matter. -The individual responsible for the statements has been arrested and is currently in custody. -School and District officials are coordinating with the Martin County Sheriff’s Office and will continue to follow law enforcement’s guidance regarding any necessary safety measures. -To protect the privacy of the student referenced in the statements, we will not be sharing identifying information or discussing the student’s circumstances. We anticipate that the Sheriff’s Office will release additional information about this investigation. Because this remains a law enforcement matter, we encourage families to rely on official communications from MCSO for details rather than information circulating on social media. Please know that we remain committed to maintaining a safe, secure, and supportive learning environment for every child and adult on our campus. We appreciate the work of our law enforcement partners and thank you for your continued trust and support. Williams Elementary is located in Stuart. Davis is being held in the Lee County Jail on $100,000 bail for the Martin County arrest warrant.

entry.article_text: Two South Florida men were arrested Friday after deputies said they stole 34 aluminum light poles from a Fort Pierce property while St. Lucie County was under a state of emergency due to flooding. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies and the South Florida Criminal Apprehension Team investigated suspicious activity Friday night at a property in the 3500 block of Eleven Mile Road. With help from the Fort Pierce Police Department , investigators used a drone to confirm two people were removing property and loading it into a truck, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies tracked the truck as it left the area and stopped it on Okeechobee Road. See also: Woman accused of inventing newborn baby to scam two West Palm Beach adoption agencies The suspects, identified as Pablo Rojas Castro, 33, of Pembroke Pines, and Alberto Guia Hernandez, 35, of Miami, were taken into custody without incident, according to the sheriff’s office. Investigators said about 34 aluminum light poles, valued at $6,800, were stolen. Castro and Hernandez were booked into the St. They face charges of burglary of an unoccupied dwelling during a state of emergency, traveling across county lines to commit burglary, grand theft during a state of emergency and possession of burglary tools. Lucie County remains under a state of emergency following this week’s historic flooding.
