Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”Supporters of the California tax started running ads recently in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Virginia, states that will vote early in the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, that criticize Newsom for his opposition to the measure.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council approved the site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One , clearing another step for the project planned near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The council held a brief discussion before approving the plan, which calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet on city-owned land. The development would include the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. The stadium is proposed to stand 61 feet tall. Its LED scoreboard could reach 85 feet, while field-light poles could rise to 135 feet. The project is planned in four phases, beginning with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The site-plan approval comes as the city advances related zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. The city’s agenda listed those measures for second reading Monday. Staff recommended approval of the site plan subject to recording a replat; the project also has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. RELATED: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC , a United Soccer League League One team. The club is expected to begin play in 2027, with matches at the new stadium planned to begin in 2028. The venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. The stadium is part of the broader Walton & One redevelopment, envisioned as a mix of residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the district in 2022 and that the stadium is intended to help spur development there. Parking for stadium events would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement. The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site . The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published project terms, the developer could be reimbursed for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners revisit proposed train quiet zones - WFLX
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners revisit proposed train quiet zones    WFLX
entry.article_text: The debate over train horns in Martin County is back before county commissioners Tuesday morning as residents continue pushing for quiet zones along the Florida East Coast Railway. Commissioners are scheduled to hear an update from Public Works staff at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county's evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones along the railroad. Quiet zones would eliminate the requirement for trains to routinely sound their horns at designated crossings, provided those crossings meet federal safety requirements. Train engineers would still be able to sound their horns when necessary for safety. For neighbors living near the tracks, the issue comes down to finding a balance between safety and quality of life. "Safety considerations may not be as important, but they need to have the ability to sound that horn," said Glenn Malone of Hobe Sound, "If they can regulate it down just a bit so the option for safety is still viable." Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor. The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones. "We don’t have a problem with that. We just don’t want the inherent noise all day and night long," said Jeffry Aderman of Hobe Sound, "All these big counties around us have quiet zones and here we are in this beautiful quiet, quaint little area and we’ve got train bars blowing 24/7." At a March 11, 2025, meeting, commissioners decided not to pursue quiet zones after reviewing options presented by county staff. However, following continued concerns from residents, commissioners revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility. Tuesday's presentation will outline the potential risks and benefits of quiet zones, along with the safety requirements and improvements that would be necessary to establish them in Martin County. Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and provide direction to staff on how to move forward. WPTV will continue following the discussion and any decisions made by county leaders.

entry.title: Fort Pierce police union declares impasse, says city cited Amendment 3 in 0% raise offer - cw34.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce police union declares impasse, says city cited Amendment 3 in 0% raise offer    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Fort Pierce Police Officers Association says it declared an impasse in contract negotiations after the city proposed no raises or step increases for officers. In a Facebook post dated Nov. 7, the association said officers and representatives from the Coastal Florida Police Benevolent Association met with the city Nov. 5 for a fourth round of negotiations. The union said the city’s proposal included 0% raises and no step increases. The association said city representatives cited Amendment 3 and an anticipated $6 million budget shortfall. It also said representatives indicated city employees could potentially go without raises for two to three years. The city’s website estimates Amendment 3 could reduce Fort Pierce’s property-tax revenue by about $3.5 million in fiscal year 2028 and an additional $1.5 million in fiscal year 2029, for a combined estimated reduction of about $5 million. The city says it may consider cost reductions and other revenue sources to address the impact. 3 election, Florida law enforcement groups warned that the amendment could reduce money available for public safety and lead to fewer deputies, slower 911 response times and service cuts. The Florida Sheriffs Association ran an ad campaign opposing the measure, while police and fire leaders also raised concerns about the lack of a replacement funding plan. Those were warnings about potential effects, not announcements of specific cuts to Fort Pierce’s police department. Declaring an impasse moves negotiations into a formal process for resolving disagreements. The association said it will continue advocating for what it called fair and competitive wages and keep members and the community updated. The negotiations come as Fort Pierce police have been part of a major multi-agency operation targeting the 23rd Street gang . Officials said the nearly two-year investigation led to nearly 40 arrests, five search warrants and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash. Fort Pierce police said investigators linked people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings over the past decade.

entry.summary: Beds will be rolling down Flagler Avenue in Stuart as Family Promise of Martin County brings its annual Bed Races back to Sailfish Ballpark, turning an unusual competition into a community effort to help families with children facing homelessness. The free event is scheduled for Saturday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Sailfish Ballpark, 600 SE Flagler Ave. Why are people racing beds down a Stuart street? Teams turn beds into racing machines, with runners pushing a rider toward the finish line. But behind the costumes, competition and laughs are a serious mission. Madeleine Bozone Greenwood, executive director of Family Promise of Martin County, said the organization works to prevent and end family homelessness in Martin County. 'We serve parents with children that are here in Martin County,' Greenwood said. 'We provide shelter, transitional housing. A path to return to home ownership or their own rental housing.' Family Promise says its work includes homelessness prevention, shelter and services designed to help families find stable housing while keeping parents and children together. entry.title: Palm Beach County shelter dog with endless energy lands new career in police K-9 work
entry.summary: A dog that arrived at Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control spinning in circles in his kennel is now headed toward a future in police work. The dog, named Bayblade, caught attention for the very energy that made him stand out at the shelter. 'He had a tendency to spin, which is typically something that dogs will do when they are really backed up with energy and they need something to do,' Arielle Weinberger, a public releations specialist with Palm Beach County Animal Care Control, said. That energy caught the attention of animal rescue advocate Jim Bradley. 'I work with all sorts of rescues. Malinois, Dutch Shepherd Rescue, so a lot of local rescues. Oftentimes they might have a more challenging dog,' Bradley said. He put Bayblade to the test, looking at his energy, focus and drive to work. 'A working dog they are genetically just a complete different dog. Their energy, their drive, their tenacity, their desire to bite and grip into whole things,' Bradley said. He recognized those traits could make Bayblade ideal for police work. So Bradley contacted a canine organization in Ohio, and Bayblade was accepted. 'They'll be doing some bite work because he'll be a dual-purpose canine that can do apprehensions and also find drugs or weapons,' Bradley said. Now, Bayblade is getting a chance to put all that energy to work. 'That cute little puppy with the pointy ears that in 6 months you've got a working dog who needs to work, who needs to move, who needs to do his what he was bred to do. And so I'm happy that Bayblade is going to get that chance,' Bradley said. From providing video of the dog in the kennel to the flight to Ohio, several people were instrumental in getting Bayblade who is now called Blade to his destination. Those involved included Fabienne with the Canine Enrichment Team, Alpha Pack K9 training, plane owners Harrison Gevirtz and Adam Young, and Wendy Cristantiello.

entry.title: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding - WPTV
entry.summary: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding    WPTV
entry.article_text: Residents and farmers in western St. Lucie County are seeking answers and long-term drainage solutions after historic flooding left homes, farms and roads underwater last week.The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear concerns from people in the area, including farmers, residents and representatives from Save the Chimps. District members said the drainage system can handle only so much water during an extreme rainfall event and discussed engineering as part of a possible long-term plan.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Some of the hardest-hit areas are now seeing significant improvement, including Save the Chimps in western St. But residents and farmers say they want to know what can be done to reduce the risk of similar flooding during the next extreme rainfall event.For one resident, the flooding has already changed how they view their future in the area."I will be selling my house cause I am not going to risk my investment," the resident said during Monday's meeting.Water control district hears concerns from western St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear from people affected by the flooding.Farmers, residents and representatives of Save the Chimps attended as district members discussed the drainage system and the scale of last week's flooding.President Steve Cassens said there are limits to what the existing system can handle when extraordinary amounts of rain fall in a short period."If we have a rainfall event like that, my personal feeling is you can have gates open, shut, it doesn't matter," said Cassens. "We can manage water maybe 3, 4, 5, 6 inches. We can't manage water in the quantities that we got."District officials also discussed maintaining waterways and ditches, including concerns about a creek in Western Fort Pierce that serves as a primary drainage route. The district said it systematically cleans ditches within its boundaries.The district said it could examine engineering as part of developing a long-range plan.Conditions improve at Save the ChimpsSave the Chimps, a sanctuary in western St. Lucie County, was among the places hit hard by the flooding.WPTV previously reported that staff members had to use drones to deliver food to chimpanzees because several roads through the sanctuary were underwater.When WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache returned days later, staff said conditions had significantly improved."A short 40 hours after that, we're almost completely dry on our roads," said Mark Yohannan.The improvement came after days of challenges caused by standing water at the sanctuary.West Fort Pierce farmer raises concernsThe concerns extended beyond residential neighborhoods.Justin Akerley, who helps operate Saint Lucie Farm Preserve in west Fort Pierce, spoke later Monday at a Port St. Lucie City Council meeting after attending the water control district meeting.Akerley told council members he believes continued development is adding pressure to the area's drainage infrastructure."I just spent my morning in a meeting with the North St. Lucie River Water Control District trying to figure out what we can do to alleviate the water issues, and there's really no right answer except for stop building," Akerley said.Akerley shared a video with WPTV showing flooding at Saint Lucie Farm Preserve, a working agritourism farm operated by Akerley and Michael Hale. The farm produces hay, cut flowers, beef and assorted vegetables and hosts community agricultural events.Akerley told council members the consequences extend to other farms and families."I've got friends that have calves dying that are flooded; they can't get out," he said. "It's a terrible, terrible situation for everybody. There's people that have lost their homes."He urged city leaders to reconsider the effect future development could have on flooding and drainage."Just please reconsider because it's not a good situation for everybody, and it's only gonna get worse," Akerley said.Officials consider what comes nextDuring Monday's Port St. Lucie City Council meeting, Councilman David Pickett also called for greater scrutiny of flooding and the city's stormwater infrastructure.Pickett said he sent two memos to the city manager earlier in the week addressing floodwaters and wants the city to expedite a planned stormwater study rather than wait until 2029.He also raised concerns about flooding in Tradition and called for the city to examine stormwater systems before distributing certain stormwater fees to community development districts.Meanwhile, the North St. Lucie River Water Control District has said engineering options can be assessed as officials consider a long-term plan.For residents and farmers still recovering from last week's flooding, those discussions are now turning toward a larger question: what can be done before the next extreme rainfall event?This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Fire heavily damages India Grill and Bar in Royal Palm Beach
entry.summary: A fire heavily damaged India Grill and Bar in Royal Palm Beach, but firefighters prevented the flames from spreading to neighboring businesses, according to Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. Crews responded to reports of a commercial fire on Royal Palm Beach Boulevard, just north of Southern Boulevard. Watch video of the fire: Fire heavily damages India Grill and Bar in Royal Palm Beach When firefighters arrived, they found the restaurant heavily involved in flames. PBCFR said a large fire was visible from the front of the building, while thick, dark smoke billowed from the rear. Firefighters prevent flames from spreading It took firefighters about 30 minutes to bring the fire under control. An aggressive attack prevented the fire from going to neighboring businesses or running along the overhead space, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue said in a statement. Adjacent businesses experienced some smoke intrusion, according to PBCFR, but no injuries were reported. India Grill and Bar sustained considerable fire damage. Cause remains under investigation PBCFR fire investigators remained at the scene throughout the night as they worked to determine where and how the fire started. The fire remains under investigation, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue said.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council approved the site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One , clearing another step for the project planned near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The council held a brief discussion before approving the plan, which calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet on city-owned land. The development would include the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. The stadium is proposed to stand 61 feet tall. Its LED scoreboard could reach 85 feet, while field-light poles could rise to 135 feet. The project is planned in four phases, beginning with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The site-plan approval comes as the city advances related zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. The city’s agenda listed those measures for second reading Monday. Staff recommended approval of the site plan subject to recording a replat; the project also has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. RELATED: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC , a United Soccer League League One team. The club is expected to begin play in 2027, with matches at the new stadium planned to begin in 2028. The venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. The stadium is part of the broader Walton & One redevelopment, envisioned as a mix of residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the district in 2022 and that the stadium is intended to help spur development there. Parking for stadium events would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement. The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site . The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published project terms, the developer could be reimbursed for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million.

entry.title: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary recovers after historic flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary recovers after historic flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: Save the Chimps, a 150-acre chimpanzee sanctuary in Fort Pierce, is recovering after 19 inches of rain caused historic flooding, disrupting operations and making it difficult for staff to care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. Mark Yohannan, facilities director at Save the Chimps, said water levels have dropped significantly, allowing staff to regain access to most of the sanctuary’s roads. "We've probably lost at least 7 or 8 inches of water. Now we have 1.2 miles of road here on property, 90% of that we can actually see and drive on. We expect the last little bit to dry up overnight," Yohannan said. Before the water began receding, staff faced challenges, including delivering food to a chimpanzee via drone. The sanctuary has 12 islands that house 11-21 chimpanzees in a family group. In total, there are 211 chimpanzees on the property. "We saw that we had a situation. Caleb was the one that stayed out; he loves his island as many others do," said Ana Paula Tavares, CEO of Save the Chimps. "He decided he was going to stay out until he realized that he was not going to be able to go indoors anymore because of the land bridge that connects the island to his indoor house got flooded as well. Not on all the islands, but on that island. That's when we had to get creative and think, how can we drop fluid and food?" The sanctuary’s chimps live on islands with care houses situated on higher ground, but staff struggled to navigate the flooded property. "We have a lot of golf carts that care staff use to move themselves, staff, 3,000 pounds of food a day, and so, those were rendered inoperable because you couldn't see the road; they're battery carts... Not to mention some were damaged," Yohannan said. Employees have been relying on tractors, trailers, and large off-road vehicles to access the sanctuary. An overflowing header canal has slowed the water’s recession. On Monday, Yohannan met with the St. Lucie Water River District to discuss the flooding. "We left with the understanding that everyone already knows. This rain event was a 200-year event, and I think that the county's working as hard as they can to get stuff moving," Yohannan said. Despite the historic flood, rescue leaders felt they were mostly prepared but acknowledged areas for improvement. "The one thing that came to mind is we have insurance...very good insurance but not flood insurance because we didn't have floods in Florida. So now we do, or now we will look into that...that was one lesson learned," Tavares said. Yohannan added, "We would have needed some very large pumps, watched the forecast a little better maybe...but other than that I think we're in the same boat as all the other neighbors. It's the first thing that's rained this hard in 200 years; I don't know what we could've done to be more prepared." entry.title: NTSB recovers cockpit voice recorder from Learjet that crashed near Greenacres
entry.summary: Federal investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres earlier this month. The National Transportation Safety Board said in a Monday evening post on X that investigators found the cockpit voice recorder, commonly known as a CVR, at the site of the plane's initial impact. WATCH REPORT BELOW: NTSB recovers cockpit voice recorder from Learjet crash The recorder has been sent to the NTSB's Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C., where it is being evaluated. Cockpit voice recorders can provide investigators with information about sounds and conversations inside an aircrafts cockpit leading up to a crash. The NTSB also announced that excavation work at the initial impact site has been completed. PREVIOUS COVERAGE: NTSB completes most on-scene work related to crash NTSB completes most on-scene work in Learjet crash The Learjet 60 crashed near Greenacres on Nov. 1. The NTSB did not provide additional details about what may have been captured on the recorder or when information from its examination could become available. The agency said Sunday that it had completed most of its on-scene investigative work. The investigation into the crash remains ongoing.

First time I've seen something like this," Pahzoor said.To find answers, I got on the phone, connecting with officials at Palm Beach County, the City of West Palm Beach, Hamilton Bay's property management company, and the Hamal Community Development District — which includes several flooded neighborhoods off of Okeechobee Boulevard.Dwayne Barrett, Hamal's operations manager, told me the district has been working with the county and the city, and is currently pumping water into a canal that the county allowed them to use."This is at least 16 inches (deep) right here," Pahzoor said as he drove his SUV around his neighborhood.West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James sent the following statement Monday afternoon:“I understand the frustration and hardship that residents of Briar Bay, The Cove at Briar Bay, and Hamilton Bay continue to experience following last week's historic rainfall. With significant standing water remaining in these communities, the City is focused on residents’ safety and is continuing to coordinate with the agencies responsible for drainage while providing direct assistance where possible.The Hamal Community Development District (CDD) is responsible for maintaining the community’s surface water management system. Its existing system has two pumps that currently cannot operate simultaneously. The Northern Palm Beach County Improvement District (NPBCID) has provided two additional pumps, and Hamal CDD informed the City this morning that an electrician is being brought in to enable its two pumps to operate concurrently.Since the beginning of this event, the City has maintained ongoing communication with the NPBCID and has also made direct outreach to Hamal CDD, offering personnel, equipment, and technical assistance. Both districts have informed us that there is nothing further the City can do at this time to assist with drainage operations. The City is not withholding permits, delaying improvements on the current pumping and drainage efforts. We will continue monitoring conditions, coordinating with the responsible agencies and offering assistance as needs change.While the drainage system is outside our jurisdiction, our commitment to these residents is not. The City partially activated its Emergency Operations Center on November 2. Since then, City crews have been working around the clock to respond to flooding throughout West Palm Beach, while continuing to provide direct assistance to residents in these communities. This includes offering transportation to shelters for residents unable to leave their neighborhoods and helping hospice nurses reach patients when they were flooded in. The City will continue coordinating with the responsible agencies, monitoring conditions, and providing assistance wherever possible. Our priority remains the safety and well-being of every resident.” For questions regarding drainage operations and floodwater removal, residents should contact the Hamal Community Development District:District Manager: Jamie OteroPhone: (561) 571-0010Email: info@hamalcdd.comWebsite: https://hamalcdd.com/contactResidents experiencing a medical emergency should call 911. entry.article_text: Florida Highway Patrol is investigating a fatal crash that occurred in Indian River County Monday afternoon. FHP says that at around 3:43 p.m. on Monday, a 2018 Toyota Rav 4 SUV and a 2017 Harley Davidson Electra Guide Motorcycle collided near 1850 37th Street within unincorporated Indian River County. According to FHP , the driver of the Rav 4 SUV an 82-year-old female was traveling east on 37th Street before coming to a stop in the roadway and waiting to turn left into Indian River MRI. At the same time, the driver of the Harley Davidson a 58-year-old male was traveling west before colliding with the SUV, who turned into the path of the motorcycle as it approached. See also: Vero Beach family citrus grove reels after historic South Florida flooding damages crops The 82-year-old woman came away with minor injuries, while the 58-year-old male on the motorcycle was pronounced dead after being transported HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. As a result, Westbound 37th Street between U.S. Highway 1 and 17th Avenue is currently closed. This remains an active investigation.

entry.summary: Vero Beach family citrus grove reels after historic South Florida flooding damages crops    WPEC
entry.article_text: Many businesses are reeling in the effects of last week’s historic flooding event across South Florida, including a local Vero Beach citrus grove farm. CBS12 News Photojournalist Chris Pollock visited Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach, a family-owned farm business that spans multiple generations. The farm has been amongst the hardest hit from the historic flooding. Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and were anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. That amount of rain over all of this land, it’s crazy, Greene said.

entry.title: WPTV finds $15.5 million in political contributions tied to fight over Florida's 'free kill' law
entry.summary: Florida lawmakers overwhelmingly voted to repeal one of the state's most controversial medical malpractice provisions earlier this year. But despite bipartisan support, the legislation never became law. Now, a WPTV investigation is following the money behind the political fight over what critics call Florida's 'free kill' law uncovering more than $15.5 million in campaign contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying groups to political committees tied to lawmakers who opposed the repeal and to Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ultimately vetoed it. A mother's fight for answers In a previous investigation , WPTV introduced viewers to Beth Miller, whose only daughter, Dawn, died just hours after being discharged from the hospital following gallbladder surgery. 'It's on your mind, 24/7,' Miller said. 'We were very close, to say the least. She was my only child, my only living relative.' A medical expert who reviewed Dawn's records told WPTV she should not have been discharged from the hospital. Miller said her request for an autopsy was denied, leaving her with unanswered questions about her daughter's death. 'I don't have an answer to this day,' she said. No court has determined whether medical negligence contributed to Dawn's death. But when Miller explored her legal options, she encountered another obstacle. Because Dawn was older than 25, unmarried and had no children, Florida law prevents Miller from recovering certain wrongful-death damages in a medical malpractice lawsuit. The restriction is part of Florida's Wrongful Death Act. Critics argue it creates a disparity in accountability by limiting the damages available to certain surviving family members based on the deceased person's age and family circumstances. 'It's completely arbitrary,' said Jordan Dulcie, a trial attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart Shipley. Dulce, who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is now among the attorneys advocating for repeal. 'Trying to value life from the Legislature's standpoint, I think, is always improper,' he said. Lawmakers voted to repeal it. The governor said no. State Rep. Dana Trabulsy, a R-Fort Pierce, sponsored House Bill 6017 , legislation aimed at removing the controversial restriction from Florida's Wrongful Death Act. The proposal passed both chambers of the Florida Legislature with overwhelming support, but in May, DeSantis vetoed the bill. Critics argue it creates a disparity in accountability by limiting the damages available to certain surviving family members based on the deceased person's age and family circumstances."It's completely arbitrary," said Jordan Dulcie, a trial attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart & Shipley.Dulce, who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is now among the attorneys advocating for repeal."Trying to value life from the Legislature's standpoint, I think, is always improper," he said.State Rep. Dana Trabulsy, a R-Fort Pierce, sponsored House Bill 6017, legislation aimed at removing the controversial restriction from Florida's Wrongful Death Act.The proposal passed both chambers of the Florida Legislature with overwhelming support, but in May, DeSantis vetoed the bill.The governor argued that expanding the damages families could recover without additional safeguards, including caps on damages and attorney fees, could increase costs for Floridians."That imposes costs, as those costs are put through the system that helps drive the price that people pay for normal products and premiums they pay," DeSantis said.Critics of the law argue Florida remains the only state with this particular restriction on medical malpractice wrongful-death claims.Dulcie believes politics, rather than fairness, is standing in the way of reform."It's politics. That's all it is, is politics," he said. "When you look at the end of the day, no one thinks this law is fair."So WPTV examined the campaign contributions flowing to the political figures who opposed the repeal.WPTV reviewed hundreds of campaign finance records, tracking contributions made between 2017 and 2026 to political committees tied to the 10 lawmakers who voted against HB 6017 — four senators and six representatives — and DeSantis, who vetoed it.The investigation identified more than $15.5 million in contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying organizations with a stake in the debate.Of that total:More than $12 million came from hospitals, healthcare networks, physician groups, insurance companies, nursing homes and other health care interestsMore than $3 million came from lobbying organizations that opposed HB 6017 and efforts to repeal the provisionAmong the lawmakers who opposed the bill, WPTV identified several who received substantial contributions from the groups examined.Sen. Gayle Harrell, a Republican representing part of the Treasure Coast, received more than $700,000 from the tracked groups since 2017, including $28,000 in the weeks leading up to the vote.Sen. Tom Leek, a Republican from northeast Florida, received more than $400,000 since 2024, including $15,000 in the weeks before the vote.Rep. James Buchanan, a Republican from Sarasota County, received more than $300,000 since 2018, including $46,000 in the month before the vote.But the vast majority of the contributions WPTV tracked went to political committees tied to DeSantis.Those committees, primarily his Political Action Committee Florida Freedom Fund, received approximately $12.7 million since 2017, including $170,000 in the weeks and months preceding his veto.The contributions were made over multiple election cycles and were not necessarily connected to HB 6017. Campaign finance records do not establish that the money influenced any lawmaker's vote or the governor's veto.Still, Dulcie argues the financial resources available to groups opposing changes to the law create an imbalance in Tallahassee."Unfortunately, the victims of medical negligence don't have hundreds of lobbyists that they can pay millions of dollars to go to Tallahassee year after year to campaign to change this law," he said.WPTV contacted all 10 lawmakers who voted against the bill, as well as DeSantis, requesting interviews and asking about the contributions and their positions on the legislation.Despite multiple calls and emails, none responded to WPTV's requests.Dr. Aubrey Jewett, a political science professor at the University of Central Florida, said campaign contributions are an essential part of modern politics."There's an old saying that money is the mother's milk of politics," Jewett said, describing the importance of fundraising to political campaigns.He said businesses and lobbying organizations frequently contribute to politicians they believe will support their interests."I mean, it is 100% crystal clear. Most people that give are trying to get access and influence," Jewett said.But he emphasized an important distinction: political contributions alone are not evidence that a politician changed a vote or policy decision in exchange for money.Donors may support a politician because that politician already shares their views."The candidates will say, 'Well, you know, they're not like buying my vote. Instead, they support the position that I hold,'" Jewett explained.And while DeSantis vetoed HB 6017, Jewett pointed out that the governor did not rule out supporting a different version of the legislation."Gov. DeSantis did say that he would sign off on a similar bill as long as it had some caps," Jewett said.That leaves open the possibility of another attempt at repeal.With DeSantis leaving office, WPTV took the question directly to Gov.-elect Byron Donalds while he was on the campaign trail.Would he support repealing Florida's so-called "free kill" law?Donalds stopped short of committing to a position."I'm aware of Gov. DeSantis's veto on this measure. Also aware of how many members of the Legislature supported it," Donalds said. "We're just going to sit down, take a look at the issue, and render a decision. I've not made one at this time, but we're going to do what's in the best interest of the people of Florida."For families like Beth Miller's, the future of the law could determine whether others facing similar circumstances have an opportunity to seek accountability through the courts.And the debate is far from over.Since WPTV's first investigation aired, numerous viewers have reached out to share their own experiences involving alleged medical negligence and the legal barriers they encountered afterward.WPTV is continuing to investigate those cases, examine the law's impact on Florida families and seek answers from the elected

entry.title: Delray Beach cancels 2027 St. Patrick's Day Parade, Pride event under new Florida law
entry.summary: The City of Delray Beach announced Tuesday it will not host its annual St. Patrick's Day Parade or Pride event in 2027, citing a new Florida law restricting local governments from funding or promoting certain diversity, equity and inclusion activities. The city said it made the decision following a review of Senate Bill 1134 , which takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. The law prohibits municipalities from funding or promoting, directly or indirectly, or taking official action related to activities that fall under its definition of diversity, equity and inclusion. Under the law, DEI includes certain programming or activities designed or implemented with reference to race, color, sex, ethnicity, gender identity or sexual orientation. Delray Beach officials said they determined that the restrictions legally prohibit the city from organizing, funding or promoting these events in 2027. 'The City recognizes that these annual events have provided opportunities for members of the community to gather, celebrate, and connect,' the city said in a Facebook post. 'We appreciate the residents, participants, volunteers, and community partners who have contributed to these events over the years.' The legislation also prohibits municipalities from spending money to support DEI offices or officers and bars them from authorizing municipal funds to be used by employees, contractors, volunteers, vendors or agents to promote DEI initiatives. A resident may bring an action in circuit court against a municipality accused of violating the law. However, the law includes several exceptions. Municipalities may still recognize or promote certain federal and state holidays and observances. The law also specifically allows cities to issue event permits in a content-neutral manner and provide public safety services. That provision means the law does not categorically prohibit privately organized events that obtain permits from a municipality. Delray Beach's announcement specifically addresses events organized, funded or promoted by the city. 'We remain committed to serving all residents and providing opportunities for community engagement consistent with applicable state and federal laws,' the city said. The new law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

entry.title: Stuart bed races put fun on wheels to help Martin County families facing homelessness - WFLX
entry.summary: Stuart bed races put fun on wheels to help Martin County families facing homelessness    WFLX
entry.article_text: Beds will be rolling down Flagler Avenue in Stuart as Family Promise of Martin County brings its annual Bed Races back to Sailfish Ballpark, turning an unusual competition into a community effort to help families with children facing homelessness. The free event is scheduled for Saturday from 10 a.m. at Sailfish Ballpark, 600 SE Flagler Ave. Teams turn beds into racing machines, with runners pushing a rider toward the finish line. But behind the costumes, competition and laughs are a serious mission. Madeleine Bozone Greenwood, executive director of Family Promise of Martin County, said the organization works to prevent and end family homelessness in Martin County. "We serve parents with children that are here in Martin County," Greenwood said. "We provide shelter, transitional housing. A path to return to home ownership or their own rental housing." Pastor Chad Fair, board chair of Family Promise of Martin County, said homelessness does not always look the way people might expect. "We kind of think that it hits just those people we see on the street corner, but it's families, it's nurses, it's school teachers, it's people that are integral in our community and do the work with our kids, with our families, and they're experiencing homelessness," Fair said. Family Promise says its work includes homelessness prevention, shelter and services designed to help families find stable housing while keeping parents and children together. That work gives the bed races a literal connection to the organization's mission: The race may be entertaining, but the bed represents something every family needs at the end of the day, a safe place to sleep. Paige Cortes, director of operations for Family Promise of Martin County, said spectators can attend Saturday's event for free . "This Saturday, bed races 10 to 1 at the Sailfish Ballpark," Cortes said. "So we are ready for fun too, and you can join us in the race to end childhood homelessness." The event combines the spectacle of beds on wheels with the broader goal of connecting Martin County residents with an issue that can sometimes remain largely invisible. For working families facing a housing crisis, Fair said homelessness can affect people who are already contributing to the community every day. That gives Saturday's race a purpose beyond deciding which team can push its bed across the finish line fastest. It gives residents an opportunity to learn about family homelessness in Martin County and the organizations working to help families regain stable housing. entry.title: Deputies fatally shoot man found stabbing woman inside Jupiter-area home, PBSO says
entry.summary: The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office (PBSO) responded to a domestic disturbance near Jupiter early Tuesday morning that ended in a deputy-involved shooting. WATCH: PBSO Chief Deputy Bobby Allen gives update on deputy-involved shooting PBSO gives update on knife-wielding man killed in deputy-involved shooting According to PBSO, deputies responded around 1:39 a.m. to the 6500 block of Jupiter Gardens Boulevard, where they found the man attacking a woman with a knife. A deputy then shot the knife-wielding suspect. The victim was taken to a local hospital for treatment of her injuries. The man was pronounced dead at the scene. Chief Deputy Bobby Allen laid out a detailed timeline of the events during a news conference on Tuesday. He said said the incident began with a series of 911 calls, hours before deputies made entry into the home. 'At 12:14 this morning, we had a 911 hang-up call, which isn't that unusual. At 12:19 a.m., deputies get another 911 call, and they hear a male talking in the background, and they hang up,' Allen said. 'At 12:21 a.m., they called the number back to see if there was a problem there. A male answered the phone, and he said the calls were accidental, which is not that uncommon.' Allen said deputies first arrived at the residence to check on the occupants but found nothing unsual. 'At 1:07 a.m., they receive another call, and they can hear someone crying in the background. So at 1:27 a.m., our deputies arrive at the residence to check, make sure everybody's okay, and it's all quiet,' he said. 'Nothing is heard from inside. The deputies knock and knock, walk around. They can't hear or see nothing out of the ordinary.' Deputies said the situation quickly escalated when a later call revealed the victim was in danger. 'At 1:39 a.m., we receive another call for service, and they can hear the victim is whispering that her boyfriend was holding her at knife point. While they're talking to the victim, at 1:40 a.m., the victim stated she had been sexually battered by her boyfriend earlier that evening. At 1:41 a.m., the victim tells our operator that she is hiding in the bathroom, and the suspect was in the bedroom,' Allen said. Allen said deputies were dispatched with additional resources as the victim remained on the line with a communications officer, where the officer asks the victim if she is able to safely exit the apartment. Minutes later, the victim tells the communication officer that the suspect is trying to enter the bathroo
entry.article_text: Minutes later, the victim tells the communication officer that the suspect is trying to enter the bathroom.That is when deputies arrived and forced their way inside, after hearing screaming and found the suspect attacking the woman."They find the suspect on top of the victim with a knife, trying and attempting to stab her. The deputies attempt to physically intervene and stop the male from stabbing the victim. They were eventually forced to discharge her firearms, killing suspect at the scene," Allen said.The woman was taken to a hospital with with "stab wounds and some other lacerations, a possible severe concussion," Allen said.The suspect's identity has not been confirmed yet, the chief deputy said. Meanwhile, the two deputies who fired their weapons have been placed on administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation.Detectives with PBSO's Violent Crimes Division and Crime Scene Investigators are investigating alongside the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the State Attorney's Office.

entry.title: Palm Beach County shelter dog with endless energy lands new career in police K-9 work
entry.summary: A dog that arrived at Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control spinning in circles in his kennel is now headed toward a future in police work. WATCH BELOW: From shelter spins to police K-9 meet Blade! Shelter dog's endless energy earns him a police K-9 future in Ohio The dog, named Bayblade, caught attention for the very energy that made him stand out at the shelter. 'He had a tendency to spin, which is typically something that dogs will do when they are really backed up with energy and they need something to do,' Arielle Weinberger, a public releations specialist with Palm Beach County Animal Care Control, said. That energy caught the attention of animal rescue advocate Jim Bradley. 'I work with all sorts of rescues. Malinois, Dutch Shepherd Rescue, so a lot of local rescues. Oftentimes they might have a more challenging dog,' Bradley said. He put Bayblade to the test, looking at his energy, focus and drive to work. 'A working dog they are genetically just a complete different dog. Their energy, their drive, their tenacity, their desire to bite and grip into whole things,' Bradley said. He recognized those traits could make Bayblade ideal for police work. So Bradley contacted a canine organization in Ohio, and Bayblade was accepted. 'They'll be doing some bite work because he'll be a dual-purpose canine that can do apprehensions and also find drugs or weapons,' Bradley said. Now, Bayblade is getting a chance to put all that energy to work. 'That cute little puppy with the pointy ears that in 6 months you've got a working dog who needs to work, who needs to move, who needs to do his what he was bred to do. And so I'm happy that Bayblade is going to get that chance,' Bradley said. From providing video of the dog in the kennel to the flight to Ohio, several people were instrumental in getting Bayblade who is now called Blade to his destination. Those involved included Fabienne with the Canine Enrichment Team, Alpha Pack K9 training, plane owners Harrison Gevirtz and Adam Young, and Wendy Cristantiello.

entry.title: Fort Pierce police union declares impasse, says city cited Amendment 3 in 0% raise offer - cw34.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce police union declares impasse, says city cited Amendment 3 in 0% raise offer    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Fort Pierce Police Officers Association says it declared an impasse in contract negotiations after the city proposed no raises or step increases for officers. In a Facebook post dated Nov. 7, the association said officers and representatives from the Coastal Florida Police Benevolent Association met with the city Nov. 5 for a fourth round of negotiations. The union said the city’s proposal included 0% raises and no step increases. The association said city representatives cited Amendment 3 and an anticipated $6 million budget shortfall. It also said representatives indicated city employees could potentially go without raises for two to three years. The city’s website estimates Amendment 3 could reduce Fort Pierce’s property-tax revenue by about $3.5 million in fiscal year 2028 and an additional $1.5 million in fiscal year 2029, for a combined estimated reduction of about $5 million. The city says it may consider cost reductions and other revenue sources to address the impact. 3 election, Florida law enforcement groups warned that the amendment could reduce money available for public safety and lead to fewer deputies, slower 911 response times and service cuts. The Florida Sheriffs Association ran an ad campaign opposing the measure, while police and fire leaders also raised concerns about the lack of a replacement funding plan. Those were warnings about potential effects, not announcements of specific cuts to Fort Pierce’s police department. Declaring an impasse moves negotiations into a formal process for resolving disagreements. The association said it will continue advocating for what it called fair and competitive wages and keep members and the community updated. The negotiations come as Fort Pierce police have been part of a major multi-agency operation targeting the 23rd Street gang . Officials said the nearly two-year investigation led to nearly 40 arrests, five search warrants and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash. Fort Pierce police said investigators linked people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings over the past decade.

entry.title: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding
entry.summary: Residents and farmers in western St. Lucie County are seeking answers and long-term drainage solutions after historic flooding left homes, farms and roads underwater last week. The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear concerns from people in the area, including farmers, residents and representatives from Save the Chimps. District members said the drainage system can handle only so much water during an extreme rainfall event and discussed engineering as part of a possible long-term plan. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County residents seek answers after widespread flooding Some of the hardest-hit areas are now seeing significant improvement, including Save the Chimps in western St. Lucie County. But residents and farmers say they want to know what can be done to reduce the risk of similar flooding during the next extreme rainfall event. For one resident, the flooding has already changed how they view their future in the area. 'I will be selling my house cause I am not going to risk my investment,' the resident said during Monday's meeting. entry.title: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council approved the site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One , clearing another step for the project planned near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The council held a brief discussion before approving the plan, which calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet on city-owned land. The development would include the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. The stadium is proposed to stand 61 feet tall. Its LED scoreboard could reach 85 feet, while field-light poles could rise to 135 feet. The project is planned in four phases, beginning with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The site-plan approval comes as the city advances related zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. The city’s agenda listed those measures for second reading Monday. Staff recommended approval of the site plan subject to recording a replat; the project also has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. RELATED: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC , a United Soccer League League One team. The club is expected to begin play in 2027, with matches at the new stadium planned to begin in 2028. The venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. The stadium is part of the broader Walton & One redevelopment, envisioned as a mix of residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the district in 2022 and that the stadium is intended to help spur development there. Parking for stadium events would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement. The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site . The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published project terms, the developer could be reimbursed for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million.

entry.title: Palm Beach County school district employee accused of soliciting person he believed was 14-year-old boy
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County School District employee was arrested after police said he had sexually explicit conversations with an undercover detective posing as a 14-year-old boy. Boynton Beach police said Donald Rush, 65, of Lake Worth was arrested following an investigation by the department's Human Exploitation Task Force. According to police, detectives posed as a 14-year-old boy advertising lawn mowing services on Craigslist's Community messaging board. Investigators said they were contacted by someone using the screen name 'Palm Guy,' who was later identified by police as Rush. Police said Rush asked the person his age, whether adult men had approached him about sexual activity and whether he had told his parents about those interactions. The conversation later moved to text messages, according to police. Detectives said they again made clear that the person Rush was communicating with was supposedly 14 years old. Despite the stated age, police allege Rush continued the conversation, asking sexually explicit questions and making statements about his own sexual activity. With assistance from the Palm Beach County School Board Police Department, detectives located and interviewed Rush. Boynton Beach police said Rush admitted his involvement during that interview. Police said Rush also claimed during the investigation that he was a youth pastor. The department did not identify a church or organization with which he was allegedly affiliated. Rush faces charges of solicitation of a minor to engage in sexual conduct and unlawful use of a two-way communications device, according to police. He was being held at the Palm Beach County Jail. Police identified Rush as an employee of the Palm Beach County School District. Sean Cooley, the school district's chief of communications, said in a statement Tuesday that Rush is an electrician. Cooley also said the district immediately revoked Rush's access to all school facilities after learning of his arrest. Investigators said they believe there could be additional victims. entry.title: Dolphins lose veteran defensive tackle Zach Sieler for rest of season to ruptured biceps, AP source says
entry.summary: Miami Dolphins veteran defensive lineman Zach Sieler ruptured his biceps in the team's 19-9 loss to the Detroit Lions last weekend and will undergo season-ending surgery, a person familiar with the injury told The Associated Press on Tuesday. The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because neither the team nor Sieler announced the injury. ESPN first reported the injury, saying that it happened on the first play of the game on Sunday. The expected recovery timeline for the injury is five to six months, meaning Sieler will miss the rest of the Dolphins' season. He played the entire game on Sunday, recording one quarterback hurry and a tackle while aiding a Dolphins front that successfully pressured Jared Goff for much of the game. Sieler has 24 tackles, seven tackles for loss and two sacks this season, which is his eighth in Miami. He is the only player older than 30 on Miami's roster, which is the youngest in the NFL, and first-year coach Jeff Hafley has praised his leadership throughout the season. 'It's valuable to me. It's valuable to our young players,' Hafley said in October. 'To have a guy like that around the youth of this team and having a guy that I can lean on, because not only does he do all that, but hes one of the best people ever. Theres not a much better person out there than Zach Sieler.'

entry.title: Tequesta Chili Cook-Off moves to Carlin Park in Jupiter for 15th year
entry.summary: The Tequesta Chili Cook-Off returns Saturday, Nov. 14, with thousands of people expected to gather for chili, live music, and a celebration of veterans, but organizers say one of the event's biggest changes this year is its move to the Seabreeze Amphitheater at Carlin Park in Jupiter. The 15th annual event runs from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. and brings together more than 30 teams of firefighters, public safety personnel and community sponsors for an afternoon organizers describe as a combination of chili competition, entertainment and patriotism. Tequesta Chili Cook-Off moves to Carlin Park After 14 years, the cook-off is moving to a larger location at Carlin Park. Captain David McGovern of Tequesta Fire Rescue told WPTV the venue gives the growing event more room while offering easier parking and a different atmosphere near the ocean. Bigger, beautiful location, easier to park, and just that lovely little sea breeze coming in as well, McGovern said. The Seabreeze Amphitheater also offers paved walkways, permanent restrooms, a permanent stage and additional space for the chili teams, entertainment and guests, according to event organizers. Chili competition comes with a patriotic purpose While chili may bring people through the gates, McGovern said honoring veterans remains at the heart of the event. We'll have (around) 4,000 people show up on Saturday to honor our veterans, give medals to our veterans, McGovern said. So we say thank you for all their sacrifices and everything else. The event includes a Veterans Award Ceremony recognizing veterans and Gold Star families, along with military flyovers and performances by pipes and drums. Organizers say 100% of the event's proceeds benefit organizations serving veterans and first responders, including Wounded Veterans Relief Fund, Operation 300, Southeast Florida Honor Flight, Warriors Renewal Coalition, and Tequesta Friends of Public Safety Inc. I have covered and judged the event in previous years, and the community surrounding the cook-off is part of its appeal. This year at the judges' table will be WPTV's Ashley Glass and Janny Rodriguez. Everybody at the station makes fun of me because I talk about this event all year and say it's my favorite thing, but my favorite thing about it is the community comes together as one, and it's just so patriotic, I said. entry.title: Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, cut off his ankle monitor, DOJ says
entry.summary: The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, cut an electronic monitoring device off his ankle, just days after his arrest for keeping child sexual abuse material in storage units in California, authorities said Tuesday. Thomas Markle was in custody awaiting a hearing in federal court in Tampa, Florida, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said. He was arrested shortly after he cut off the ankle bracelet at 1:45 a.m., Essayli said. Markles arrest on Friday followed the seizure of approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images in storage in the Los Angeles area, Essayli said. During his arrest last week, he was taken from a senior care center in Lakeland by ambulance. Hours later, a judge allowed Markle to be released on the condition that he be electronically monitored, which typically means wearing an ankle tether. The judge also ordered a mental competency exam and a report by Nov. 20. His daughter, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, married Prince Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. She is an American citizen and actor who starred in the U.S. television drama Suits. Meghan recently said she was deeply distressed by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her fathers former home. She also revealed that a letter containing troubling allegations about him had been sent to police in London in 2019. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated, Meghan said of the letter. I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them. Thomas Markle was living in the Philippines this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S. His arrest followed reports by The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghans half-brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their fathers home in the Philippines. That discovery led to information about two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.

entry.article_text: Many businesses are reeling in the effects of last week’s historic flooding event across South Florida, including a local Vero Beach citrus grove farm. CBS12 News Photojournalist Chris Pollock visited Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach, a family-owned farm business that spans multiple generations. The farm has been amongst the hardest hit from the historic flooding. Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and were anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. That amount of rain over all of this land, it’s crazy, Greene said.

entry.summary: One person is dead following a crash in Indian River County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 58-year-old Sebastian man is dead following a crash in Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. FHP said the crash happened at around 3:40 p.m. on Monday along 37th Street. The westbound lanes between U.S. Highway 1 and 17th Avenue were closed at the time. According to FHP, an 82-year-old woman from Barefoot Bay driving an SUV was traveling east on 37th Street and stopped in the roadway to turn left into Hope Imaging Indian River MRI, a medical diagnostic imaging center. The 58-year-old man was riding a motorcycle traveling west on the same street. The woman made an improper left turn into the path of the man on the motorcycle, resulting in a collision between the front right corner of the SUV and the front of the motorcycle within the westbound lane, FHP said. Both vehicles came to rest on the north shoulder of 37th Street. According to FHP, the woman sustained minor injuries and was transported to Cleveland Clinic Indian River Hospital. The man was transported to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 4:33 p.m. FHP is still investigating the deadly crash.

entry.title: Independence Middle School honors veterans while teaching students meaning of service
entry.summary: Independence Middle School in Jupiter celebrated Veterans Day early, filling its gym with the school band and patriotic songs to honor military veterans. WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with veterans who were part of the event. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Jupiter students salute veterans The ceremony marked 15 years of a tradition at the school, where the panel of veterans from the Army, Navy and Marines shared their stories with students, who honored each one of them one by one. Michael Gallo, a civics teacher at Independence Middle School, said the event is about teaching students to appreciate those who served. 'These are the people who fight for our freedom and keep us safe. We want to show students what this holiday's about, how to appreciate veterans and they should always take the opportunity to say thank you for your service,' Gallo said. Francisco Nova, a Navy veteran, reflected on his time in the military. 'It was a great experience for me. I'll never regret the decision that I made to join the military. And it's just one of the main things people can think about doing in their future careers,' Nova said. Barbara Wirth, an Army veteran, said the day serves as a meaningful reminder. 'It's a good reminder about serving the bigger cause,' Wirth said. The students stayed locked in and listening as the veterans spoke about pressing forward. 'The challenge was to continue to press forward because that was the vision to press forward.' Trim spoke to the students with crowd participation, asking them to yell 'Go Navy' on a count of three. entry.title: Riviera Beach residents face costly recovery after flooding leaves homes damaged, many without flood insurance
entry.summary: More than a week after record rainfall flooded neighborhoods across Palm Beach County, residents in the Lone Pine Estates community of Riviera Beach are getting a clearer picture of what they lost and what it could take to recover. WPTV reporter Christy Waite listened to neighbors' heartbreaking stories about their recovery process. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Riviera Beach residents face costly flood recovery For residents like Patricia Brown Campbell, the damage is overwhelming. 'My house is completely, absolutely nothing,' Brown Campbell said. Brown Campbell has called Lone Pine Estates home for nine years. She said the recent flooding tore through her home, with water coming in from multiple directions. 'We had water coming from the back and the front. It was horrific,' she said. Brown Campbell estimates the damage to her home could top $100,000. She does not have flood insurance to help cover the cost. Brown Campbell is not alone. Rochelle Baker-Hughes, president of the neighborhoods homeowners association, said many residents are now facing significant losses and need financial help. 'A lot of them are going to need financial assistance because these people lost everything,' Baker-Hughes said. Baker-Hughes said Lone Pine Estates is not in a flood zone, leaving some homeowners without flood insurance and wondering where to turn next. 'I am going to pray and wait on the Lord to send us an angel to bail us out of it,' Brown Campbell said. Waite took those concerns to insurance attorney Aaron Bass, who said people without flood insurance should reach out to FEMA and other organizations to find out what assistance may be available. 'You are going to have to call FEMA and see if they will help you. And you need to call non-government agencies,' Bass said. Bass also encourages homeowners to consider purchasing flood insurance even if they do not live in a designated flood zone, because severe flooding can happen outside those areas. For residents looking for immediate assistance, Palm Beach County has set up a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Wells Recreation Center in Riviera Beach. The center brings county and partner agencies together in one location to help people affected by the flooding. The resource center is open until 7 p.m. Tuesday, and transportation is available for residents who need help getting there. Wells Recreation Center is located at 2409 Avenue H West in Riviera Beach.

entry.title: Palm Beach County school district employee accused of soliciting person he believed was 14-year-old boy
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County School District employee was arrested after police said he had sexually explicit conversations with an undercover detective posing as a 14-year-old boy. Boynton Beach police said Donald Rush, 65, of Lake Worth was arrested following an investigation by the department's Human Exploitation Task Force. According to police, detectives posed as a 14-year-old boy advertising lawn mowing services on Craigslist's Community messaging board. Investigators said they were contacted by someone using the screen name 'Palm Guy,' who was later identified by police as Rush. Police said Rush asked the person his age, whether adult men had approached him about sexual activity and whether he had told his parents about those interactions. The conversation later moved to text messages, according to police. Detectives said they again made clear that the person Rush was communicating with was supposedly 14 years old. Despite the stated age, police allege Rush continued the conversation, asking sexually explicit questions and making statements about his own sexual activity. With assistance from the Palm Beach County School Board Police Department, detectives located and interviewed Rush. Boynton Beach police said Rush admitted his involvement during that interview. Police said Rush also claimed during the investigation that he was a youth pastor. The department did not identify a church or organization with which he was allegedly affiliated. Rush faces charges of solicitation of a minor to engage in sexual conduct and unlawful use of a two-way communications device, according to police. He was being held at the Palm Beach County Jail. Police identified Rush as an employee of the Palm Beach County School District. Sean Cooley, the school district's chief of communications, said in a statement Tuesday that Rush is an electrician. Cooley also said the district immediately revoked Rush's access to all school facilities after learning of his arrest. In an update Tuesday, Cooley said the district is now processing Rush's termination following court action that prohibits him from being on school district property or having contact with employees or students. Rush's termination will take effect Wednesday, Nov. 11. Investigators said they believe there could be additional victims. entry.title: After 20 years, The King's Academy are once again state champs
entry.summary: In the gym at The Kings Academy, a strong serve sets the tone; the Lions are always on the prowl, and what theyve been hunting for for years is a regional title. You just dont know how far ahead the competition is and how strong its going to be, so we were always watching film and just preparing ourselves, said Head Coach, Bethany Avila, who prepared her girls for a showdown with the powerhouse Cardinal Mooney High School in Sarasota, and they beat them 3-0. I think we all just worked really hard at practice, knowing that we could do anything we put our minds to, said setter, Jordan Molnar. With their biggest obstacle out of the way, the girls were looking at a state championship title as they took on Pine Crest. It was definitely something that we had as a goal from the beginning of the season, to get that trophy. And I think it was something we all knew we could do, and we were going to do it, said pin hitter Miranda Knoll. Got to love the confidence, but the girls had a tough challenge in Pine Crest High School standing in their way. They immediately took the first set, but Pine Crest took the second, and we had a matchup. Then, in the fourth and final set, Anabelle Bencosme hit Pine Crest with the dagger to bring home the first championship in 20 years. I definitely shed a few tears, but nothing like that. It was definitely emotional for me personally it was my last volleyball game ever so it was really beautiful and special that the ending got to be the final game us being number one, said Ava Maldonado, middle blocker.

entry.article_text: Florida Highway Patrol is investigating a fatal crash that occurred in Indian River County Monday afternoon. FHP says that at around 3:43 p.m. on Monday, a 2018 Toyota Rav 4 SUV and a 2017 Harley Davidson Electra Guide Motorcycle collided near 1850 37th Street within unincorporated Indian River County. According to FHP , the driver of the Rav 4 SUV an 82-year-old female was traveling east on 37th Street before coming to a stop in the roadway and waiting to turn left into Indian River MRI. At the same time, the driver of the Harley Davidson a 58-year-old male was traveling west before colliding with the SUV, who turned into the path of the motorcycle as it approached. See also: Vero Beach family citrus grove reels after historic South Florida flooding damages crops The 82-year-old woman came away with minor injuries, while the 58-year-old male on the motorcycle was pronounced dead after being transported HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. As a result, Westbound 37th Street between U.S. Highway 1 and 17th Avenue is currently closed. This remains an active investigation.

entry.title: Treasure Coast woman loses second home in 2 years after devastating Fort Pierce flooding
entry.summary: A Treasure Coast woman who lost her home two years ago to a tornado from Hurricane Milton has lost another home to devastating flooding in Fort Pierce. 'I'm starting to feel like I'm invincible at this point,' says Terry Polk as she watched the debris pile of drywall and ruined furniture in front of her home get bigger. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Treasure Coast woman loses a second home in 2 years The water in her home was measured in feet, not inches, as the heavy rain in the first weekend of November flooded her block. 'We were actually in the house,' Polk said. 'When we were wading around, like around knee-deep water, I started getting scared.' She said they were rescued by kayaks and returned when the water receded, leaving so much damage. 'You know, to keep your focus, you just have to realize there are people out there that have it way worse. There are people out there that are so much worse, you know, and I have to be thankful that we got out with our lives,' she said. Two years ago she was living in the Spanish Lakes community of St. Lucie County when Hurricane Milton's winds created widespread tornadoes. One of the twisters, an EF3, struck the community, killing six people and destroying homes, including Terry's. 'Terry is one of the most amazing people I've met,' said friend Cindy McGee. 'She's very strong, does a lot for the community, a lot for the neighborhood.' Polk said she has flood insurance, but the damage is so extensive, she's not sure if there is enough coverage to fix everything. 'I already explained to the cats, who are looking at me like, we didn't exactly sign up for your survivor world,' she said.

entry.title: 17-year-old killed in Boynton Beach shooting, police say
entry.summary: Police are investigating after a 17-year-old was fatally shot Monday evening in Boynton Beach. The Boynton Beach Police Department said officers responded to a shooting at approximately 8 p.m. near the 100 block of Southwest 3rd Avenue. WATCH REPORT BELOW: 17-year-old fatally shot in Boynton Beach Police identified the victim as 17-year-old Franck Jeannoute of Boynton Beach. Jeannoute was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead shortly after arriving, according to police.
