entry.title: Martin County to establish some quiet zones to combat train noise
entry.summary: To combat complaints over train horns, Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to enact some quiet zones in the county. A motion was first made to turn all 27 railroad crossings into quiet zones, but then a second motion narrowed the scope. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County to establish some train quiet zones That second motion passed 3-2. This vote comes after County Commissioners had unanimously voted against quiet zones last year. Opponents of quiet zones talked about safety, while supporters said it was a quality of life issue. 'The horn all day and all night. And as I'm listening to that noisy disruption, I can visualize the intersection with four gates down, deployed, and cars safely behind them with that horn pointlessly bothering people,' said Doug Farley, a quiet zone supporter. The areas that will first be worked on to become quiet zones will be two crossings at County Line Road and Skyline Drive in Jensen Beach. The third is along Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound near Mariner Sands. The city of Stuart recently received a $1.86 million grant to enhance rail corridor safety. St. Lucie County has established a quiet zone in the southern end of the county at three crossings. In Palm Beach County, both Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens recently set up quiet zones.

I'm not a prosecutor, so I don't know that, and I wouldn't. That's not something I would be able to speculate," Weiss said.If an investigation finds problems with how city business was conducted, Weiss told WPTV he wants changes to follow."I'd like to see corrective action taking place, making sure it's an open, transparent, and fair, um, how we go about and award contracts in the city," Weiss said.West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James strongly pushed back against Weiss' allegations in a statement to WPTV, calling them "misleading and baseless false accusations.""The City of West Palm Beach strongly rejects Gregg Weiss' misleading and baseless false accusations. After years on the County Commission, it is deeply disappointing that Weiss is choosing to spend his final week in office launching politically motivated attacks rather than doing something meaningful for our community," James said.James said residents have a right to question development, public property and government decisions, but said those questions should be based on facts."The City conducts its business in accordance with applicable laws, established procedures, and appropriate public oversight," James said. entry.title: Independence Middle School honors veterans while teaching students meaning of service
entry.summary: Independence Middle School in Jupiter celebrated Veterans Day early, filling its gym with the school band and patriotic songs to honor military veterans. WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with veterans who were part of the event. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Jupiter students salute veterans The ceremony marked 15 years of a tradition at the school, where the panel of veterans from the Army, Navy and Marines shared their stories with students, who honored each one of them one by one. Michael Gallo, a civics teacher at Independence Middle School, said the event is about teaching students to appreciate those who served. 'These are the people who fight for our freedom and keep us safe. We want to show students what this holiday's about, how to appreciate veterans and they should always take the opportunity to say thank you for your service,' Gallo said. Francisco Novoa, a Navy veteran, reflected on his time in the military. 'It was a great experience for me. I'll never regret the decision that I made to join the military. And it's just one of the main things people can think about doing in their future careers,' Novoa said. Barbara Wirth, an Army veteran, said the day serves as a meaningful reminder. 'It's a good reminder about serving the bigger cause,' Wirth said. The students stayed locked in and listening as the veterans spoke about pressing forward. 'The challenge was to continue to press forward because that was the vision to press forward.' Trim spoke to the students with crowd participation, asking them to yell 'Go Navy' on a count of three. The students responded loudly, followed by Mr. Gallo thanking the veterans who participated in a salute to those who served. entry.title: WPTV finds $15.5 million in political contributions tied to fight over Florida's 'free kill' law
entry.summary: Florida lawmakers overwhelmingly voted to repeal one of the state's most controversial medical malpractice provisions earlier this year. But despite bipartisan support, the legislation never became law. Now, a WPTV investigation is following the money behind the political fight over what critics call Florida's 'free kill' law uncovering more than $15.5 million in campaign contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying groups to political committees tied to lawmakers who opposed the repeal and to Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ultimately vetoed it. entry.article_text: Florida lawmakers overwhelmingly voted to repeal one of the state's most controversial medical malpractice provisions earlier this year. But despite bipartisan support, the legislation never became law.Now, a WPTV investigation is following the money behind the political fight over what critics call Florida's "free kill" law — uncovering more than $15.5 million in campaign contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying groups to political committees tied to lawmakers who opposed the repeal and to Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ultimately vetoed it.WATCH REPORT BELOW: In a previous investigation, WPTV introduced viewers to Beth Miller, whose only daughter, Dawn, died just hours after being discharged from the hospital following gallbladder surgery."It's on your mind, 24/7," Miller said. "We were very close, to say the least. She was my only child, my only living relative."A medical expert who reviewed Dawn's records told WPTV she should not have been discharged from the hospital. Miller said her request for an autopsy was denied, leaving her with unanswered questions about her daughter's death."I don't have an answer to this day," she said.No court has determined whether medical negligence contributed to Dawn's death.But when Miller explored her legal options, she encountered another obstacle.Because Dawn was older than 25, unmarried and had no children, Florida law prevents Miller from recovering certain wrongful-death damages in a medical malpractice lawsuit.The restriction is part of Florida's Wrongful Death Act. Critics argue it creates a disparity in accountability by limiting the damages available to certain surviving family members based on the deceased person's age and family circumstances."It's completely arbitrary," said Jordan Dulcie, a trial attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart & Shipley.Dulce, who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is now among the attorneys advocating for repeal."Trying to value life from the Legislature's standpoint, I think, is always improper," he said.State Rep. Dana Trabulsy, a R-Fort Pierce, sponsored House Bill 6017, legislation aimed at removing the controversial restriction from Florida's Wrongful Death Act.The proposal passed both chambers of the Florida Legislature with overwhelming support, but in May, DeSantis vetoed the bill.The governor argued that expanding the damages families could recover without additional safeguards, including caps on damages and attorney fees, could increase costs for Floridians."That imposes costs, as those costs are put through the system that helps drive the price that people pay for normal products and premiums they pay," DeSantis said.Critics of the law argue Florida remains the only state with this particular restriction on medical malpractice wrongful-death claims.Dulcie believes politics, rather than fairness, is standing in the way of reform."It's politics. That's all it is, is politics," he said. "When you look at the end of the day, no one thinks this law is fair."So WPTV examined the campaign contributions flowing to the political figures who opposed the repeal.WPTV reviewed hundreds of campaign finance records, tracking contributions made between 2017 and 2026 to political committees tied to the 10 lawmakers who voted against HB 6017 — four senators and six representatives — and DeSantis, who vetoed it.The investigation identified more than $15.5 million in contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying organizations with a stake in the debate.Of that total:More than $12 million came from hospitals, healthcare networks, physician groups, insurance companies, nursing homes and other health care interestsMore than $3 million came from lobbying organizations that opposed HB 6017 and efforts to repeal the provisionAmong the lawmakers who opposed the bill, WPTV identified several who received substantial contributions from the groups examined.Sen. Gayle Harrell, a Republican representing part of the Treasure Coast, received more than $700,000 from the tracked groups since 2017, including $28,000 in the weeks leading up to the vote.Sen. Tom Leek, a Republican from northeast Florida, received more than $400,000 since 2024, including $15,000 in the weeks before the vote.Rep. James Buchanan, a Republican from Sarasota County, received more than $300,000 since 2018, including $46,000 in the month before the vote.But the vast majority of the contributions WPTV tracked went to political committees tied to DeSantis.Those committees, primarily his Political Action Committee Florida Freedom Fund, received approximately $12.7 million since 2017, including $170,000 in the weeks and months preceding his veto.The contributions were made over multiple election cycles and were not necessarily connected to HB 6017. Campaign finance records do not establish that the money influenced any lawmaker's vote or the governor's veto.Still, Dulcie argues the financial resources available to groups opposing changes to the law create an imbalance in Tallahassee."Unfortunately, the victims of medical negligence don't have hundreds of lobbyists that they can pay millions of dollars to go to Tallahassee year after year to campaign to change this law," he said.WPTV contacted all 10 lawmakers who voted against the bill, as well as DeSantis, requesting interviews and asking about the contributions and their positions on the legislation.Despite multiple calls and emails, none responded to WPTV's requests.Dr. Aubrey Jewett, a political science professor at the University of Central Florida, said campaign contributions are an essential part of modern politics."There's an old saying that money is the mother's milk of politics," Jewett said, describing the importance of fundraising to political campaigns.He said businesses and lobbying organizations frequently contribute to politicians they believe will support their interests."I mean, it is 100% crystal clear. Most people that give are trying to get access and influence," Jewett said.But he emphasized an important distinction: political contributions alone are not evidence that a politician changed a vote or policy decision in exchange for money.Donors may support a politician because that politician already shares their views."The candidates will say, 'Well, you know, they're not like buying my vote. Instead, they support the position that I hold,'" Jewett explained.And while DeSantis vetoed HB 6017, Jewett pointed out that the governor did not rule out supporting a different version of the legislation."Gov. DeSantis did say that he would sign off on a similar bill as long as it had some caps," Jewett said.That leaves open the possibility of another attempt at repeal.With DeSantis leaving office, WPTV took the question directly to Gov.-elect Byron Donalds while he was on the campaign trail.Would he support repealing Florida's so-called "free kill" law?Donalds stopped short of committing to a position."I'm aware of Gov. DeSantis's veto on this measure. Also aware of how many members of the Legislature supported it," Donalds said. "We're just going to sit down, take a look at the issue, and render a decision. I've not made one at this time, but we're going to do what's in the best interest of the people of Florida."For families like Beth Miller's, the future of the law could determine whether others facing similar circumstances have an opportunity to seek accountability through the courts.And the debate is far from over.Since WPTV's first investigation aired, numerous viewers have reached out to share their own experiences involving alleged medical negligence and the legal barriers they encountered afterward.WPTV is continuing to investigate those cases, examine the law's impact on Florida families and seek answers from the elected

entry.title: Delray Beach cancels 2027 St. Patrick's Day Parade, Pride event under new Florida law
entry.summary: The City of Delray Beach announced Tuesday it will not host its annual St. Patrick's Day Parade or Pride event in 2027, citing a new Florida law restricting local governments from funding or promoting certain diversity, equity and inclusion activities. The city said it made the decision following a review of Senate Bill 1134 , which takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Delray Beach cancels St. Patrick's Day, Pride events under new Florida law The law prohibits municipalities from funding or promoting, directly or indirectly, or taking official action related to activities that fall under its definition of diversity, equity and inclusion. Under the law, DEI includes certain programming or activities designed or implemented with reference to race, color, sex, ethnicity, gender identity or sexual orientation. Delray Beach officials said they determined that the restrictions legally prohibit the city from organizing, funding or promoting these events in 2027. 'The City recognizes that these annual events have provided opportunities for members of the community to gather, celebrate, and connect,' the city said in a Facebook post. 'We appreciate the residents, participants, volunteers, and community partners who have contributed to these events over the years.' The legislation also prohibits municipalities from spending money to support DEI offices or officers and bars them from authorizing municipal funds to be used by employees, contractors, volunteers, vendors or agents to promote DEI initiatives. A resident may bring an action in circuit court against a municipality accused of violating the law. However, the law includes several exceptions. Municipalities may still recognize or promote certain federal and state holidays and observances. The law also specifically allows cities to issue event permits in a content-neutral manner and provide public safety services. That provision means the law does not categorically prohibit privately organized events that obtain permits from a municipality. Delray Beach's announcement specifically addresses events organized, funded or promoted by the city. 'We remain committed to serving all residents and providing opportunities for community engagement consistent with applicable state and federal laws,' the city said. The new law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

entry.title: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding - WPTV
entry.summary: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding    WPTV
entry.article_text: Residents and farmers in western St. Lucie County are seeking answers and long-term drainage solutions after historic flooding left homes, farms and roads underwater last week.The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear concerns from people in the area, including farmers, residents and representatives from Save the Chimps. District members said the drainage system can handle only so much water during an extreme rainfall event and discussed engineering as part of a possible long-term plan.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Some of the hardest-hit areas are now seeing significant improvement, including Save the Chimps in western St. But residents and farmers say they want to know what can be done to reduce the risk of similar flooding during the next extreme rainfall event.For one resident, the flooding has already changed how they view their future in the area."I will be selling my house cause I am not going to risk my investment," the resident said during Monday's meeting.Water control district hears concerns from western St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear from people affected by the flooding.Farmers, residents and representatives of Save the Chimps attended as district members discussed the drainage system and the scale of last week's flooding.President Steve Cassens said there are limits to what the existing system can handle when extraordinary amounts of rain fall in a short period."If we have a rainfall event like that, my personal feeling is you can have gates open, shut, it doesn't matter," said Cassens. "We can manage water maybe 3, 4, 5, 6 inches. We can't manage water in the quantities that we got."District officials also discussed maintaining waterways and ditches, including concerns about a creek in Western Fort Pierce that serves as a primary drainage route. The district said it systematically cleans ditches within its boundaries.The district said it could examine engineering as part of developing a long-range plan.Conditions improve at Save the ChimpsSave the Chimps, a sanctuary in western St. Lucie County, was among the places hit hard by the flooding.WPTV previously reported that staff members had to use drones to deliver food to chimpanzees because several roads through the sanctuary were underwater.When WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache returned days later, staff said conditions had significantly improved."A short 40 hours after that, we're almost completely dry on our roads," said Mark Yohannan.The improvement came after days of challenges caused by standing water at the sanctuary.West Fort Pierce farmer raises concernsThe concerns extended beyond residential neighborhoods.Justin Akerley, who helps operate Saint Lucie Farm Preserve in west Fort Pierce, spoke later Monday at a Port St. Lucie City Council meeting after attending the water control district meeting.Akerley told council members he believes continued development is adding pressure to the area's drainage infrastructure."I just spent my morning in a meeting with the North St. Lucie River Water Control District trying to figure out what we can do to alleviate the water issues, and there's really no right answer except for stop building," Akerley said.Akerley shared a video with WPTV showing flooding at Saint Lucie Farm Preserve, a working agritourism farm operated by Akerley and Michael Hale. The farm produces hay, cut flowers, beef and assorted vegetables and hosts community agricultural events.Akerley told council members the consequences extend to other farms and families."I've got friends that have calves dying that are flooded; they can't get out," he said. "It's a terrible, terrible situation for everybody. There's people that have lost their homes."He urged city leaders to reconsider the effect future development could have on flooding and drainage."Just please reconsider because it's not a good situation for everybody, and it's only gonna get worse," Akerley said.Officials consider what comes nextDuring Monday's Port St. Lucie City Council meeting, Councilman David Pickett also called for greater scrutiny of flooding and the city's stormwater infrastructure.Pickett said he sent two memos to the city manager earlier in the week addressing floodwaters and wants the city to expedite a planned stormwater study rather than wait until 2029.He also raised concerns about flooding in Tradition and called for the city to examine stormwater systems before distributing certain stormwater fees to community development districts.Meanwhile, the North St. Lucie River Water Control District has said engineering options can be assessed as officials consider a long-term plan.For residents and farmers still recovering from last week's flooding, those discussions are now turning toward a larger question: what can be done before the next extreme rainfall event?This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Dolphins place QB Malik Willis on injured reserve, sidelining him at least 4 games
entry.summary: The Miami Dolphins placed Malik Willis on injured reserve on Tuesday, sidelining the quarterback for at least four games. Willis has been dealing with a nagging groin injury that appeared to significantly limit his mobility in last weekend's 19-9 loss to the Detroit Lions . He said after the game his groin felt a little tight,' and coach Jeff Hafley echoed those words. 'It was tight today, and you could see it,' Hafley said last Sunday. You could see he couldnt really open up. There were a couple plays where I give him credit. He pulled it and he ran and he got us yards and he got out of trouble against a good defensive line. But you could see he just wasnt quite able to go full speed. Willis has completed 121 of 208 passes with six touchdowns and six interceptions this season for the 1-7 Dolphins. The Ringer first reported the news, saying it is not expected to be a season-ending injury. Backup Kyle McCord, who the Dolphins acquired in August from Green Bay, will be in line to start this week at Indianapolis. McCord spent the 2025 season on the practice squad of the Philadelphia Eagles, who drafted him in the sixth round a year ago. The Packers signed him on Jan. 20. He went 46 of 70 for 446 yards with four touchdowns and no interceptions while getting sacked six times in three preseason games with Green Bay. The Dolphins also placed defensive lineman Zach Sieler on IR on Tuesday after he suffered a ruptured biceps against Detroit.

entry.title: The King's Academy volleyball wins first state championship in 20 years
entry.summary: The King's Academy volleyball team brought home the school's first championship in 20 years, defeating the Pine Crest Panthers on Nov. 4. 'You just dont know how far ahead the competition is and how strong it's going to be, so we were always watching film and just preparing ourselves,' said head Coach Bethany Avila. The Lions finished with a 26-5-1 overall record, sweeping Pensacola Catholic (30) in the state semifinals and Cardinal Mooney in Sarasota (30) in the regional round. 'I think we all just worked really hard at practice, knowing that we could do anything we put our minds to,' said setter Jordan Molnar. In the title game, The King's Academy took the first set, but Pine Crest took the second. The Lions bounced back to take the third set. Then, in the fourth and final set, Anabelle Bencosme hit Pine Crest with the dagger to bring home the school's first volleyball championship since 2006. 'It was definitely something that we had as a goal from the beginning of the season, to get that trophy. And I think it was something we all knew we could do, and we were going to do it,' said pin hitter Miranda Knoll. 'I definitely shed a few tears, but nothing like that. It was definitely emotional for me personally; it was my last volleyball game ever, so it was really beautiful and special that the ending got to be the final game us being number one,' said Ava Maldonado, middle blocker.

entry.title: Keiser football faces must-win season finale with playoff streak on the line
entry.summary: Since 2019, the Keiser University football team has made the NAIA football playoffs each season, including making it to the title game the last four years, but that streak could be in jeopardy. 'We always talk about process over results, and I know the results have shown us going to countless amount of national championships but we continue to focus on the process of what got us there,' said head coach Myles Russ. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Keiser's playoff streak comes down to season finale Keiser's push to national prominence is thanks to an all-in approach by every man on the team, and for the last few years the leader of that attack was Shea Spencer, the former quarterback who led Keiser to two straight national title appearances. These days, however, a new signal caller, JT Tabora, has taken over. 'It's been awesome being the quarterback here at Keiser. I've been backup for the past two years, and it's been great learning behind him, and giving me the opportunity to start this year has been great,' said Tabora. In seven games this season, the sophomore has passed for 1,300 yards and 13 touchdowns. While his numbers are strong, the Seahawks find themselves in uncharted waters. They're 6-3 and ranked 15th overall in the country, and after suffering a loss Saturday, the fellas could fall out of the top 15. Sounds like no problem, right? Well, only the top 15 teams are guaranteed a spot in the NAIA Playoffs, making Saturday's season finale against Warner a must-win. 'I think we can clean up some things, that's our mindset: just clean up some things, and once we get those things (fixed), were a tough team to beat,' Tabora said.

entry.title: Judge jails Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, after he cut off his ankle monitor
entry.summary: The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was ordered to jail Tuesday because he removed an electronic monitoring device from his ankle, just days after he was charged with possession of child sexual abuse material. Thomas Markle was arrested and appeared in federal court in Tampa, Florida, after authorities learned he had cut off the device at 1:45 a.m., First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said. 'Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions,' he said. Markle's arrest on Friday in Lakeland, Florida, followed the seizure of approximately 78 items from storage units in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, said Essayli, a federal prosecutor in California. He was living in a senior care center at the time, but U.S. Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin agreed Tuesday that Markle now must be kept in custody. Authorities have not said where Markle will be held while his case remains in court ahead of a likely transfer to California. In her written order, Griffin noted Markle's 'housing situation' had become 'untenable,' but did not elaborate. Essayli told The Associated Press that he didn't know why the ankle device was cut off. The judge last week ordered a mental competency exam for Markle and a report by Nov. 20. entry.title: Port St. Lucie cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills, independence - WPTV
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills, independence    WPTV
entry.article_text: A recent cooking class in Port St. Lucie is helping adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities learn valuable life skills and gain more independence.The participants are part of the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County’s Guardian Advocacy Program, which provides guardianship support to people with developmental disabilities.WATCH: Cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills for independent livingSome of the participants are young adults who have aged out of foster care and don't have family members to rely on for support.Through a partnership with GL Homes that has lasted nearly a decade, participants are given hands-on experiences and opportunities to develop skills that can help them in everyday life.During the latest class in October, participants learned how to prepare a healthier meal, with Mediterranean chicken on the menu.From chopping vegetables and preparing ingredients to following a recipe and practicing kitchen safety, the lesson was about more than just cooking.Organizers say the goal is to give participants experiences and opportunities that are often not readily available to them while helping them become more self-sufficient."We wanted to give them these experiences that they just don't have and the rest of us take for granted," said Sarah Alsofrom, Vice President of Community Relations at GL Homes.Jessica Kelson with the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County says watching participants learn new skills and take part in activities can make a meaningful difference."Being able to watch them learn a new skill or participate in something that's not typically offered to them is just really heartwarming and nice to see them be able to grow," Kelson said.By the end of the class, participants had prepared their meal and sat down to enjoy what they made.For one participant, the accomplishment was something to be proud of."I'm proud of it," she said. "I am going to try this at home."Organizers hope these experiences will give participants the confidence and practical skills to take greater control of their daily lives — one meal at a time.

entry.title: 'We’re homeless': Martin County residents voice frustrations over flooding at commission meeting - WPBF
entry.summary: 'We’re homeless': Martin County residents voice frustrations over flooding at commission meeting    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County residents gathered at the commission chambers Tuesday morning to express their concerns about ongoing flooding in their neighborhoods and demand action from county leaders. "For 40 years, I’ve raised my family here, built my life here, and in the hours, watched everything we worked for become submerged in flood water and sewage," Jensen Beach resident Mary Berner said. Resident Lisa French described the impact of the flooding, saying, "Today, we’re homeless. We have nowhere to have Christmas. We don’t have much to come home to." Some residents questioned whether drainage infrastructure and development contributed to the flooding, while Yamila Rollan Escalona, who's with the Yaya por Vida Foundation, raised concerns about response efforts. MARTIN COUNTY FLOODING: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall "Take Rich, a historic Black American in a Bahamian neighborhood inhabited and preserved for generations by a majority Black Americans. With a capital 'B.' They still have not been properly mitigated. Standing water, no pumps, no headlines, not a peep on social media, and just one article in the news today! Katrina much?" Rollan Escalona said. County leaders said crews are pumping water around the clock and assured residents that once the immediate flooding is addressed, they will explore ways to reduce future risks. Some proposed solutions include having one agency, such as the South Florida Water Management District, manage the nearby Savannas as a single watershed and exploring additional drainage options. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "I do expect you to make additional funding available to your staff today to mitigate this emergency as efficiently as possible. Thank you for your time and expect to continue to hear from us," resident Kyle Pond said. Commissioner Sarah Heard responded, saying, "Jensen Beach residents, we’ve heard you loud and clear. You are our top priority." County leaders also said they plan to review the county’s warning system and will address the flooding issue again at their next meeting, where they will provide updates and discuss a potential grant program. entry.title: Martin County to establish some quiet zones to combat train noise - WFLX
entry.summary: Martin County to establish some quiet zones to combat train noise    WFLX
entry.article_text: To combat complaints over train horns, Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to enact some quiet zones in the county. A motion was first made to turn all 27 railroad crossings into quiet zones, but then a second motion narrowed the scope. WATCH REPORT BELOW: That second motion passed 3-2. This vote comes after County Commissioners had unanimously voted against quiet zones last year. Opponents of quiet zones talked about safety, while supporters said it was a quality of life issue. "The horn all day and all night. And as I'm listening to that noisy disruption, I can visualize the intersection with four gates down, deployed, and cars safely behind them with that horn pointlessly bothering people," said Doug Farley, a quiet zone supporter. The areas that will first be worked on to become quiet zones will be two crossings at County Line Road and Skyline Drive in Jensen Beach. The third is along Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound near Mariner Sands. The city of Stuart recently received a $1.86 million grant to enhance rail corridor safety. Lucie County has established a quiet zone in the southern end of the county at three crossings. In Palm Beach County, both Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens recently set up quiet zones.

entry.title: WPTV finds $15.5 million in political contributions tied to fight over Florida's 'free kill' law
entry.summary: Florida lawmakers overwhelmingly voted to repeal one of the state's most controversial medical malpractice provisions earlier this year. But despite bipartisan support, the legislation never became law. Now, a WPTV investigation is following the money behind the political fight over what critics call Florida's 'free kill' law uncovering more than $15.5 million in campaign contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying groups to political committees tied to lawmakers who opposed the repeal and to Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ultimately vetoed it. WATCH REPORT BELOW: WPTV follows the money behind Florida's 'free kill' law A mother's fight for answers In a previous investigation , WPTV introduced viewers to Beth Miller, whose only daughter, Dawn, died just hours after being discharged from the hospital following gallbladder surgery. 'It's on your mind, 24/7,' Miller said. 'We were very close, to say the least. She was my only child, my only living relative.' A medical expert who reviewed Dawn's records told WPTV she should not have been discharged from the hospital. Miller said her request for an autopsy was denied, leaving her with unanswered questions about her daughter's death. 'I don't have an answer to this day,' she said. No court has determined whether medical negligence contributed to Dawn's death. But when Miller explored her legal options, she encountered another obstacle. Because Dawn was older than 25, unmarried and had no children, Florida law prevents Miller from recovering certain wrongful-death damages in a medical malpractice lawsuit. The restriction is part of Florida's Wrongful Death Act. Critics argue it creates a disparity in accountability by limiting the damages available to certain surviving family members based on the deceased person's age and family circumstances. 'It's completely arbitrary,' said Jordan Dulcie, a trial attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart Shipley. Dulce, who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is now among the attorneys advocating for repeal. entry.article_text: Florida lawmakers overwhelmingly voted to repeal one of the state's most controversial medical malpractice provisions earlier this year. But despite bipartisan support, the legislation never became law.Now, a WPTV investigation is following the money behind the political fight over what critics call Florida's "free kill" law — uncovering more than $15.5 million in campaign contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying groups to political committees tied to lawmakers who opposed the repeal and to Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ultimately vetoed it.WATCH REPORT BELOW: In a previous investigation, WPTV introduced viewers to Beth Miller, whose only daughter, Dawn, died just hours after being discharged from the hospital following gallbladder surgery."It's on your mind, 24/7," Miller said. "We were very close, to say the least. She was my only child, my only living relative."A medical expert who reviewed Dawn's records told WPTV she should not have been discharged from the hospital. Miller said her request for an autopsy was denied, leaving her with unanswered questions about her daughter's death."I don't have an answer to this day," she said.No court has determined whether medical negligence contributed to Dawn's death.But when Miller explored her legal options, she encountered another obstacle.Because Dawn was older than 25, unmarried and had no children, Florida law prevents Miller from recovering certain wrongful-death damages in a medical malpractice lawsuit.The restriction is part of Florida's Wrongful Death Act. Critics argue it creates a disparity in accountability by limiting the damages available to certain surviving family members based on the deceased person's age and family circumstances."It's completely arbitrary," said Jordan Dulcie, a trial attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart & Shipley.Dulce, who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is now among the attorneys advocating for repeal."Trying to value life from the Legislature's standpoint, I think, is always improper," he said.State Rep. Dana Trabulsy, a R-Fort Pierce, sponsored House Bill 6017, legislation aimed at removing the controversial restriction from Florida's Wrongful Death Act.The proposal passed both chambers of the Florida Legislature with overwhelming support, but in May, DeSantis vetoed the bill.The governor argued that expanding the damages families could recover without additional safeguards, including caps on damages and attorney fees, could increase costs for Floridians."That imposes costs, as those costs are put through the system that helps drive the price that people pay for normal products and premiums they pay," DeSantis said.Critics of the law argue Florida remains the only state with this particular restriction on medical malpractice wrongful-death claims.Dulcie believes politics, rather than fairness, is standing in the way of reform."It's politics. That's all it is, is politics," he said. "When you look at the end of the day, no one thinks this law is fair."So WPTV examined the campaign contributions flowing to the political figures who opposed the repeal.WPTV reviewed hundreds of campaign finance records, tracking contributions made between 2017 and 2026 to political committees tied to the 10 lawmakers who voted against HB 6017 — four senators and six representatives — and DeSantis, who vetoed it.The investigation identified more than $15.5 million in contributions from healthcare interests and lobbying organizations with a stake in the debate.Of that total:More than $12 million came from hospitals, healthcare networks, physician groups, insurance companies, nursing homes and other health care interestsMore than $3 million came from lobbying organizations that opposed HB 6017 and efforts to repeal the provisionAmong the lawmakers who opposed the bill, WPTV identified several who received substantial contributions from the groups examined.Sen. Gayle Harrell, a Republican representing part of the Treasure Coast, received more than $700,000 from the tracked groups since 2017, including $28,000 in the weeks leading up to the vote.Sen. Tom Leek, a Republican from northeast Florida, received more than $400,000 since 2024, including $15,000 in the weeks before the vote.Rep. James Buchanan, a Republican from Sarasota County, received more than $300,000 since 2018, including $46,000 in the month before the vote.But the vast majority of the contributions WPTV tracked went to political committees tied to DeSantis.Those committees, primarily his Political Action Committee Florida Freedom Fund, received approximately $12.7 million since 2017, including $170,000 in the weeks and months preceding his veto.The contributions were made over multiple election cycles and were not necessarily connected to HB 6017. Campaign finance records do not establish that the money influenced any lawmaker's vote or the governor's veto.Still, Dulcie argues the financial resources available to groups opposing changes to the law create an imbalance in Tallahassee."Unfortunately, the victims of medical negligence don't have hundreds of lobbyists that they can pay millions of dollars to go to Tallahassee year after year to campaign to change this law," he said.WPTV contacted all 10 lawmakers who voted against the bill, as well as DeSantis, requesting interviews and asking about the contributions and their positions on the legislation.Despite multiple calls and emails, none responded to WPTV's requests.Dr. Aubrey Jewett, a political science professor at the University of Central Florida, said campaign contributions are an essential part of modern politics."There's an old saying that money is the mother's milk of politics," Jewett said, describing the importance of fundraising to political campaigns.He said businesses and lobbying organizations frequently contribute to politicians they believe will support their interests."I mean, it is 100% crystal clear. Most people that give are trying to get access and influence," Jewett said.But he emphasized an important distinction: political contributions alone are not evidence that a politician changed a vote or policy decision in exchange for money.Donors may support a politician because that politician already shares their views."The candidates will say, 'Well, you know, they're not like buying my vote. Instead, they support the position that I hold,'" Jewett explained.And while DeSantis vetoed HB 6017, Jewett pointed out that the governor did not rule out supporting a different version of the legislation."Gov. DeSantis did say that he would sign off on a similar bill as long as it had some caps," Jewett said.That leaves open the possibility of another attempt at repeal.With DeSantis leaving office, WPTV took the question directly to Gov.-elect Byron Donalds while he was on the campaign trail.Would he support repealing Florida's so-called "free kill" law?Donalds stopped short of committing to a position."I'm aware of Gov. DeSantis's veto on this measure. Also aware of how many members of the Legislature supported it," Donalds said. "We're just going to sit down, take a look at the issue, and render a decision. I've not made one at this time, but we're going to do what's in the best interest of the people of Florida."For families like Beth Miller's, the future of the law could determine whether others facing similar circumstances have an opportunity to seek accountability through the courts.And the debate is far from over.Since WPTV's first investigation aired, numerous viewers have reached out to share their own experiences involving alleged medical negligence and the legal barriers they encountered afterward.WPTV is continuing to investigate those cases, examine the law's impact on Florida families and seek answers from the elected

entry.title: Fort Pierce police union declares impasse, says city cited Amendment 3 in 0% raise offer - WPEC
entry.summary: Fort Pierce police union declares impasse, says city cited Amendment 3 in 0% raise offer    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Fort Pierce Police Officers Association says it declared an impasse in contract negotiations after the city proposed no raises or step increases for officers. In a Facebook post dated Nov. 7, the association said officers and representatives from the Coastal Florida Police Benevolent Association met with the city Nov. 5 for a fourth round of negotiations. The union said the city’s proposal included 0% raises and no step increases. The association said city representatives cited Amendment 3 and an anticipated $6 million budget shortfall. It also said representatives indicated city employees could potentially go without raises for two to three years. The city’s website estimates Amendment 3 could reduce Fort Pierce’s property-tax revenue by about $3.5 million in fiscal year 2028 and an additional $1.5 million in fiscal year 2029, for a combined estimated reduction of about $5 million. The city says it may consider cost reductions and other revenue sources to address the impact. 3 election, Florida law enforcement groups warned that the amendment could reduce money available for public safety and lead to fewer deputies, slower 911 response times and service cuts. The Florida Sheriffs Association ran an ad campaign opposing the measure, while police and fire leaders also raised concerns about the lack of a replacement funding plan. Those were warnings about potential effects, not announcements of specific cuts to Fort Pierce’s police department. Declaring an impasse moves negotiations into a formal process for resolving disagreements. The association said it will continue advocating for what it called fair and competitive wages and keep members and the community updated. The negotiations come as Fort Pierce police have been part of a major multi-agency operation targeting the 23rd Street gang . Officials said the nearly two-year investigation led to nearly 40 arrests, five search warrants and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash. Fort Pierce police said investigators linked people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings over the past decade.

entry.title: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond    WPEC
entry.article_text: Less than 12 hours after he was booked into jail, a Cape Coral man accused of making TikTok threats involving a Stuart elementary school was out on a $100,000 bond. By Monday morning, deputies were watching the school entrance, and Jessica and John Greisen had decided to keep their third grader home. Wanted to vomit, Jessica Greisen said. She recalled thinking, My child is not going to school. Their daughter, Teigan, attends Felix A. Williams Elementary School. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the entrance. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would also add deputies at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. How detectives found the threats A tip late Friday led detectives to TikTok videos in which Michael George Davis, 51, threatened to kill law enforcement officers, the sheriff’s office said. Sheriff John Budensiek said the videos were repeatedly posted and taken down. In one video reviewed by CBS12 News, Davis said he was going to shoot people. As many as I can, dawg, as soon as I get there, he said. Budensiek said the threat in that video was directed at law enforcement officers. As detectives looked through the account, they found a separate post naming Felix A. So it went from threatening law enforcement to threatening Jews to threatening one of our students here in Martin County, Budensiek said. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The sheriff said the post also threatened a local family. Tuthill described the threats against the school as vague and said the posts referenced a specific student. Budensiek said the student hasn’t attended Felix A. Williams in years, but Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. An alleged dispute dating back to 2006 2014 Davis lives in Cape Coral, but Budensiek said he surfed in Martin County years ago. The sheriff said Davis appeared to link the family he named online to a dispute he claims happened sometime between 2006 and 2014. Budensiek also described a later incident Davis claims happened at a gym. According to that account, people Davis associated with a surf group were supposed to spot him while he lifted weights. Davis claims they failed to do so and a significant amount of weight fell on his chest. Budensiek said investigators found no direct connection between the alleged dispute and the family. They have no idea what he’s talking about, he said. Arrested Saturday night, released Sunday afternoon Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night on a felony warrant for written threats to kill. The sheriff’s office said Davis initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said deputies found no weapons when they arrested Davis. He said investigators were unaware of any prior arrests or any instances in which Davis was taken for an involuntary mental health evaluation under Florida’s Baker Act. Lee County jail records show Davis was booked at 2:53 a.m. Sunday and released at 2:12 p.m. on a $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant. The records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. I was hoping that $100,000 bond he would still be sitting in jail, and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry, Budensiek said. The Greisens said they want to know whether Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Why was he even released first off? Budensiek said Davis rides an e-bike, his driver’s license was suspended and deputies don’t know of a car he uses. The sheriff said that makes it harder to track his movements. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat, Budensiek said. What happens next Budensiek urged parents to stay vigilant and asked anyone who sees Davis in Martin County to call the sheriff’s office. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams and that his office would support parents as they decide what’s best for their children. Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers about the precautions in place. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Detectives are still working with Cape Coral police. Budensiek said investigators recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to search it. His office also sent preservation requests to TikTok. We are working diligently to come up with other cases and other charges that may change that, but we are not there yet, Budensiek said. He said he expects more charges in Martin County and that other jurisdictions could also bring charges.

entry.title: One-year emergency contract sets phased MARTY transit return in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: One-year emergency contract sets phased MARTY transit return in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Following a brief pause, the Martin County Board of Commissioners announced on Tuesday that the county has reached a resolution to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit services. The county says it has reached a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC to begin the phased restoration of public transportation services following an abrupt disruption due to a contract breach by the prior vendor. Last month, MARTY public transit services in Martin County abruptly stopped after its operator withdrew from its contract due to rising operating costs. This left many people without a regular bus service. The county now says it will be taking a phased approach to resuming operations, prioritizing riders who rely on ADA paratransit services, then working towards restoring fixed-route services. See also: Delray Beach says new Florida law will block St. Patrick’s Day, Pride events For those who with disabilities who cannot use regular fixed-route bus services, ADA paratransit services are expected to resume on Thursday, Nov. Details regarding scheduling and reservations are available at 772-463-2822 , the county says. A start date for restoration of full services has yet to be announced. Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer, said Ash Beecher, Martin County Transit Administrator. We recognize the disruption this has caused for our riders and the broader community, and we are working to reestablish service in a thoughtful, coordinated manner.

entry.title: Delray Beach Veterans Day ceremony honors service with message of unity and appreciation
entry.summary: The message at the Veterans Day ceremony held in Delray Beach was that unity and appreciation are the best way to honor the brave men and women who have fought for freedom. Dozens gathered Wednesday inside the vintage gym at Old School Square in the heart of Delray Beach to commemorate those who have served the country. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Delray Beach honors veterans with message of unity The ceremony featured several speakers who talked about the sacrifices men and women in uniform go through, along with a performance from the Plumosa School of the Arts choir. The choir took the stage with two special songs honoring veterans' bravery. WPTV's Delray Beach reporter Victor Jorges connected with James Bassa, a former Marine, whose message focused on how we can all come together, put differences aside and show appreciation to those who served. 'Anyone who wakes up in the morning and says, 'I'm gonna join a force that fights for freedom, for people I don't even know, people I may never meet.' I think they realize there has to be something different about those people. That motivates me to do more and help people understand more what veterans really are,' Bassa said. We also asked him what we can do every day to honor those who fought for the country. 'Show understanding, feel mutual admiration; no matter what our conflicts are, disagreements, we have the ability to always show love,' Bassa said. entry.summary: A special program at Atlantic Community High School in Delray Beach gives students a look at what it's like to be a 911 dispatcher and a chance to graduate ready to step straight into the career. Students are learning to stay calm, ask the right questions and gather critical details for first responders. On one recent simulation, the voices sounded like a real emergency, but it was all practice. Victoria Simpson, a senior, is one of the students training to field those calls. 'It can be any extra thing, so clothing, weapons, any extra info that you can get that can help the officers or anyone that's arriving on scene,' Simpson said. Her classmate Liliana Munoz, also a senior, works the other side of the line, coming up with emergencies to put those skills to the test. 'We definitely do really hard calls with each other,' Munoz said. Simpson and Munoz are two of 28 students currently training to become certified 911 dispatchers. Michael Byrd, the school's criminal justice teacher, said the course mirrors professional training. 'It gives some real-world experience with us using the simulators. It also teaches them teamwork, communication, and gets them ready for the career field,' Byrd said. 'This is the same course an adult would take to become a 911 dispatcher.' Students will test for their certification at the end of the school year. If they pass, they become career-ready and could begin working as a dispatcher immediately.

entry.title: Martin County to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit service
entry.summary: Martin County will begin restoring public transportation services this week after securing a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC. The announcement comes after the county's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement last month, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County begins restoring MARTY transit service The county said Tuesday that it will take a phased approach to restoring MARTY service after what officials described as an abrupt disruption caused by a contract breach involving the previous vendor. ADA paratransit service will be the first to return, with operations expected to resume Thursday. The service is available to eligible riders with disabilities who are unable to use regular fixed-route buses. MARTY customer service representatives are contacting active registered paratransit riders directly about the resumption of service. Riders can call 772-463-2822 for information about scheduling and reservations. As buses are prepared and drivers become available, the county said it will begin restoring fixed-route service, starting with the heavily traveled U.S. 1 corridor. The Indiantown route will also be among the priorities as service returns. 'Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer,' Martin County Transit Administrator Ash Beecher said. Beecher acknowledged the disruption has affected riders and the broader community and said the county is working to reestablish service in a coordinated manner. During the interruption, United Way of Martin County helped coordinate transportation for people with critical travel needs. The county said additional routes will return as buses and drivers become available. Start dates, schedules and rider instructions will be announced as each phase is finalized. Residents can find updates through Martin County's transit website or call transit customer service at 772-463-2860 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday.

entry.title: More workers say extra work is a must to cover holiday costs this year
entry.summary: As the holidays approach, many workers say it's adding pressure to budgets that are already stretched thin. Between gifts, travel and hosting, a new survey reveals how some are planning to cover the cost. New research from resume.io found 56% of workers have considered changing jobs or seeking a higher salary because of the cost of living or holiday expenses, while more than 53.6% have taken on or plan to take on extra work to cover holiday costs. WATCH: Workers look to additional employment hours to cover holiday expenses More workers say extra work is a must to cover holiday costs this year The study reveals at least one in four workers plan to borrow money to get through the holidays by either using credit cards or Buy Now Pay Later methods. Some also plan to lean on family and friends for financial support. While gifts are often seen as the biggest holiday expense, everyday costs are the top reason workers are taking on extra work. Nearly 23% say covering food and household expenses is their main reason, ahead of paying for Christmas gifts or existing debts or bills.

entry.title: Lighthouse for the Blind teaches skills that help people navigate independently in West Palm Beach
entry.summary: Learning to navigate without relying on sight requires skills many people may never have considered, from using a white cane to technology that reads or magnifies what's on a computer screen. At Lighthouse for the Blind of the Palm Beaches, Treasure Coast Okeechobee in West Palm Beach, those tools are helping people who are blind or visually impaired build greater independence. The organization serves people ranging from babies to seniors across five counties, executive director Lisa Stella told WPTV. For children, that can include activities designed to be sensory-oriented and inclusive in the community. Walker put on a blindfold and attempted a mobility exercise with Elizabeth Prus, Lighthouse for the Blind's youth services director. Prus instructed Walker to sweep the cane back and forth roughly the width of his shoulders as he walked. The cane provided information about objects in his path, including a chair and a kitchen island. 'This is a tool that people who are visually impaired use to navigate environments,' Prus said. The training can begin at a young age. 'We start with little kids, teaching them how to use a cane so that way they can travel independently,' Prus said. For Walker, temporarily navigating without sight offered a firsthand look at how a white cane can provide information about the environment around him. entry.title: School bus crashes into Okeechobee County home after collision; no injuries reported
entry.summary: A school bus veered into a home Wednesday morning after crashing with another vehicle, the Okeechobee County School District said. District officials said preliminary information indicates the driver of the other vehicle failed to stop at a stop sign, causing the collision. The impact sent the school bus into a nearby residence. No students were on the bus at the time of the crash. Officials said no one was injured, including the bus driver, the occupants of the other vehicle and the people inside the home. Officials did not immediately provide additional details about the crash, including its location and whether any citations were issued.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home
entry.summary: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home. entry.title: Martin County to establish some quiet zones to combat train noise - WFLX
entry.summary: Martin County to establish some quiet zones to combat train noise    WFLX
entry.article_text: To combat complaints over train horns, Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to enact some quiet zones in the county. A motion was first made to turn all 27 railroad crossings into quiet zones, but then a second motion narrowed the scope. That second motion passed 3-2. This vote comes after County Commissioners had unanimously voted against quiet zones last year. Opponents of quiet zones talked about safety, while supporters said it was a quality of life issue. “The horn all day and all night. And as I’m listening to that noisy disruption, I can visualize the intersection with four gates down, deployed, and cars safely behind them with that horn pointlessly bothering people,” said Doug Farley, a quiet zone supporter. The areas that will first be worked on to become quiet zones will be two crossings at County Line Road and Skyline Drive in Jensen Beach. The third is along Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound near Mariner Sands. The city of Stuart recently received a $1.86 million grant to enhance rail corridor safety. Lucie County has established a quiet zone in the southern end of the county at three crossings. In Palm Beach County, both Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens recently set up quiet zones.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council approved the site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One , clearing another step for the project planned near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The council held a brief discussion before approving the plan, which calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet on city-owned land. The development would include the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. The stadium is proposed to stand 61 feet tall. Its LED scoreboard could reach 85 feet, while field-light poles could rise to 135 feet. The project is planned in four phases, beginning with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The site-plan approval comes as the city advances related zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. The city’s agenda listed those measures for second reading Monday. Staff recommended approval of the site plan subject to recording a replat; the project also has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. RELATED: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC , a United Soccer League League One team. The club is expected to begin play in 2027, with matches at the new stadium planned to begin in 2028. The venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. The stadium is part of the broader Walton & One redevelopment, envisioned as a mix of residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the district in 2022 and that the stadium is intended to help spur development there. Parking for stadium events would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement. The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site . The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published project terms, the developer could be reimbursed for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million.

The third is along Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound near Mariner Sands.The city of Stuart recently received a $1.86 million grant to enhance rail corridor safety.St. Lucie County has established a quiet zone in the southern end of the county at three crossings.In Palm Beach County, both Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens recently set up quiet zones.

entry.title: Dolphins place QB Malik Willis on injured reserve, sidelining him at least 4 games
entry.summary: The Miami Dolphins placed Malik Willis on injured reserve on Tuesday, sidelining the quarterback for at least four games. Willis has been dealing with a nagging groin injury that appeared to significantly limit his mobility in last weekend's 19-9 loss to the Detroit Lions . He said after the game his groin felt a little tight,' and coach Jeff Hafley echoed those words. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Dolphins QB Malik Willis placed on IR; Zach Sieler out for season 'It was tight today, and you could see it,' Hafley said last Sunday. You could see he couldnt really open up. There were a couple plays where I give him credit. He pulled it and he ran and he got us yards and he got out of trouble against a good defensive line. But you could see he just wasnt quite able to go full speed. Willis has completed 121 of 208 passes with six touchdowns and six interceptions this season for the 1-7 Dolphins. The Ringer first reported the news, saying it is not expected to be a season-ending injury. Backup Kyle McCord, who the Dolphins acquired in August from Green Bay, will be in line to start this week at Indianapolis. McCord spent the 2025 season on the practice squad of the Philadelphia Eagles, who drafted him in the sixth round a year ago. The Packers signed him on Jan. 20. He went 46 of 70 for 446 yards with four touchdowns and no interceptions while getting sacked six times in three preseason games with Green Bay. The Dolphins also placed defensive lineman Zach Sieler on IR on Tuesday after he suffered a ruptured biceps against Detroit.

entry.title: Dolphins lose veteran defensive tackle Zach Sieler for rest of season to ruptured biceps, AP source says
entry.summary: Miami Dolphins veteran defensive lineman Zach Sieler ruptured his biceps in the team's 19-9 loss to the Detroit Lions last weekend and will undergo season-ending surgery, a person familiar with the injury told The Associated Press on Tuesday. The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because neither the team nor Sieler announced the injury. ESPN first reported the injury, saying that it happened on the first play of the game on Sunday. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Dolphins QB Malik Willis placed on IR; Zach Sieler out for season The expected recovery timeline for the injury is five to six months, meaning Sieler will miss the rest of the Dolphins' season. He played the entire game on Sunday, recording one quarterback hurry and a tackle while aiding a Dolphins front that successfully pressured Jared Goff for much of the game. Sieler has 24 tackles, seven tackles for loss and two sacks this season, which is his eighth in Miami. He is the only player older than 30 on Miami's roster, which is the youngest in the NFL, and first-year coach Jeff Hafley has praised his leadership throughout the season. 'It's valuable to me. It's valuable to our young players,' Hafley said in October. 'To have a guy like that around the youth of this team and having a guy that I can lean on, because not only does he do all that, but hes one of the best people ever. Theres not a much better person out there than Zach Sieler.'

entry.title: Stuart bed races put fun on wheels to help Martin County families facing homelessness
entry.summary: Beds will be rolling down Flagler Avenue in Stuart as Family Promise of Martin County brings its annual Bed Races back to Sailfish Ballpark, turning an unusual competition into a community effort to help families with children facing homelessness. The free event is scheduled for Saturday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Sailfish Ballpark, 600 SE Flagler Ave. Why are people racing beds down a Stuart street? Teams turn beds into racing machines, with runners pushing a rider toward the finish line. But behind the costumes, competition and laughs are a serious mission. Madeleine Bozone Greenwood, executive director of Family Promise of Martin County, said the organization works to prevent and end family homelessness in Martin County. 'We serve parents with children that are here in Martin County,' Greenwood said. 'We provide shelter, transitional housing. A path to return to home ownership or their own rental housing.' Family homelessness can be difficult to see Pastor Chad Fair, board chair of Family Promise of Martin County, said homelessness does not always look the way people might expect. 'We kind of think that it hits just those people we see on the street corner, but it's families, it's nurses, it's school teachers, it's people that are integral in our community and do the work with our kids, with our families, and they're experiencing homelessness,' Fair said. Family Promise says its work includes homelessness prevention, shelter and services designed to help families find stable housing while keeping parents and children together. That work gives the bed races a literal connection to the organization's mission: The race may be entertaining, but the bed represents something every family needs at the end of the day, a safe place to sleep. entry.summary: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now    WPEC
entry.article_text: A day after Jensen Beach residents told Martin County commissioners that flooding forced them from their homes, families can go to Hoke Library for recovery help while they wait for word on federal aid. The flood recovery center is open Wednesday even though regular library services are closed for Veterans Day. State agencies and local nonprofits are there to connect residents with recovery resources, and the county says more agencies and services will be added throughout the week. At Tuesday’s commission meeting, residents pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned. Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes and that assessment teams planned to visit each one to document the damage. Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

entry.article_text: Following a brief pause, the Martin County Board of Commissioners announced on Tuesday that the county has reached a resolution to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit services. The county says it has reached a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC to begin the phased restoration of public transportation services following an abrupt disruption due to a contract breach by the prior vendor. Last month, MARTY public transit services in Martin County abruptly stopped after its operator withdrew from its contract due to rising operating costs. This left many people without a regular bus service. The county now says it will be taking a phased approach to resuming operations, prioritizing riders who rely on ADA paratransit services, then working towards restoring fixed-route services. See also: Delray Beach says new Florida law will block St. Patrick’s Day, Pride events For those who with disabilities who cannot use regular fixed-route bus services, ADA paratransit services are expected to resume on Thursday, Nov. Details regarding scheduling and reservations are available at 772-463-2822 , the county says. A start date for restoration of full services has yet to be announced. Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer, said Ash Beecher, Martin County Transit Administrator. We recognize the disruption this has caused for our riders and the broader community, and we are working to reestablish service in a thoughtful, coordinated manner.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners revisit proposed train quiet zones - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners revisit proposed train quiet zones    WPTV
entry.article_text: The debate over train horns in Martin County is back before county commissioners Tuesday morning as residents continue pushing for quiet zones along the Florida East Coast Railway.Commissioners are scheduled to hear an update from Public Works staff at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county's evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones along the railroad.Quiet zones would eliminate the requirement for trains to routinely sound their horns at designated crossings, provided those crossings meet federal safety requirements. Train engineers would still be able to sound their horns when necessary for safety.For neighbors living near the tracks, the issue comes down to finding a balance between safety and quality of life."Safety considerations may not be as important, but they need to have the ability to sound that horn," said Glenn Malone of Hobe Sound, "If they can regulate it down just a bit so the option for safety is still viable."Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor.The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones."We don’t have a problem with that. We just don’t want the inherent noise all day and night long," said Jeffry Aderman of Hobe Sound, "All these big counties around us have quiet zones and here we are in this beautiful quiet, quaint little area and we’ve got train bars blowing 24/7."At a March 11, 2025, meeting, commissioners decided not to pursue quiet zones after reviewing options presented by county staff.However, following continued concerns from residents, commissioners revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility.Tuesday's presentation will outline the potential risks and benefits of quiet zones, along with the safety requirements and improvements that would be necessary to establish them in Martin County.Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and provide direction to staff on how to move forward.WPTV will continue following the discussion and any decisions made by county leaders.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.
