entry.title: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding - WPTV
entry.summary: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding    WPTV
entry.article_text: Residents and farmers in western St. Lucie County are seeking answers and long-term drainage solutions after historic flooding left homes, farms and roads underwater last week.The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear concerns from people in the area, including farmers, residents and representatives from Save the Chimps. District members said the drainage system can handle only so much water during an extreme rainfall event and discussed engineering as part of a possible long-term plan.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Some of the hardest-hit areas are now seeing significant improvement, including Save the Chimps in western St. But residents and farmers say they want to know what can be done to reduce the risk of similar flooding during the next extreme rainfall event.For one resident, the flooding has already changed how they view their future in the area."I will be selling my house cause I am not going to risk my investment," the resident said during Monday's meeting.Water control district hears concerns from western St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear from people affected by the flooding.Farmers, residents and representatives of Save the Chimps attended as district members discussed the drainage system and the scale of last week's flooding.President Steve Cassens said there are limits to what the existing system can handle when extraordinary amounts of rain fall in a short period."If we have a rainfall event like that, my personal feeling is you can have gates open, shut, it doesn't matter," said Cassens. "We can manage water maybe 3, 4, 5, 6 inches. We can't manage water in the quantities that we got."District officials also discussed maintaining waterways and ditches, including concerns about a creek in Western Fort Pierce that serves as a primary drainage route. The district said it systematically cleans ditches within its boundaries.The district said it could examine engineering as part of developing a long-range plan.Conditions improve at Save the ChimpsSave the Chimps, a sanctuary in western St. Lucie County, was among the places hit hard by the flooding.WPTV previously reported that staff members had to use drones to deliver food to chimpanzees because several roads through the sanctuary were underwater.When WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache returned days later, staff said conditions had significantly improved."A short 40 hours after that, we're almost completely dry on our roads," said Mark Yohannan.The improvement came after days of challenges caused by standing water at the sanctuary.West Fort Pierce farmer raises concernsThe concerns extended beyond residential neighborhoods.Justin Akerley, who helps operate Saint Lucie Farm Preserve in west Fort Pierce, spoke later Monday at a Port St. Lucie City Council meeting after attending the water control district meeting.Akerley told council members he believes continued development is adding pressure to the area's drainage infrastructure."I just spent my morning in a meeting with the North St. Lucie River Water Control District trying to figure out what we can do to alleviate the water issues, and there's really no right answer except for stop building," Akerley said.Akerley shared a video with WPTV showing flooding at Saint Lucie Farm Preserve, a working agritourism farm operated by Akerley and Michael Hale. The farm produces hay, cut flowers, beef and assorted vegetables and hosts community agricultural events.Akerley told council members the consequences extend to other farms and families."I've got friends that have calves dying that are flooded; they can't get out," he said. "It's a terrible, terrible situation for everybody. There's people that have lost their homes."He urged city leaders to reconsider the effect future development could have on flooding and drainage."Just please reconsider because it's not a good situation for everybody, and it's only gonna get worse," Akerley said.Officials consider what comes nextDuring Monday's Port St. Lucie City Council meeting, Councilman David Pickett also called for greater scrutiny of flooding and the city's stormwater infrastructure.Pickett said he sent two memos to the city manager earlier in the week addressing floodwaters and wants the city to expedite a planned stormwater study rather than wait until 2029.He also raised concerns about flooding in Tradition and called for the city to examine stormwater systems before distributing certain stormwater fees to community development districts.Meanwhile, the North St. Lucie River Water Control District has said engineering options can be assessed as officials consider a long-term plan.For residents and farmers still recovering from last week's flooding, those discussions are now turning toward a larger question: what can be done before the next extreme rainfall event?This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: One-year emergency contract sets phased MARTY transit return in Martin County - cw34.com
entry.summary: One-year emergency contract sets phased MARTY transit return in Martin County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Following a brief pause, the Martin County Board of Commissioners announced on Tuesday that the county has reached a resolution to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit services. The county says it has reached a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC to begin the phased restoration of public transportation services following an abrupt disruption due to a contract breach by the prior vendor. Last month, MARTY public transit services in Martin County abruptly stopped after its operator withdrew from its contract due to rising operating costs. This left many people without a regular bus service. The county now says it will be taking a phased approach to resuming operations, prioritizing riders who rely on ADA paratransit services, then working towards restoring fixed-route services. See also: Delray Beach says new Florida law will block St. Patrick’s Day, Pride events For those who with disabilities who cannot use regular fixed-route bus services, ADA paratransit services are expected to resume on Thursday, Nov. Details regarding scheduling and reservations are available at 772-463-2822 , the county says. A start date for restoration of full services has yet to be announced. Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer, said Ash Beecher, Martin County Transit Administrator. We recognize the disruption this has caused for our riders and the broader community, and we are working to reestablish service in a thoughtful, coordinated manner.

entry.title: Stuart bed races put fun on wheels to help Martin County families facing homelessness - WFLX
entry.summary: Stuart bed races put fun on wheels to help Martin County families facing homelessness    WFLX
entry.article_text: Beds will be rolling down Flagler Avenue in Stuart as Family Promise of Martin County brings its annual Bed Races back to Sailfish Ballpark, turning an unusual competition into a community effort to help families with children facing homelessness. The free event is scheduled for Saturday from 10 a.m. at Sailfish Ballpark, 600 SE Flagler Ave. Teams turn beds into racing machines, with runners pushing a rider toward the finish line. But behind the costumes, competition and laughs are a serious mission. Madeleine Bozone Greenwood, executive director of Family Promise of Martin County, said the organization works to prevent and end family homelessness in Martin County. "We serve parents with children that are here in Martin County," Greenwood said. "We provide shelter, transitional housing. A path to return to home ownership or their own rental housing." Pastor Chad Fair, board chair of Family Promise of Martin County, said homelessness does not always look the way people might expect. "We kind of think that it hits just those people we see on the street corner, but it's families, it's nurses, it's school teachers, it's people that are integral in our community and do the work with our kids, with our families, and they're experiencing homelessness," Fair said. Family Promise says its work includes homelessness prevention, shelter and services designed to help families find stable housing while keeping parents and children together. That work gives the bed races a literal connection to the organization's mission: The race may be entertaining, but the bed represents something every family needs at the end of the day, a safe place to sleep. Paige Cortes, director of operations for Family Promise of Martin County, said spectators can attend Saturday's event for free . "This Saturday, bed races 10 to 1 at the Sailfish Ballpark," Cortes said. "So we are ready for fun too, and you can join us in the race to end childhood homelessness." The event combines the spectacle of beds on wheels with the broader goal of connecting Martin County residents with an issue that can sometimes remain largely invisible. For working families facing a housing crisis, Fair said homelessness can affect people who are already contributing to the community every day. That gives Saturday's race a purpose beyond deciding which team can push its bed across the finish line fastest. It gives residents an opportunity to learn about family homelessness in Martin County and the organizations working to help families regain stable housing. entry.title: Martin County to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit service
entry.summary: Martin County will begin restoring public transportation services this week after securing a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC. The announcement comes after the county's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement last month, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County begins restoring MARTY transit service The county said Tuesday that it will take a phased approach to restoring MARTY service after what officials described as an abrupt disruption caused by a contract breach involving the previous vendor. ADA paratransit service will be the first to return, with operations expected to resume Thursday. The service is available to eligible riders with disabilities who are unable to use regular fixed-route buses. MARTY customer service representatives are contacting active registered paratransit riders directly about the resumption of service. Riders can call 772-463-2822 for information about scheduling and reservations. As buses are prepared and drivers become available, the county said it will begin restoring fixed-route service, starting with the heavily traveled U.S. 1 corridor. The Indiantown route will also be among the priorities as service returns. 'Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer,' Martin County Transit Administrator Ash Beecher said. Beecher acknowledged the disruption has affected riders and the broader community and said the county is working to reestablish service in a coordinated manner. During the interruption, United Way of Martin County helped coordinate transportation for people with critical travel needs. The county said additional routes will return as buses and drivers become available. Start dates, schedules and rider instructions will be announced as each phase is finalized. Residents can find updates through Martin County's transit website or call transit customer service at 772-463-2860 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday.

entry.title: Martin County signs emergency contract to restore MARTY bus services - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County signs emergency contract to restore MARTY bus services    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County has signed a one-year emergency contract to restore the MARTY bus services, which will resume in phases. The service ended abruptly on Oct. 8 after the last vendor, Martin County Transit LLC, canceled services, citing rising costs of fuel and maintenance. The county signed the emergency contract with MTM Transit, which has operated these buses in the past. The first phase begins Thursday and will prioritize eligible riders with disabilities who cannot use the regular fixed-route bus service. For details on scheduling and reservations, residents should call 772-463-2822. As for regular services, there is still no official start date. The county is working to restore buses and rehire bus drivers who were let go by the previous vendor.

But his attorney is questioning the state's evidence, telling investigative reporter Katie LaGrone she hasn't seen proof of her client's wrongdoing beyond a voter card the state sent him even though he was ineligible to vote. entry.article_text: A Tampa father accused of voting illegally is now behind bars — one of 20 defendants charged with voter fraud as part of the state's latest sweep. But his attorney is questioning the state's evidence, telling investigative reporter Katie LaGrone she hasn't seen proof of her client's wrongdoing beyond a voter card the state sent him even though he was ineligible to vote.WATCH KATIE LAGRONE'S REPORT BELOW: In a Hillsborough County courtroom recently, Donta White sat in the inmate section, dressed in an orange jumpsuit, his expression stoic. This court appearance was about scheduling his trial, but for the people waiting for the 44-year-old to return home, the consequences of his latest arrest have already settled in."I thought it was a prank. There's officers here to arrest you for voting? He's like, 'I didn't do it,'" said Taquilla Allen, White's girlfriend. She's helping to care for his two young children while he remains in jail."It's been rough, but you know, we're just gonna take it a day at a time," Allen said.The state is accusing White of illegally voting. At the time, the convicted felon was still serving a 10-year probation for grand theft when, according to a press release issued by Florida's Attorney General's Office, White signed a state form warning him not to register or vote until after he completed his sentence.But according to prosecutors, White submitted two voter registration applications falsely claiming his voting rights had been restored, and then voted early in the 2024 general election. White is now charged with illegal voting and two counts of false swearing.A spokesperson for the AG's office said White admitted to authorities that he registered and voted, but his attorney, Lynley Flagler, is questioning the state's case."There is no clear-cut evidence that would support the fact that he actually went to the polls and voted himself," Flagler said.In addition, despite White not being eligible to vote because of his felony conviction, Flagler says the state sent him a voter ID card as if he was eligible."I feel that there's an entrapment issue. They want to prosecute voting, but they have not put any checks and balances in place to let people know when they're able to vote and when they can't vote," Flagler said.While a voter ID card does not, by itself, grant someone the right to vote, under Florida law certain convicted felons can get their voting rights restored once they complete their sentence, including probation. In White's case, his illegal voting charges triggered a violation of probation, which is how he landed back in jail."He runs a body shop. He's just, overall, really changed his life. So to see him in this position saddens me on a personal level as well as a professional level," Flagler said.Questions around voter eligibility for convicted felons aren't new in Florida. Ron DeSantis announced the arrests of 20 former felons who cast a ballot despite having disqualifying convictions. Several said they thought they could vote."What we discovered from a review of all those cases was there was more confusion than fraud," said Ramon De La Cabada, a Florida criminal defense attorney who co-chairs a committee formed after those arrests.De La Cabada believes White's case may be another example of that confusion — as is the recent arrest of Astrid Navarette Quintana. She's sitting in a Lee County jail after the state charged her for voting as a non-citizen. LaGrone recently investigated her case and found she's a permanent resident, married to a U.S. veteran and was also sent a voter ID card. When asked why voters shouldn't be responsible for knowing if they're eligible to vote, De La Cabada responded, "Absolutely, but I think the better question is why isn't the government creating better communication about eligibility? What you're finding in all these cases is massive confusion as to eligibility."Donta White's jury trial is set for early next year. He faces up to 15 years in prison for illegally voting and 30 years for his probation violation, which stemmed from his recent voting charges.In the meantime, he and his family remain apart, waiting for what's next."Who would throw their life away to vote? That's what it all boils down to," his girlfriend said. "It's petty, but we're dealing with it."

entry.title: Drowsy driving risks in focus as data shows hundreds of truck crashes on Florida's Turnpike
entry.summary: Drowsy driving can be dangerous for anyone behind the wheel, but fatigue involving a large commercial truck can have deadly consequences. During Drowsy Driving Prevention Week , crash data from the Florida Department of Transportation and Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration is putting renewed attention on the risks of driver fatigue, including here in Palm Beach County. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Drowsy driving puts truckers and motorists at risk on South Florida roads In 2025, West Palm Beach recorded 51 reported truck crashes, resulting in one fatality and 23 injuries, according to the data provided to WPTV. The numbers are even larger along Florida's Turnpike. There were 451 reported truck crashes, resulting in 21 fatalities and 245 injuries. Statewide data also points to the morning commute as a key period for truck crashes. Nearly 20% of reported truck crashes occurred between 6 a.m. and 9 a.m. Fatigue can affect a driver's reaction time, concentration and ability to make quick decisions. Those risks are especially concerning when the driver is operating a large commercial vehicle. Federal hours-of-service regulations limit how long commercial drivers can remain behind the wheel and require rest periods. But regardless of how much driving time remains under those limits, drivers are responsible for stopping when fatigue makes continuing unsafe. The message during Drowsy Driving Prevention Week is straightforward: recognize the warning signs of fatigue and don't try to push through them. For truck drivers and other motorists alike, getting off the road and resting could prevent a serious or deadly crash.

entry.title: President Donald J. Trump International Airport named cheapest major U.S. airport for parking
entry.summary: Paying to park at the airport can eat up a good chunk of your travel budget. But one airport in South Florida was just named the cheapest major U.S. airport for parking. In an analysis by Florida Rentals, President Donald J. Trump International Airport in West Palm Beach ranked as the No. 1 least expensive major airport in the country for parking in a study of 'America's Most Expensive Airport Parking'. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida airport named one of the cheapest for parking in the U.S. Drivers will pay about $56 a week for general airport parking. The next least expensive major airport in Florida for parking is Miami International Airport . Parking at MIA will set drivers back at about $129 per week. Tampa International Airport came in as the most expensive parking airport in Florida. The weekly cost to leave your vehicle at TPA is roughly $168. Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood was second on the list at about $140. Orlando International and Southwest Florida International in Fort Myers came in around $133 for weekly parking The study, which examined parking rates at 50 of the busiest airports, found parking at all of Florida's largest airports is cheaper than the average airport cost, which is roughly $215 for parking a week or about $30 a day. LaGuardia was named the most expensive major airport in the U.S. to park for a week, costing drivers close to $525.

entry.title: Businesses impacted by Military Trail closure after Learjet crash can apply for grants of up to $5,000
entry.summary: Starting Thursday, Palm Beach County is making $250,000 available to help businesses and nonprofits that lost revenue after the Nov. 1 Learjet crash forced the partial closure of Military Trail near Greenacres. The Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners approved funding for the Military Trail Business Interruption Grant Program on Tuesday. County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo initially launched the program Nov. 2 under local emergency authority. PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: $250K in grants for Palm Beach County businesses impacted by Learjet crash Eligible businesses and nonprofits can receive a one-time grant of up to $5,000, while funding remains available. County officials said the closure of Military Trail near the crash site disrupted businesses by limiting access for customers and deliveries. The county's Department of Housing and Economic Development will administer the grants. Businesses can use the money for operating expenses including rent, payroll, utilities and essential inventory. The county will use an applicant's latest filed business tax return to estimate revenue losses based on a 30-day interruption. Grants will be awarded on a first-come, first-served basis until the $250,000 is exhausted or all eligible applicants have been served. Who is eligible? The eligible area stretches along Military Trail from Broadway Street on the south to Kelly Drive and Sussex Avenue on the north. Businesses and nonprofits must have been operating at a physical location within the designated area before Nov. 1. Applicants must also certify that the road closure disrupted their operations or access and that they intend to continue or resume operations. The county will verify addresses using the official program map. How to apply Applications and full program criteria will be available Thursday, Nov. 12, on the Palm Beach County Department of Housing and Economic Development website. Applicants will need to submit: A signed application A W-9 Their latest filed business tax return Proof of the business address Photo identification for the authorized signer Applicable Sunbiz documentation A business tax receipt or documentation showing an exemption Awards are capped at $5,000 for each eligible business or nonprofit.

entry.title: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050 - WPEC
entry.summary: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050    WPEC
entry.article_text: As the Treasure Coast prepares for decades of growth, water managers face a critical question: How will the region supply enough freshwater for more people while protecting the farms, waterways and wildlife that also depend on it? Water is a necessity that is being planned for at all times, years in advance. With the explosive growth in population unfolding now, the plan is even more critical. The South Florida Water Management District’s 2026 Upper East Coast Water Supply Plan looks ahead to 2050, outlining future needs in Martin and St. Lucie counties and northeastern Okeechobee County. The district says the region’s limited freshwater resources make conservation and alternative water supplies essential to planning for that growth. What we’re seeing is about a 36-percent increase in the population in the planning area by 2050, said Carolina Maran, Chief of District Resiliency with SFWMD, describing a population approaching three-quarters of a million people. The demand for water, however, is not necessarily increasing at the same rate, Maran says. Demand for water supplied to homes and businesses, along with commercial, landscaping, and recreational uses, is expected to rise. Agricultural water use, which is the region’s largest category, is projected to decline. See also: WPB police ask public for information on sidewalk assault outside Hook Fish and Chicken Meeting the shifting needs will depend on more than population forecasts. It will also require infrastructure, efficient water use, and planning for uncertain conditions, including drought and storms. Inside a University of Florida laboratory in Fort Pierce, Dr. Sandra Guzman and her team study how water moves through soil and across different land uses. Guzman is an Associate Professor of Smart Irrigation and Hydrology with the UF/IFAS Agricultural and Biological Engineering department. A demonstration table with sand and simulated farm fields shows how water’s movement changes depending on the ground beneath it. In another area, there are charts demonstrating how immediate communication can connect area farmers with real-time agriculture and weather data. I always tell my team: water is a blessing and a curse, Guzman said. The challenge is not simply whether water is available. Its quality also determines how it can be used. We suffer from a lot of issues regarding deficit of water because it’s not only the volume of water; it’s also the quality of water, Guzman said. That creates a balancing act: supplying people and farms while protecting the lagoons, estuaries, and wildlife that depend on the region’s water resources. The district’s approach includes alternative water sources, expanded treatment and storage, and conservation. What that means is that investing in reuse, investing in efficient water uses, and also alternative water sources like the Floridan Aquifer, Maran said. Projects described in the plan include reverse-osmosis treatment, reclaimed-water expansions, and stormwater storage. In coming years, some of the infrastructure needed to support future demand must still be built. SFWMD describes the plan as a framework for local governments, utilities, agricultural operations, and other water users to guide water supply decisions. Its recommendations are intended to inform local comprehensive plans, facility work plans and ordinances. Having a plan, however, does not guarantee that every project will be completed on time. Carrying it out will require follow-through by the communities and water providers preparing for growth. On farms, part of the solution is knowing more precisely when crops need water, and how much of it. Guzman’s team works on tools that help farmers measure soil moisture and irrigate more efficiently, directing water where crops need it. The research connects decisions made in the field to the broader challenge of stretching the region’s water supply. So, in this lab, we work for that: every single drop of water that is coming out of whatever aquifer or freshwater system becomes food to your table, Guzman said. As the Treasure Coast grows, its water future will depend both on the infrastructure communities build and on how efficiently people use the supplies already available. entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County animal shelter is urgently seeking homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency 'Empty the Shelters' adoption event on Nov. 13 and 14. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13, and Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: MARTY bus service begins phased return in Martin County after monthlong shutdown - WFLX
entry.summary: MARTY bus service begins phased return in Martin County after monthlong shutdown    WFLX
entry.article_text: MARTY public transportation is beginning a phased return in Martin County after more than a month without regular bus service, starting with ADA paratransit before service expands to the U.S. Highway 1 and Indiantown routes, according to the county. The restoration will not happen all at once. Martin County said additional service will be added as buses are prepared and drivers become available. The county has not announced a date for full MARTY service to return. For riders who rely on public transportation to get to work, buy groceries or reach medical appointments, the phased restart offers some relief after weeks of limited transportation options. MARTY riders were left scrambling Oct. 8 when the county’s transit provider abruptly stopped service. One rider, Joe, told WFLX at the time that he received no warning. For him, losing bus service was more than an inconvenience. He told WFLX that injuries limited his mobility and made finding another way to get around difficult. “I’ve had two broken necks, three broken backs. I can’t feel my feet, so I’m not getting anywhere,” he said. As the shutdown continued, United Way of Martin County stepped in to help residents who had lost their usual transportation. Carol Houwaart-Diez with United Way of Martin County said the organization contacted the county and offered assistance through Ride United, a program that helps provide transportation for critical needs. “We made the call to the county administrator and said, ‘Hey, how can we help?’” Houwaart-Diez said. “And we have a ride program that helps provide critical services in our community, and they said, ‘Please help us.’” Through Ride United, the nonprofit began scheduling Lyft rides for people who needed to make essential trips. Houwaart-Diez said United Way has helped 108 individual clients with 754 rides during the MARTY disruption. Those trips included transportation to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and physical therapy, according to United Way. The temporary transportation solution could not help everyone. Houwaart-Diez said the Lyft vehicles being used through the program were generally unable to accommodate people who are fully wheelchair-bound. “For those that were fully wheelchair bound, we couldn’t help them, which made me sad,” she said. “We did look into to see if we could do that.” The limitation makes the return of ADA paratransit an important first step for riders with disabilities who could not use the temporary Lyft option. Martin County said ADA paratransit is expected to return first, followed by the U.S. Highway 1 and Indiantown MARTY routes. United Way plans to continue providing other transportation assistance as MARTY service is restored. “Once that starts, we still will be able to provide the other services until everything gets back up in full gear,” Houwaart-Diez said. “I’m not sure how long that’s going to be, though.” Martin County said it will add service as buses are prepared and drivers become available. A date for the complete restoration of MARTY service has not been announced. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: MARTY bus service begins phased return in Martin County after monthlong shutdown
entry.summary: MARTY public transportation is beginning a phased return in Martin County after more than a month without regular bus service, starting with ADA paratransit before service expands to the U.S. Highway 1 and Indiantown routes, according to the county. WATCH: MARTY bus service begins returning in Martin County MARTY Bus Service in Martin County: Phased Return Begins The restoration will not happen all at once. Martin County said additional service will be added as buses are prepared and drivers become available. The county has not announced a date for full MARTY service to return. For riders who rely on public transportation to get to work, buy groceries or reach medical appointments, the phased restart offers some relief after weeks of limited transportation options. MARTY shutdown left riders without regular transportation MARTY riders were left scrambling Oct. 8 when the county's transit provider abruptly stopped service. One rider, Joe, told WPTV at the time that he received no warning. 'No warning at all. Nothing. Zero,' Joe said. For him, losing bus service was more than an inconvenience. He told WPTV that injuries limited his mobility and made finding another way to get around difficult. 'I've had two broken necks, three broken backs. I can't feel my feet, so I'm not getting anywhere,' he said. United Way steps in with more than 750 rides As the shutdown continued, United Way of Martin County stepped in to help residents who had lost their usual transportation. Carol Houwaart-Diez with United Way of Martin County said the organization contacted the county and offered assistance through Ride United, a program that helps provide transportation for critical needs. 'We made the call to the county administrator and said, 'Hey, how can we help?'' Houwaart-Diez said. 'And we have a ride program that helps provide critical services in our community, and they said, 'Please help us.'' Through Ride United, the nonprofit began scheduling Lyft rides for people who needed to make essential trips. Houwaart-Diez said United Way has helped 108 individual clients with 754 rides during the MARTY disruption. Those trips included transportation to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and physical therapy, according to United Way. entry.title: Palm Beach County Thanksgiving pies help feed local seniors for a week
entry.summary: Palm Beach County residents can take one Thanksgiving task off their list while helping feed a neighbor in need through Pie It Forward , a fundraiser benefiting Meals on Wheels of the Palm Beaches. Meals on Wheels Special Events Director Maura Sartory said local chefs from restaurants and country clubs donate pies that are sold through the campaign. Proceeds from each pie sold help feed a senior for one week. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Time is running out to Pie It Forward for Palm Beach County seniors 'We sell them online now through Nov. 18, and each pie we sell is available for pickup that Tuesday of Thanksgiving week,' Sartory said. 'You get a pie and the proceeds feed a senior for a week.' The campaign includes traditional Thanksgiving favorites such as pumpkin, pecan and apple pies, along with key lime pies. Orders are available through Nov. 18, although organizers say pies can sell out before the deadline. A pie without the pie People who will be traveling for Thanksgiving or simply don't need another dessert can still participate. Sartory said Pie It Forward offers a virtual pie, which allows people to make a donation without receiving a physical pie. 'A lot of people travel during the holidays, so they can still support,' Sartory said. 'We have a way they can buy a virtual pie, which is simply a donation. No physical pie is received, and you feed a senior for a week.' And there is one additional benefit to the virtual version. When WPTV's T.A. Walker asked Sartory how many calories were in a virtual pie, her answer was simple: 'Zero.' Students and Girl Scouts pitch in The community effort extends beyond the chefs making the pies. Students from the Palm Beach School for Autism help assemble the boxes used for the fundraiser. 'Our students train in a number of Duffy's restaurants, and we're helping Meals on Wheels, kind of putting the boxes together and just helping this great cause,' Patrick Pierre Jr. said. Girl Scouts are also lending a hand by decorating boxes with Thanksgiving messages for the people who receive them. Melinda Glasco of Girl Scouts of Southeast Florida said the project is a natural fit with the organization's mission. 'Part of the Girl Scout mission is making the world a better place, and this is a great way to partner with some amazing organizations and do just that,' Glasco said. entry.title: Lighthouse for the Blind teaches skills that help people navigate independently in West Palm Beach
entry.summary: Learning to navigate without relying on sight requires skills many people may never have considered, from using a white cane to technology that reads or magnifies what's on a computer screen. At Lighthouse for the Blind of the Palm Beaches, Treasure Coast Okeechobee in West Palm Beach, those tools are helping people who are blind or visually impaired build greater independence. The organization serves people ranging from babies to seniors across five counties, executive director Lisa Stella told WPTV. For children, that can include activities designed to be sensory-oriented and inclusive in the community. Learning to navigate with a white cane One of the skills taught at the Lighthouse is how to use a white cane to navigate an environment. During WPTV's visit, Shining A Light reporter T.A. Walker put on a blindfold and attempted a mobility exercise with Elizabeth Prus, Lighthouse for the Blind's youth services director. Prus instructed Walker to sweep the cane back and forth roughly the width of his shoulders as he walked. The cane provided information about objects in his path, including a chair and a kitchen island. 'This is a tool that people who are visually impaired use to navigate environments,' Prus said. The training can begin at a young age. 'We start with little kids, teaching them how to use a cane so that way they can travel independently,' Prus said. For Walker, temporarily navigating without sight offered a firsthand look at how a white cane can provide information about the environment around him. Technology provides another tool for independence The Lighthouse also helps clients use technology designed to make computers more accessible to people who are blind or have low vision. Brandon Butzberger demonstrated ZoomText Fusion, software he uses on a computer. 'It's called ZoomText Fusion,' Butzberger said. 'It's a software that has the screen reading (narration) capabilities that Tekesha is showing, as well as magnification.' Tekesha Saffold also demonstrated audio software she uses to navigate her computer. entry.title: Treasure Coast woman loses second home in 2 years after devastating Fort Pierce flooding - WPTV
entry.summary: Treasure Coast woman loses second home in 2 years after devastating Fort Pierce flooding    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Treasure Coast woman who lost her home two years ago to a tornado from Hurricane Milton has lost another home to devastating flooding in Fort Pierce."I'm starting to feel like I'm invincible at this point," says Terry Polk as she watched the debris pile of drywall and ruined furniture in front of her home get bigger.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The water in her home was measured in feet, not inches, as the heavy rain in the first weekend of November flooded her block."We were actually in the house," Polk said. "When we were wading around, like around knee-deep water, I started getting scared."She said they were rescued by kayaks and returned when the water receded, leaving so much damage. "You know, to keep your focus, you just have to realize there are people out there that have it way worse. There are people out there that are so much worse, you know, and I have to be thankful that we got out with our lives," she said. Two years ago she was living in the Spanish Lakes community of St. Lucie County when Hurricane Milton's winds created widespread tornadoes. One of the twisters, an EF3, struck the community, killing six people and destroying homes, including Terry's. "Terry is one of the most amazing people I've met," said friend Cindy McGee. "She's very strong, does a lot for the community, a lot for the neighborhood." Polk said she has flood insurance, but the damage is so extensive, she's not sure if there is enough coverage to fix everything.

entry.title: 2 northbound lanes of Military Trail reopened near Learjet crash site in Greenacres
entry.summary: Two northbound lanes of Military Trail in Palm Beach County were reopened to traffic Thursday, 11 days after a fatal Learjet crashed at the site. The Florida Department of Transportation said they worked Wednesday to repair utilities and to fill the crater left by the plane crash. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Northbound Military Trail reopened near Learjet crash site Crews worked overnight and into Thursday morning to open the northbound lanes, which were previously closed from 10th Avenue to Forest Hill Boulevard. FDOT said in a Facebook post that crews plan to pave southbound lanes Thursday. Starting Thursday, Palm Beach County is making $250,000 available to help businesses and nonprofits that lost revenue after the crash forced road closures this month. Nine people were killed when the Learjet, which departed Austin, Texas, en route to the Bahamas, crashed near Greenacres earlier this month. No one on the ground was seriously injured.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new 6,000-seat soccer stadium in December
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie is getting closer to welcoming its first professional soccer team , with a groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat stadium scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12. Port St. Lucie Sports Club announced Thursday that construction will begin at Walton One, where the stadium will sit on approximately six acres. Port St. Lucie council approves 6,000-seat professional soccer stadium The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027, and the new stadium is expected to serve as more than just a place to watch soccer. Plans call for a year-round destination where families and community members can gather for entertainment and other events. The development group will fully fund construction of the stadium and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land. 'From day one, we knew this had to be about much more than building a soccer club,' said Gustavo Surez, founder and CEO of Port St. Lucie Sports Club. 'We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape.' The groundbreaking ceremony will begin at noon on Dec. 12, bringing together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., featuring food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages. The club says more details about the event will be announced in the coming weeks.

entry.title: Nikki Haley rules out 2028 run, warns Republicans to ‘hear the signs’
entry.summary: Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley announced this week that she does not intend to run for president in 2028, four years after an unsuccessful bid for the Republican nomination. Nikki Haley reiterated that decision in an interview with CNBC this week. Haley told CNBC that Republicans need to hear the signs after the party suffered major losses in last weeks midterm elections. I am not running in 2028, but I will continue to talk about the things that I care about, Haley said in an interview with CNBC . I will continue to push good policy. I will continue to support good candidates, and we want a strong America. She added she does not have a favored candidate for 2028, saying the Democrats have a 'talented' slate of candidates. RELATED STORY | Democrats are most excited to support three candidates for 2028 Haleys 2024 campaign struggled to gain traction as Donald Trump secured the GOP nomination for a third consecutive presidential election. Although Haley served in the Donald Trump administration as U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, she became a prominent critic of him during the campaign. Although Haley struggled to win over the partys conservative base, she attracted support from some moderate Republicans, including Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins. While many initially expected Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis to emerge as Donald Trumps strongest challenger in 2024, Haley ultimately mounted the most sustained opposition to him. She finished second in the New Hampshire primary and went on to win Vermonts primary. Still, her 97 delegates were a fraction of the more than 2,000 Donald Trump accumulated during the primary campaign. With Haley ruling out a 2028 bid, several other prominent Republicans have yet to fully address their plans. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are among the names being discussed as potential candidates, though neither has formally entered the race. entry.title: Delray Beach veteran says he's nearly been hit 9 times, wants red-light camera installed
entry.summary: A Delray Beach resident says reckless drivers have made him scared to cross the road connecting his neighborhood, and he's asking for a red-light camera to make people think twice about speeding. Marine Corps veteran Rolando Fernandez says he has almost been hit nine times in a single month simply trying to cross the road. He lives at the Bridge View community on Lake Ida and Petal roads. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Delray Beach veteran seeks red-light camera after near-misses crossing road 'I don't want to get in my car and just cross the street, so I don't get plowed by somebody who doesn't want to stop for a red light,' Fernandez said. He says drivers have been hostile toward him along the way. 'I've been given the finger. The guy has even gone through the light, stopped, rolled down his window, and told me, 'Don't have a heart attack',' Fernandez said. Fernandez said the near-misses have taken a toll. 'To the point that I asked the Lord to help me safely (cross the road) because these people, everybody's in a hurry,' Fernandez said. He believes a red-light camera installed by the Florida Department of Transportation would be a fix. 'People unfortunately understand only pain, whether it is physical or financial. You run that light, and it costs you $200 and two points on your license, you'll think about not only this light you're running, but in all the places,' Fernandez said. Fernandez said he reached out to the Florida Department of Transportation and U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel, but he couldn't find answers, so he turned to WPTV. The fear of getting hit has even cut into his daily walks with his service dog, Scout. He says other residents share his concern. 'We have a lot of people on this side, elderly people. They cross because we have the lake over there and stuff to walk around there. ... I see them when they walk in the street because they know what's coming,' Fernandez said. This court appearance was about scheduling his trial, but for the people waiting for the 44-year-old to return home, the consequences of his latest arrest have already settled in. 'I thought it was a prank. Like, what do you mean? There's officers here to arrest you for voting? He's like, 'I didn't do it,'' said Taquilla Allen, White's girlfriend. They want to prosecute voting, but they have not put any checks and balances in place to let people know when they're able to vote and when they can't vote," Flagler said.While a voter ID card does not, by itself, grant someone the right to vote, under Florida law certain convicted felons can get their voting rights restored once they complete their sentence, including probation. In White's case, his illegal voting charges triggered a violation of probation, which is how he landed back in jail."He runs a body shop. He's just, overall, really changed his life. So to see him in this position saddens me on a personal level as well as a professional level," Flagler said.Questions around voter eligibility for convicted felons aren't new in Florida. Ron DeSantis announced the arrests of 20 former felons who cast a ballot despite having disqualifying convictions. Several said they thought they could vote."What we discovered from a review of all those cases was there was more confusion than fraud," said Ramon De La Cabada, a Florida criminal defense attorney who co-chairs a committee formed after those arrests.De La Cabada believes White's case may be another example of that confusion — as is the recent arrest of Astrid Navarette Quintana. She's sitting in a Lee County jail after the state charged her for voting as a non-citizen. LaGrone recently investigated her case and found she's a permanent resident, married to a U.S. veteran and was also sent a voter ID card. When asked why voters shouldn't be responsible for knowing if they're eligible to vote, De La Cabada responded, "Absolutely, but I think the better question is why isn't the government creating better communication about eligibility? entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service
entry.summary: Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony. WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Veterans honored at Port St. Lucie event Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service 'It's all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it's very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there,' Greene told Trim. Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized. 'It's good to get the recognition that we didn't get,' Thomas said. The Port St. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on. That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel. 'I'm one of the few left. I just thank God. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they're really important to support the veterans,' Vogel told Trim. Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. Vincent Lavelle Jr. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

entry.title: New women's high-tech golf league makes its Palm Beach Gardens debut at the SoFi Center
entry.summary: A new type of golf kicked off in Palm Beach Gardens, as the high-tech Women's Tomorrow's Golf League made its debut and brought a different kind of experience to the sport. Golfers compete in Womens Tomorrows Golf League Some of the world's best female golfers competed inside the SoFi Center. The new women's golf league combines technology with traditional golf, bringing a whole new energy to the game. The league features 25 of the world's top female golfers competing on five teams: the Atlanta Drive GC, Boston Common Golf, Los Angeles Golf Club, Motor City Golf Club and New York Golf Club. Golfers compete in the WTGL in Palm Beach Gardens When you think of professional golf, you're probably thinking beautiful fairways, sand traps and lots of sun. Throw in a giant simulator screen and mix it all up, and that's where you get the WTGL. Instead of playing on a traditional golf course, players hit shots into a massive simulator screen before moving to a real green to finish each hole. When it's time to chip or putt, they move to a short game area. The matches are fast-paced, featuring 15 holes of team competition inside the SoFi Center. Every player has 40 seconds to hit a shot. Every player is mic'd up, so you can hear them talking strategy or trash. There's also a referee, and the greens rotate and can be contoured to make holes harder.

Before his flight, Orloff shared some of his memories from his years of flying. 'It's amazing when I think about it. I've flown over thousands and thousands of miles of water. All I ever saw was water, clouds and rain, thunder and lightning, but I made it, as you see,' Orloff said. Orloff's flight was organized by retired U.S. Coast Guard Cmdr. Phil Perry and Aamro Aviation.

entry.title: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050 - WPEC
entry.summary: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050    WPEC
entry.article_text: As the Treasure Coast prepares for decades of growth, water managers face a critical question: How will the region supply enough freshwater for more people while protecting the farms, waterways and wildlife that also depend on it? Water is a necessity that is being planned for at all times, years in advance. With the explosive growth in population unfolding now, the plan is even more critical. The South Florida Water Management District’s 2026 Upper East Coast Water Supply Plan looks ahead to 2050, outlining future needs in Martin and St. Lucie counties and northeastern Okeechobee County. The district says the region’s limited freshwater resources make conservation and alternative water supplies essential to planning for that growth. entry.article_text: Lucie County animal shelter is urgently seeking homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency “Empty the Shelters” adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it’s facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman’s arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.summary: A handwritten note reading 'HELP US' helped police in Central Florida find children hiding inside a home during a domestic disturbance. Kissimmee Police Department officers said they responded to a domestic disturbance involving Andre Janard Smithson on Oct. 26. Family members told police that children were inside the residence and feared for their safety. Officers used a drone to search the home and located the children hiding in a room. Police said the children safely left the residence while Smithson was distracted. Smithson eventually surrendered peacefully, police said. Kissimmee police said he is now facing charges of false imprisonment and an outstanding active warrant. The-CNN-Wire 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros. Discovery Company. entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County beaches are recovering after a nor’easter and king tides caused erosion along the coastline, with officials noting improvements in shoreline conditions. Erosion officials said water levels had risen almost as high as a sign at Tracking Station Beach, but the sand has already begun shifting back into place. Waves and high water significantly impacted the county’s coastline. “This is a great example of coastal resistance at work,” officials said. Johnnie Sabin, a coastal specialist with Indian River County’s Department of Natural Resources, said the shoreline at Tracking Station Beach is already showing signs of recovery. “Much of the sand we placed on the beach, while it shifted briefly, has already been returning. I mean, these beaches, these berms, there's a lot more space. They're a little higher, a little wider so folks aren't in jeopardy to visit the beaches anymore,” Sabin said. Sabin explained that Tracking Station Beach experienced five to ten feet of erosion. He credited dune plants for helping hold the sand together and said the county’s Sector Five Beach Restoration Project performed as expected. “Luckily because of the sand being there, it buffered all private properties, the roads, all the infrastructure we care about and it did its job,” Sabin said. While major parks in the central beach area are open, some beach access points remain closed. Sabin advised visitors to check the county’s website before heading out. The county plans to repair beach parks where needed. Beachgoer Erin Dobrinski has noticed some of the damage but it's not stopping her from enjoying the beach. “You know down the Sebastian riverfront area down there there's a part of the sidewalk completely blocked off and if you peep around you can see it's all eroded,” Dobrinski said. Sabin said there are no current plans for another major sand project, but with more king tides expected, the county is closely monitoring the coast. There is good news for sea turtles, as Sabin reported that less than one percent of nests were affected by the erosion event. “They're resilient creatures. This is not their first rodeo. And they're going to continue doing what they do,” Sabin said. Erosion officials are asking the public to help protect the shoreline by picking up trash and debris. What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground. "It's completely covered," Chirico said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Chirico pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Chirico, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Chirico said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new 6,000-seat soccer stadium in December
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie is getting closer to welcoming its first professional soccer team , with a groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat stadium scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12. Port St. Lucie Sports Club announced Thursday that construction will begin at Walton One, where the stadium will sit on approximately six acres. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new pro soccer stadium in December The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027, and the new stadium is expected to serve as more than just a place to watch soccer. Plans call for a year-round destination where families and community members can gather for entertainment and other events. The development group will fully fund construction of the stadium and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land. 'From day one, we knew this had to be about much more than building a soccer club,' said Gustavo Surez, founder and CEO of Port St. Lucie Sports Club. 'We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape.' The groundbreaking ceremony will begin at noon on Dec. 12, bringing together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., featuring food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages. The club says more details about the event will be announced in the coming weeks.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce woman is recovering from devastating flooding that destroyed her childhood home, marking the second time in two years she has lost everything. Terri Polk, who previously lost her home in the Spanish Lakes community to a tornado during Hurricane Milton, moved back into her childhood home to care for her mother, who has Alzheimer’s. Now, that home has been severely damaged by floodwaters. “The heart throb of our whole family is here,” Polk said. Polk shared that the house, built by her parents, has always been a central place for her family. “My mother’s door has always been open to everyone in the family,” she said. “This breaks your heart because I grew up in this house, I actually grew up here.” Last Monday, floodwaters rushed into the home, leaving behind destruction. “In the morning, the water was up to the tops of the beds,” Polk said. By the time the water receded, the damage was done. Polk’s belongings, including her bed and bookcases, now lie in a pile on the front lawn. Polk said she hasn’t slept in days as she tries to process the loss. The home is now filled with dehumidifiers, and Polk’s flood insurance won’t cover all the damages. Despite the challenges, she remains determined to rebuild. “No is not the answer; quit is not an option,” she said. “I’m not going to give up."
