entry.article_text: Yvette Drucker is beginning a new chapter in public service as Palm Beach County's new Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller, taking over one of the county's most significant constitutional offices.Sworn in Tuesday, Drucker steps into the role following a turbulent period for the clerk's office under former Clerk Mike Caruso. She now oversees approximately 670 employees and an $87.4 million budget while serving as the county's chief financial officer, treasurer and auditor.WATCH REPORT BELOW: In an exclusive interview with WPTV's Joel Lopez, Drucker discussed her leadership priorities, her transition from Boca Raton City Council, questions about her experience and the future of the county's controversial investments in Israel bonds."It's a new day for the clerk's office. It's been a little bit of a challenging time for the individuals that work here. I have a phenomenal staff. They've kept it afloat, so my goal is to really listen, evaluate, and then execute what we can do to make it better," Drucker said.Drucker is the first Hispanic woman to hold the position of Palm Beach County clerk and comptroller.For her, the milestone carries personal significance. Her parents immigrated from Cuba in 1957, and she says her journey represents the American dream."It's really important to me because my parents are immigrants. I still have a living grandmother who's 91, and she's still here, and I am the American dream," she said.Drucker is also the first college graduate in her family. She credits her parents with instilling the values that helped shape her career."My parents didn't really have a lot of schooling. They had good work ethic and integrity. And they respected people, so really important for me to continue to inspire and lead in a way that others can look up to me and that they can also make their impact in the world."Her swearing-in ceremony was an especially meaningful moment, with her parents by her side."My mom held the Bible while I got sworn in. My dad anchored her to the left, and they're just so proud," Drucker said.She described the ceremony as a defining moment in both her professional and personal life."A surreal moment, but I took it all in. I've learned that you have to really be in the moment and be present," she said. "A really defining moment in my career and in my life."Drucker is no stranger to public service. She spent six years on the Boca Raton City Council, serving as deputy mayor and vice chair of the city's Community Redevelopment Agency before reaching her term limit."Six years you were with the City of Boca Raton, so why clerk of courts?" Lopez asked Drucker."I was term limited, so we do have term limits in the city, and after a couple of years, like about one year, a little over one year ago, I was just approached by a former clerk to look at this position," Drucker said. "I was not done with public service. I was born to serve, and I've been doing that since my student government days, back in high school and middle school."She said the clerk's position offered an opportunity to bring together her experience in business, government and community service."I have a background in human resources and out of corporate America, I worked for ADP TotalSource. I did 14 years there, so I also had an advocacy background and then my government. So it's a good way of marrying in my private sector with my public sector and my community service sector all in one," Drucker said.Although her time on the Boca Raton council ended, Drucker made clear that her commitment to public service had not.She said she wanted to finish her responsibilities in Boca Raton before beginning her new role, making sure the work she had started was completed.In the same week, she ended her time with Boca Raton and started with Palm Beach County, a process she said usually takes two months to transition."I pride myself with not missing meetings in six years and attending and participating, and I finished everything that I started," Drucker said.Drucker inherits an office with hundreds of employees and says she wants to build on the experience already in place while identifying opportunities to improve operations.Her message to employees is straightforward: public service must come before politics."This is a new day for this office. This office has been working, but we can make it work better for the people that we serve," she said. "I will stand by what I've been saying all along, people over politics, people over party, and definitely people over power, and that's just kind of the way that I've always led with a lot of heart. And a lot of integrity for the work that I do."Drucker says her first 100 days will focus on understanding how each department operates, reviewing the budget and identifying ways to make the office more efficient."I want to understand every department, their inner workings, the budget. We also have to understand Amendment 3, which obviously passed, and we have to respect the will of the voters and also just like I said earlier, listen, really evaluate and then execute how we're gonna serve the public," she said.She also emphasized the importance of putting the right people in the right positions."This is a public-facing operation. It's really important for me to have the right people in the right places so that we can continue serving the public," Drucker said.While some have questioned whether her background adequately prepares her for the office's court administration, accounting and auditing responsibilities, Drucker acknowledged she does not expect to know everything immediately."We have a chief of legal, runs the operations and we have subject matter experts and I'm not gonna tell you that I know everything on day one," she said. "But the way that I operate and the way that I've conducted myself throughout the city and throughout my career, I will learn as needed and will make changes as needed."She says she plans to rely on the office's existing leadership and experienced employees as she continues the transition. She recently hired her chief of staff and also the executive administrator to the clerk, but those names have not been made public."Also, this office has a deputy clerk who is interim clerk, Ms. Shannon Ramsey-Chessman, who's been incredible, and she has institutional data, and I believe that we're going to be a great team as we, you know, continue to take one day at a time."One of the biggest questions facing Drucker, who identified herself as Jewish, is the county's investment in Israel bonds.Palm Beach County has approximately $1 billion invested in the bonds, making it the largest investor in the world. The investment became a point of controversy during the campaign, and Drucker had previously expressed support for it.Now in office, she says she plans to take another look at the county's investment strategy, particularly following the passage of Amendment 3.Asked whether she still supports the county investing in Israeli bonds, Drucker said investment decisions must ultimately serve taxpayers."So I say to the public, like any investment portfolio, whether you have your own or you're overseeing an investment portfolio of this size, you always have to evaluate and make sure that your investments are aligned with what is best for the taxpayer base," she said.Drucker said the bonds have served the county well up to this point, but that does not mean the investment should go without review."And now with Amendment 3 passing, we really need to evaluate, and that's something that I'm gonna sit with our director of finance and with our county administrator," she said.She stopped short of committing to either maintaining or eliminating the investment."It's not a yes or a no; it's just, does it continue to make sense? Is this something that we have to evaluate and we always have to evaluate how we invest and how we are using the taxpayer dollar is important."When asked whether she would consider reducing or eliminating the investment if it no longer made financial sense, Drucker said the county would have to evaluate that possibility."Is it safe to say if it didn't make sense, you'd be willing to reduce, if not potentially eliminate this investment?" asked Lopez."If it didn't make sense, we would have to evaluate, correct," said Drucker.She also pointed out that Israel bonds make up only part of the county's broader investment portfolio."Even though we have a large amount in Israel bonds, we have a large portfolio. Seventy-five percent of our portfolio is not invested in Israel bonds," she said.For Drucker, the next step is making sure residents understand how the county's investments work and what they mean for the community."I think education is gonna go a long way," she said.She also pushed back on making the issue political, saying the focus should remain on the county's financial interests and the taxpayers who depend on those investments."I think we're going to leave politics out of it. It's not a political discussion. I think it's really, what are the returns to help the county?" Drucker said.She plans to meet with county officials and review the investment portfolio before making any decisions.Drucker says the transition has been busy, but she is encouraged by the employees already in place and the team she is building around her.She has brought on a chief of staff and an executive administrator to help guide her through the responsibilities of the office.She also thanked the voters and supporters who helped bring her into the position, including those who crossed party lines."I'm just really excited to be here. I think that we're gonna have this office is going to continue to produce amazing things for this community. I'm just so honored," she said. "And I'm just so proud to represent this office, and I really look forward to everything that we have to do."As she begins her tenure, Drucker says her commitment is to serve everyone in Palm Beach County, regardless of political affiliation."This office is here to serve everybody regardless of who and what you are; that's my promise to them," she said.And as for what comes next, Drucker has a simple message:"The best is yet to come, and I believe that," Drucker said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: 'It feels like Lake Okeechobee': Martin County community underwater after years of drainage concerns
entry.summary: What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake. What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County community underwater after years of drainage concerns But for the families who live and work there, the flooding is more than a natural disaster. They say it's a crisis years in the making one they warned officials about as far back as 2018. Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast. Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented. 'All of our pastures ... they're all underwater' Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight. 'It feels like Lake Okeechobee,' she said. Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. 'It's completely covered,' Melissa said. 'All of our pastures ... they're all underwater.' The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers. Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close. And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining it's rising. 'We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising,' she said. Warnings dating back to 2018 For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns. In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm a raised barrier designed to control water flow. That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water. entry.article_text: What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake.What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground.WATCH REPORT BELOW: But for the families who live and work there, the flooding is more than a natural disaster. They say it's a crisis years in the making — one they warned officials about as far back as 2018.Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast.Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented.Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight."It feels like Lake Okeechobee," she said.Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. "It's completely covered," Melissa said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Melissa said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

entry.title: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Martin County Firefighters Union is asking county leaders to reconsider canceling a firefighter hiring class planned for January, saying the department is already short-staffed and the loss of new hires could increase pressure on crews. In a Facebook post, the union said the county canceled the class, which was expected to bring about 25 firefighters into Martin County Fire Rescue . The county cited budget concerns tied to Amendment 3 , according to the union. The union said the department is 17 firefighters short now and could be about 25 short by January as employees retire or leave for other departments. Fewer firefighters mean fewer available personnel to respond to emergencies, increased reliance on mandatory and voluntary overtime, and greater demands placed on the firefighters who remain, the union wrote. The union said its members recently agreed to forgo negotiating a new contract that would have taken effect in October, giving up a cost-of-living pay adjustment to help the county address financial challenges. It said members did so after being assured that Fire Rescue would not be affected by hiring freezes tied to Amendment 3. See also: Bobcat rescued after getting caught in barbed-wire fence near Stuart The union also questioned county administrative pay increases, saying administrative employees received 6% raises in October while firefighters face staffing shortages. The post calls on the Board of County Commissioners and county administrator to move forward with the hiring class. The county was not quoted in the union’s post. Martin County is taking a measured approach to hiring as it evaluates its long-term financial outlook and operational needs. With rising operating costs, inflation, and potential revenue impacts following the passage of Amendment 3 and anticipated SAFER Grant repayment obligations in the upcoming budget cycle, the County is being mindful of additional staffing commitments. While the firefighter recruitment class was planned months before Amendment 3 passed, current fiscal considerations have prompted a review of future hiring. The County is currently taking a soft hiring freeze approach, carefully evaluating vacancies and staffing needs. Maintaining public safety remains a priority for Martin County," the County said in a statement.

entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County animal shelter is urgently seeking homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency 'Empty the Shelters' adoption event on Nov. 13 and 14. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13, and Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: After magical season, Park Vista High School bowling finishes in the top 5 in Florida
entry.summary: In life, we all start somewhere, and for a group of kids, AMF Bowling Alley in Boynton Beach is where it all began. 'I started at a Saturday league here at AMF probably when I was 12,' Jett Kramer, a sophomore bowler at Park Vista High School, said. 'My aunt showed me a youth league here, so I started doing it and have been doing it for five years now,' Mateo Ruiz, a junior bowler at Park Vista High School, said. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Park Vista HS bowling team finishes top five in the state Both young men met at the bowling lanes at AMF as kids and have now forged a deep bond at Park Vista High School. In fact, they're not the only two bowlers from the school who love AMF Bowling; the entire team does. It's their practice court, and it's also the place they knew this year would be special. 'Last year we also had a great team, so I knew our team this year would be just as good if not better,' said Kramer. So, how good were they this year? The team won both the county championship and district championship and qualified for state. 'That was pretty good considering we didn't make it last year; that was pretty much an upset,' co-captain Nate Banks said. 'It was awesome. We all bowled great. We had a phenomenal season; everyone bonded together. It was a phenomenal season,' co-captain Jordan Fein said. The team was on fire all season and finished fifth at state. While it wasn't the finish they'd hoped for, it was a building block for next season. Ruiz finished as a state runner-up. 'It was definitely an amazing moment. I wish I could've gotten first, but I appreciate getting there,' Ruiz said.

entry.title: Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community faces devastation after historic flooding
entry.summary: Residents of Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community are confronting the aftermath of devastating flooding, with gutted homes, piles of belongings lining neighborhood streets and families struggling to figure out what comes next. A week after floodwaters forced residents from their homes, the damage is becoming clearer, leaving some without flood insurance and questioning whether they can afford to rebuild. The flooding has turned once-familiar homes into cleanup projects and left residents facing the loss of belongings, memories and, in some cases, their sense of security. Thomas walked Hoffman through her damaged home, where much of her belongings had been removed and left in piles along the curb. 'I'm all alone. entry.title: 'Bigger than ourselves': Florida Panthers host military appreciation night
entry.summary: Throughout the season, the Florida Panthers host themed nights at some home games. On Thursday, the Cats hosted the Detroit Red Wings for military appreciation night. Despite trailing most of the game, the Florida Panthers pulled off an epic third-period comeback. The Cats tied it up at 4 apiece, then scored in the final minutes to take the lead and send Detroit home with a loss. Watch report from Eleanor Sheahan: 'Bigger than ourselves': Florida Panthers host military appreciation night The Panthers beat the Red Wings 5-4 for their military appreciation game. Outside Amerant Bank Arena, members of the United States Coast Guard and Army welcomed fans before puck drop. Inside, military members and their families got early access to Pantherland for a first look at military appreciation merch. Then on the rink, the Panthers recognized retired Army veteran Joe St. John as their Heroes Among Us honoree of the night. Another army veteran at the game was Scott Sloane. As you get older and you recognize what you did and people serving today and what it takes to service and the sacrifice it takes and then people appreciating that, that's a warm feeling, that really makes you look back at your life a little bit and your service., Sloane said. Sloane is a part of the Panthers Warriors, a hockey club for disabled us military veterans who have served our country and want to play hockey. When you leave the military, some of us lose that camaraderie, and so we have to bring it back, and we do it through this organization, Sloane said. Panthers Warriors started in 2019. Sloane said they play in tournaments and, over the years, have built a strong community that combines veterans and Panther fans. On Thursday Sloane was among the many veterans cheering on the cats. Thank you for your service as well, like hockey it brings us together. It's a collaborative thing. All the military branches work together so that's what we learned from a young age, a collaborative environment and being a part of something bigger than ourselves, Sloane said. The Panthers Warriors are always looking for more players. To learn more, visit their Instagram @ pantherswarriorshockey . The Florida Panthers begin another road trip; they head to St. Louis to play the Blues.

entry.title: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Martin County Firefighters Union is asking county leaders to reconsider canceling a firefighter hiring class planned for January, saying the department is already short-staffed and the loss of new hires could increase pressure on crews. In a Facebook post, the union said the county canceled the class, which was expected to bring about 25 firefighters into Martin County Fire Rescue . The county cited budget concerns tied to Amendment 3 , according to the union. The union said the department is 17 firefighters short now and could be about 25 short by January as employees retire or leave for other departments. Fewer firefighters mean fewer available personnel to respond to emergencies, increased reliance on mandatory and voluntary overtime, and greater demands placed on the firefighters who remain, the union wrote. The union said its members recently agreed to forgo negotiating a new contract that would have taken effect in October, giving up a cost-of-living pay adjustment to help the county address financial challenges. It said members did so after being assured that Fire Rescue would not be affected by hiring freezes tied to Amendment 3. See also: Bobcat rescued after getting caught in barbed-wire fence near Stuart The union also questioned county administrative pay increases, saying administrative employees received 6% raises in October while firefighters face staffing shortages. The post calls on the Board of County Commissioners and county administrator to move forward with the hiring class. The county was not quoted in the union’s post. Martin County is taking a measured approach to hiring as it evaluates its long-term financial outlook and operational needs. With rising operating costs, inflation, and potential revenue impacts following the passage of Amendment 3 and anticipated SAFER Grant repayment obligations in the upcoming budget cycle, the County is being mindful of additional staffing commitments. While the firefighter recruitment class was planned months before Amendment 3 passed, current fiscal considerations have prompted a review of future hiring. The County is currently taking a soft hiring freeze approach, carefully evaluating vacancies and staffing needs. Maintaining public safety remains a priority for Martin County," the County said in a statement.

entry.title: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death - WPEC
entry.summary: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce mother is speaking out after watching body camera footage of the night her 19-year-old daughter was fatally shot in Fort Lauderdale near an Airbnb. She believes her daughter was asking police for help and wants to know whether the officers who first responded could have done more. I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking, said Alacia Ford-Barron, the mother of Myrah Zeigler. She shared the video with CBS12 News. The body camera video shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb. Officers tell everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, were taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park. In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. One officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park. Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help. Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby. An officer reports that shots were fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News is waiting to hear back from Fort Lauderdale police.

entry.title: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050 - WPEC
entry.summary: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050    WPEC
entry.article_text: As the Treasure Coast prepares for decades of growth, water managers face a critical question: How will the region supply enough freshwater for more people while protecting the farms, waterways and wildlife that also depend on it? Water is a necessity that is being planned for at all times, years in advance. With the explosive growth in population unfolding now, the plan is even more critical. The South Florida Water Management District’s 2026 Upper East Coast Water Supply Plan looks ahead to 2050, outlining future needs in Martin and St. Lucie counties and northeastern Okeechobee County. The district says the region’s limited freshwater resources make conservation and alternative water supplies essential to planning for that growth. What we’re seeing is about a 36-percent increase in the population in the planning area by 2050, said Carolina Maran, Chief of District Resiliency with SFWMD, describing a population approaching three-quarters of a million people. The demand for water, however, is not necessarily increasing at the same rate, Maran says. Demand for water supplied to homes and businesses, along with commercial, landscaping, and recreational uses, is expected to rise. Agricultural water use, which is the region’s largest category, is projected to decline. See also: WPB police ask public for information on sidewalk assault outside Hook Fish and Chicken Meeting the shifting needs will depend on more than population forecasts. It will also require infrastructure, efficient water use, and planning for uncertain conditions, including drought and storms. Inside a University of Florida laboratory in Fort Pierce, Dr. Sandra Guzman and her team study how water moves through soil and across different land uses. Guzman is an Associate Professor of Smart Irrigation and Hydrology with the UF/IFAS Agricultural and Biological Engineering department. A demonstration table with sand and simulated farm fields shows how water’s movement changes depending on the ground beneath it. In another area, there are charts demonstrating how immediate communication can connect area farmers with real-time agriculture and weather data. I always tell my team: water is a blessing and a curse, Guzman said. The challenge is not simply whether water is available. Its quality also determines how it can be used. We suffer from a lot of issues regarding deficit of water because it’s not only the volume of water; it’s also the quality of water, Guzman said. That creates a balancing act: supplying people and farms while protecting the lagoons, estuaries, and wildlife that depend on the region’s water resources. The district’s approach includes alternative water sources, expanded treatment and storage, and conservation. What that means is that investing in reuse, investing in efficient water uses, and also alternative water sources like the Floridan Aquifer, Maran said. Projects described in the plan include reverse-osmosis treatment, reclaimed-water expansions, and stormwater storage. In coming years, some of the infrastructure needed to support future demand must still be built. SFWMD describes the plan as a framework for local governments, utilities, agricultural operations, and other water users to guide water supply decisions. Its recommendations are intended to inform local comprehensive plans, facility work plans and ordinances. Having a plan, however, does not guarantee that every project will be completed on time. Carrying it out will require follow-through by the communities and water providers preparing for growth. On farms, part of the solution is knowing more precisely when crops need water, and how much of it. Guzman’s team works on tools that help farmers measure soil moisture and irrigate more efficiently, directing water where crops need it. The research connects decisions made in the field to the broader challenge of stretching the region’s water supply. So, in this lab, we work for that: every single drop of water that is coming out of whatever aquifer or freshwater system becomes food to your table, Guzman said. As the Treasure Coast grows, its water future will depend both on the infrastructure communities build and on how efficiently people use the supplies already available. entry.summary: What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake. What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground. They say it's a crisis years in the making — one they warned officials about as far back as 2018.Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast.Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented.Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight."It feels like Lake Okeechobee," she said.Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. "It's completely covered," Melissa said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Melissa said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

entry.title: One-year emergency contract sets phased MARTY transit return in Martin County - cw34.com
entry.summary: One-year emergency contract sets phased MARTY transit return in Martin County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Following a brief pause, the Martin County Board of Commissioners announced on Tuesday that the county has reached a resolution to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit services. The county says it has reached a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC to begin the phased restoration of public transportation services following an abrupt disruption due to a contract breach by the prior vendor. Last month, MARTY public transit services in Martin County abruptly stopped after its operator withdrew from its contract due to rising operating costs. This left many people without a regular bus service. The county now says it will be taking a phased approach to resuming operations, prioritizing riders who rely on ADA paratransit services, then working towards restoring fixed-route services. See also: Delray Beach says new Florida law will block St. Patrick’s Day, Pride events For those who with disabilities who cannot use regular fixed-route bus services, ADA paratransit services are expected to resume on Thursday, Nov. Details regarding scheduling and reservations are available at 772-463-2822 , the county says. A start date for restoration of full services has yet to be announced. Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer, said Ash Beecher, Martin County Transit Administrator. We recognize the disruption this has caused for our riders and the broader community, and we are working to reestablish service in a thoughtful, coordinated manner.

entry.title: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County beaches are recovering after a nor’easter and king tides caused erosion along the coastline, with officials noting improvements in shoreline conditions. Erosion officials said water levels had risen almost as high as a sign at Tracking Station Beach, but the sand has already begun shifting back into place. Waves and high water significantly impacted the county’s coastline. “This is a great example of coastal resistance at work,” officials said. Johnnie Sabin, a coastal specialist with Indian River County’s Department of Natural Resources, said the shoreline at Tracking Station Beach is already showing signs of recovery. “Much of the sand we placed on the beach, while it shifted briefly, has already been returning. I mean, these beaches, these berms, there's a lot more space. They're a little higher, a little wider so folks aren't in jeopardy to visit the beaches anymore,” Sabin said. Sabin explained that Tracking Station Beach experienced five to ten feet of erosion. He credited dune plants for helping hold the sand together and said the county’s Sector Five Beach Restoration Project performed as expected. “Luckily because of the sand being there, it buffered all private properties, the roads, all the infrastructure we care about and it did its job,” Sabin said. While major parks in the central beach area are open, some beach access points remain closed. Sabin advised visitors to check the county’s website before heading out. The county plans to repair beach parks where needed. Beachgoer Erin Dobrinski has noticed some of the damage but it's not stopping her from enjoying the beach. “You know down the Sebastian riverfront area down there there's a part of the sidewalk completely blocked off and if you peep around you can see it's all eroded,” Dobrinski said. Sabin said there are no current plans for another major sand project, but with more king tides expected, the county is closely monitoring the coast. There is good news for sea turtles, as Sabin reported that less than one percent of nests were affected by the erosion event. “They're resilient creatures. This is not their first rodeo. And they're going to continue doing what they do,” Sabin said. Erosion officials are asking the public to help protect the shoreline by picking up trash and debris. entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. Here’s a county-by-county guide to what’s planned. Palm Beach County Wellington Veterans Day Parade and Ceremony Parade at 8:15 a.m. from Village Hall, 12300 Forest Hill Blvd.; ceremony at 8:30 a.m. at the Wellington Veterans Memorial, Forest Hill and South Shore boulevards. Delray Beach Veterans Day Ceremony 9 a.m at the Vintage Gym at Old School Square, 51 N. North Palm Beach Veterans Day Ceremony 9 a.m. at Veterans Memorial Park, 303 Anchorage Drive. Royal Palm Beach Veteran’s Day Ceremony 9 a.m. to noon at the Royal Palm Beach Cultural Center, 151 Civic Center Way. Palm Beach Gardens Veterans Salute Celebration 11 a.m. at the Veterans Plaza Amphitheater, 10500 N. The program includes a keynote speaker and a performance by the Palm Beach Gardens High School Chorus. Boca Raton’s Red, White & Boca 4 to 7 p.m. at Mizner Park Amphitheater, 590 Plaza Real. The free event includes live music, speakers, a veterans marketplace and a classic car show. Lake Worth Beach Veterans Day Celebration 5 p.m. Martin County Stuart Veterans Day Parade and Ceremony Begins at 10 a.m. on East Ocean Boulevard in Stuart and concludes at Memorial Park. Lucie Veterans Day Ceremony 11 a.m. at Veterans Memorial Park, 2100 S.E. Veterans Memorial Parkway. The free ceremony includes remarks, music, a rifle salute, a flyover and Taps. Seating is limited; attendees are encouraged to arrive early and bring a chair. Fort Pierce Veterans Day Ceremony and lunch Ceremony at 11 a.m. at Veterans Memorial Park, 600 N. A free lunch and live entertainment follow at noon at VFW Post 8058, 3475 Douglas Ave. Indian River County Veterans Day Observance 5:30 p.m. The county calendar lists the event; check the calendar for venue and any additional details. Veterans Meet Up 6 to 8 p.m. A gathering for veterans at Our House Network in Vero Beach, listed on the county calendar. Okeechobee County Okeechobee KOA Veterans Day Celebration 5 to 8 p.m. at Okeechobee KOA RV Resort, 4276 U.S. Central Elementary Veterans Day celebration 8:30 a.m. The school invited families to share photos of veterans.

entry.title: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death - WPEC
entry.summary: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce mother is speaking out after watching body camera footage of the night her 19-year-old daughter was fatally shot in Fort Lauderdale near an Airbnb. She believes her daughter was asking police for help and wants to know whether the officers who first responded could have done more. I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking, said Alacia Ford-Barron, the mother of Myrah Zeigler. She shared the video with CBS12 News. The body camera video shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb. Officers tell everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, were taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park. In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. One officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park. Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help. Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby. An officer reports that shots were fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News did not receive a response from Fort Lauderdale Police before publication. Update : In a statement provided Friday, the department said it remains saddened by the loss of Myrah Zeigler and extends its condolences to her family and loved ones. Police said the lead detective has maintained regular communication with the family and encouraged any concerns about the handling of the case to be addressed directly with the department through its established complaint process. The department declined an interview, citing the active and ongoing investigation.

entry.title: Florida flooding survivors praise heroes who came to their aid
entry.summary: From high-water rescues to the heroes who live next door, people are sharing their stories about the good Samaritans who came to their aid during the recent floods that ravaged our area. Tessie Watts from Riviera Beach says first responders and the mayor of her city pulled her to safety after she fled her home and more than 20 inches of water. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Heroes emerge after historic flooding swamps Palm Beach County, Treasure Coast Nicole Vazquez from Fort Pierce shared with WPTV anchor Hollani Davis that her brother is her hero. She said he helped the family sandbag their home before leaving, then came back by boat to get them out. 'He left, and he came back Tuesday to evacuate us, and then we took shelter with him that night,' says Vazquez. The selfless acts stretched to West Palm Beach, where Miles Bradford and his friend jumped in to help stranded drivers. 'If it was me, I would want someone to get out there and help me,' says Bradford. Long after the water is gone, even though there will undoubtedly be more tough days ahead, it's these acts of kindness that people say they'll remember.

entry.title: FHP trooper-involved shooting incident shuts down I-95 in Indian River County
entry.summary: Interstate 95 in Indian River County is shut down in both directions early Friday morning, creating a major traffic disruption for drivers near the Indian River-St. Lucie County line. On Nov. 12, around 11:20 p.m., FHP said a trooper was involved in a shooting incident on I-95 near mile marker 141. According to FHP, the incident began when the trooper initiated a traffic stop, and the suspect fled, resulting in a pursuit. The pursuit escalated and turned into a gunfire exchange between the trooper and the suspect. Authorities said no troopers were injured during the shooting. FHP said the suspect sustained injuries from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound and was pronounced dead at the scene. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the highway is closed due to the ongoing investigation. All northbound and southbound lanes of I-95 are closed at this time. The southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road is also shut down. Northbound drivers were being directed off I-95 at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers were being directed to exit at Oslo Road. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road is also closed. Officials said all body cam and dash cam video will be reviewed during the investigation. The FDLE will take over as the lead on the investigation. WPTV is working to learn more about when the interstate could reopen.

entry.title: Boca Helping Hands aims to provide Thanksgiving meals for more than 4,000 Palm Beach County families
entry.summary: Boca Helping Hands is asking the community to help provide Thanksgiving meals for more than 4,000 Palm Beach County families through its annual Thanksgiving Box Brigade . The nonprofit is asking donors to contribute $29.72, the cost of a Thanksgiving box that helps provide families facing food insecurity with the ingredients for a holiday meal. WATCH REPORT BELOW: What can a $30 Thanksgiving box become? For families already stretching household budgets, Boca Helping Hands CEO Dr. Andrew Hagen said the added cost of Thanksgiving can make the holiday particularly difficult. 'You know this has been a tough year for a lot of people economically, and we want to make sure they have a good Thanksgiving,' Hagen said. Boca Helping Hands plans to distribute turkeys and Thanksgiving meal boxes to current Pantry Bag Program clients Nov. 21 and 22 at five drive-thru locations in East Boca Raton, West Boca Raton, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach and Lake Worth Beach. Volunteers pack thousands of Thanksgiving boxes Preparing thousands of Thanksgiving meals requires plenty of hands. entry.title: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death - cw34.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce mother is speaking out after watching body camera footage of the night her 19-year-old daughter was fatally shot in Fort Lauderdale near an Airbnb. She believes her daughter was asking police for help and wants to know whether the officers who first responded could have done more. I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking, said Alacia Ford-Barron, the mother of Myrah Zeigler. She shared the video with CBS12 News. The body camera video shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb. Officers tell everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, were taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park. In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. One officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park. Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help. Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby. An officer reports that shots were fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News did not receive a response from Fort Lauderdale Police before publication. Update : In a statement provided Friday, the department said it remains saddened by the loss of Myrah Zeigler and extends its condolences to her family and loved ones. Police said the lead detective has maintained regular communication with the family and encouraged any concerns about the handling of the case to be addressed directly with the department through its established complaint process. The department declined an interview, citing the active and ongoing investigation.

entry.title: Wellington man sentenced to 7 years for $2.3 million fraud scheme involving sham cosmetic surgery clinics
entry.summary: A Wellington man has been sentenced to seven years in federal prison for a fraud scheme that prosecutors say used fake cosmetic surgery clinics and the stolen identities of more than 100 people to obtain millions of dollars from medical lenders. Jacquez Dion Tullis, 42, was sentenced Thursday to 84 months in prison after previously pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. U.S. District Judge Rodolfo A. Ruiz II sentenced Tullis to 60 months for the bank fraud conspiracy charge and a consecutive 24 months for aggravated identity theft. Tullis was also ordered to serve five years of supervised release and pay more than $2.3 million in restitution. The court also ordered a forfeiture money judgment of more than $2.3 million. Prosecutors detail sham medical clinics According to court documents and Tullis' admissions in his plea, Tullis and his co-conspirators created six sham medical clinics between April 2018 and February 2024. The clinics purported to provide cosmetic surgery and other medical services but provided no actual care, prosecutors said. The conspirators registered the clinics with the Florida Department of State using stolen personal information belonging to practicing doctors and other people without their knowledge or consent, according to the Justice Department. Prosecutors said some doctors were falsely identified as clinic owners in applications seeking approval as merchants with medical lenders. Once the clinics were approved, the conspirators submitted fraudulent credit applications in the names of more than 100 people. The applications sought approximately $3.1 million and falsely claimed the money would pay for cosmetic surgery and other medical services. The people whose identities were used did not authorize the applications or receive treatment, prosecutors said. According to the Justice Department, death records showed some of the purported patients had died before the dates they supposedly received medical care. The scheme ultimately defrauded medical lenders of approximately $2.3 million, according to prosecutors. COVID-19 relief fraud Federal prosecutors said Tullis was also involved in a separate scheme targeting a pandemic-era federal relief program. entry.title: Stuart Air Show: What to know about traffic, parking and getting to Witham Field
entry.summary: The Stuart Air Show is preparing to take flight at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area. The air show is celebrating its 37th year at Witham Field. Lee Potter with the Stuart Air Show said this year's event will feature the F-16 demo team along with a variety of other aircraft arriving throughout the week. For drivers, planning the route before leaving home can help make the trip easier. Getting to the Stuart Air Show Drivers coming from Interstate 95 can take the Stuart exit and use Kanner Highway to Monterey Road. Drivers using Florida's Turnpike can take Southwest Martin Downs Boulevard. U.S. 1 and Dixie Highway are also options for reaching Monterey Road. As drivers approach Witham Field, they should follow posted signs and directions from law enforcement. The air show has two drive-in entrances off Monterey Road, with the Martin County Sheriff's Office directing traffic in the area. Where to park General parking is free in designated Stuart Air Show parking areas. Complimentary shuttle service will take visitors from the parking areas to the main gates. ADA parking is also available. Drivers should not create their own parking spots or park outside the designated areas. The best advice: stick with the official parking lots, watch for posted signs and follow law enforcement directions as you approach the air show. WPTV Traffic Reporter Johann Hoffend will be at Witham Field with traffic and transportation information for people heading to the Stuart Air Show.

entry.title: 911 caller said Palm City man was chasing her with guns, newly released video shows - WPEC
entry.summary: 911 caller said Palm City man was chasing her with guns, newly released video shows    WPEC
entry.article_text: A woman who called 911 during a Palm City standoff told dispatchers a man was chasing her with guns and had fired them, according to the call transcript released through a public records request. Please, quickly, the woman said at the start of the call. She told the dispatcher she was running down the street and that the man was so drunk and had tried to get into a car. The call adds detail to the September standoff involving Darrel Abbey, which lasted several hours and brought Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies, SWAT team members and hostage negotiators to the home. In an earlier report, investigators said Abbey allegedly threatened his ex-girlfriend and pointed a gun at her. The woman told the dispatcher Abbey had put a gun to his head and pulled the trigger about an hour and a half earlier. She said the gun did not fire and that he was not in a good state of mind. As she ran, the caller said Abbey turned around and headed back toward the home. She stopped on the side of the road, where she said another woman had pulled over to help her. The caller also told dispatchers there were multiple guns at the property, though she was unsure whether they were inside the house, in a vehicle or in an RV. Newly released sheriff’s office video shows deputies and a tactical vehicle at the property during the response. The footage is partially obscured, and the provided clip does not clearly show Abbey or the events described in the 911 call. See also: 18-year-old dies after being struck by car in St. Lucie County; family raises concerns According to the arrest report, Abbey’s ex-girlfriend went to his home after their breakup. She told investigators he appeared intoxicated and had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts. The report says he brought the guns inside, yelled at her and pointed a gun at her several times. It also says he later tried to get into his vehicle and reached for her phone when he realized she was recording. She ran down the road and called 911. Deputies later tried to contact Abbey at the home, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, according to the arrest report. He was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. The report also identifies him as a convicted felon with a prior vehicular assault conviction in Washington state.

entry.article_text: Collin O’Hara was sentenced to life in prison Tuesday for the 2020 killing of Calvin Bates in Fort Pierce. A jury found O’Hara guilty of second-degree murder on Sept. Lucie County court records. The judge denied the defense’s request for a reduced sentence. O’Hara will receive credit for 3,341 days already served. Fort Pierce police found Bates on a rear patio at an apartment complex at 601 Avenue B on June 12, 2020, with a knife in his neck. He later died during surgery at Lawnwood Hospital. According to the arrest affidavit, a witness told investigators O’Hara accused Bates of being a child rapist before stabbing him. Another witness said she saw O’Hara’s arm move toward Bates’ neck, then saw the knife in Bates’ neck as O’Hara left. Those were witness accounts recorded in the affidavit. See also: 13 state attorneys general ask Supreme Court to uphold Florida's Stop WOKE Act Police said O’Hara fled the scene and was arrested at an Anytime Fitness on Orange Avenue. He denied stabbing Bates during an interview with investigators, the affidavit says.

entry.article_text: A Tampa father accused of voting illegally is now behind bars — one of 20 defendants charged with voter fraud as part of the state's latest sweep. But his attorney is questioning the state's evidence, telling investigative reporter Katie LaGrone she hasn't seen proof of her client's wrongdoing beyond a voter card the state sent him even though he was ineligible to vote.WATCH KATIE LAGRONE'S REPORT BELOW: In a Hillsborough County courtroom recently, Donta White sat in the inmate section, dressed in an orange jumpsuit, his expression stoic. This court appearance was about scheduling his trial, but for the people waiting for the 44-year-old to return home, the consequences of his latest arrest have already settled in."I thought it was a prank. There's officers here to arrest you for voting? He's like, 'I didn't do it,'" said Taquilla Allen, White's girlfriend. She's helping to care for his two young children while he remains in jail."It's been rough, but you know, we're just gonna take it a day at a time," Allen said.The state is accusing White of illegally voting. At the time, the convicted felon was still serving a 10-year probation for grand theft when, according to a press release issued by Florida's Attorney General's Office, White signed a state form warning him not to register or vote until after he completed his sentence.But according to prosecutors, White submitted two voter registration applications falsely claiming his voting rights had been restored, and then voted early in the 2024 general election. White is now charged with illegal voting and two counts of false swearing.A spokesperson for the AG's office said White admitted to authorities that he registered and voted, but his attorney, Lynley Flagler, is questioning the state's case."There is no clear-cut evidence that would support the fact that he actually went to the polls and voted himself," Flagler said.In addition, despite White not being eligible to vote because of his felony conviction, Flagler says the state sent him a voter ID card as if he was eligible."I feel that there's an entrapment issue. They want to prosecute voting, but they have not put any checks and balances in place to let people know when they're able to vote and when they can't vote," Flagler said.While a voter ID card does not, by itself, grant someone the right to vote, under Florida law certain convicted felons can get their voting rights restored once they complete their sentence, including probation. In White's case, his illegal voting charges triggered a violation of probation, which is how he landed back in jail."He runs a body shop. He's just, overall, really changed his life. So to see him in this position saddens me on a personal level as well as a professional level," Flagler said.Questions around voter eligibility for convicted felons aren't new in Florida. Ron DeSantis announced the arrests of 20 former felons who cast a ballot despite having disqualifying convictions. Several said they thought they could vote."What we discovered from a review of all those cases was there was more confusion than fraud," said Ramon De La Cabada, a Florida criminal defense attorney who co-chairs a committee formed after those arrests.De La Cabada believes White's case may be another example of that confusion — as is the recent arrest of Astrid Navarette Quintana. She's sitting in a Lee County jail after the state charged her for voting as a non-citizen. LaGrone recently investigated her case and found she's a permanent resident, married to a U.S. veteran and was also sent a voter ID card. When asked why voters shouldn't be responsible for knowing if they're eligible to vote, De La Cabada responded, "Absolutely, but I think the better question is why isn't the government creating better communication about eligibility? What you're finding in all these cases is massive confusion as to eligibility."Donta White's jury trial is set for early next year. He faces up to 15 years in prison for illegally voting and 30 years for his probation violation, which stemmed from his recent voting charges.In the meantime, he and his family remain apart, waiting for what's next."Who would throw their life away to vote? That's what it all boils down to," his girlfriend said. "It's petty, but we're dealing with it."

entry.title: Military Trail reopens in both directions after repairs following deadly Learjet crash
entry.summary: Military Trail reopened Thursday night in both directions near Greenacres after crews completed roadway repairs following the fatal Learjet crash on Nov. 1, according to the Florida Department of Transportation. FDOT said two northbound and two southbound lanes opened to drivers as of 7:05 p.m. Thursday. Crews spent the past 48 hours repairing the roadway, including paving and striping the road. Sidewalk repairs also began Thursday. Earlier Thursday, FDOT said crews had worked overnight and into Thursday morning to reopen the northbound lanes. This area of Military Trail had been closed between 10th Avenue and Forest Hill Boulevard after the Learjet crash created a large crater in the road. The reopening restores traffic in both directions along the affected stretch of Military Trail. Nine people were killed when the Learjet, which departed Austin, Texas, en route to the Bahamas, crashed near Greenacres earlier this month. No one on the ground was seriously injured.

According to his attorney, he was also sent a voter ID card."I feel that there's an entrapment issue," attorney Lynley Flagler said. "They want to prosecute voting, but they have not put any checks and balances in place to let people know when they're able to vote and when they can't vote."LaGrone is still reviewing the list of the other defendants charged but of the 20 defendants charged, Duval County has the most with four cases, followed by Hillsborough, with three. entry.title: FHP trooper-involved shooting incident shuts down I-95 in Indian River County
entry.summary: Interstate 95 in Indian River County was shut down in both directions early Friday morning, creating a major traffic disruption for drivers near the Indian River-St. Lucie County line. On Thursday, at about 11:20 p.m., FHP said a trooper was involved in a shooting incident on I-95 near mile marker 141. According to FHP, the incident began when the trooper initiated a traffic stop, and the suspect fled, resulting in a pursuit. The pursuit escalated and turned into a gunfire exchange between the trooper and the suspect. Authorities said no troopers were injured during the shooting. FHP said the suspect sustained injuries from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound and was pronounced dead at the scene. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the highway is closed due to the ongoing investigation. All northbound and southbound lanes of I-95 are closed at this time. The southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road is also shut down. Northbound drivers were being directed off I-95 at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers were being directed to exit at Oslo Road. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road is also closed. Officials said all body cam and dash cam video will be reviewed during the investigation. The FDLE will take over as the lead on the investigation. WPTV is working to learn more about when the interstate could reopen.

entry.title: Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community faces devastation after historic flooding
entry.summary: Residents of Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community are confronting the aftermath of devastating flooding, with gutted homes, piles of belongings lining neighborhood streets and families struggling to figure out what comes next. A week after floodwaters forced residents from their homes, the damage is becoming clearer, leaving some without flood insurance and questioning whether they can afford to rebuild. The flooding has turned once-familiar homes into cleanup projects and left residents facing the loss of belongings, memories and, in some cases, their sense of security. WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman returned to Lone Pine after witnessing the flooding begin to speak with residents now trying to recover. Watch report from Michael Hoffman: Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community faces devastation after historic flooding 81-year-old resident loses everything in flooding For 81-year-old Hazeline Thomas, the damage is deeply personal. Thomas walked Hoffman through her damaged home, where much of her belongings had been removed and left in piles along the curb. 'I'm all alone. And all my life saving is on the sidewalk,' Thomas said. She described being trapped inside her home as floodwaters rose around her. Thomas said the water eventually reached her neck before firefighters rescued her by boat. 'The water was up to my neck,' Thomas said. 'So the firefighters, the men, had to pick me up and put me in the boat.' She said rescuers also helped evacuate neighbors across the street. Now, Thomas is facing the financial burden of cleaning out her home. She said she has had to pay people to remove damaged belongings, using money she can hardly afford to spend. entry.title: 'It feels like Lake Okeechobee': Martin County community underwater after years of drainage concerns
entry.summary: What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake. What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground.
