Trump International Airport continued to face flight cancellations and delays Saturday, a day after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop that disrupted air travel across the country. WATCH: Travelers Stranded as FAA Ground Stop Fallout Continues Travelers Stranded as FAA Ground Stop Fallout Continues The FAA's air traffic control system was back at full operations Saturday, but federal officials warned that delays and cancellations would continue as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said airlines expected to return to full schedules by the end of Sunday. The disruption remained significant Saturday. FlightAware reported more than 6,000 U.S. flight cancellations and over 7,000 delays as of Saturday evening. For some South Florida travelers, those numbers translated into hours spent bouncing between airports and transportation options in hopes of simply getting home. Veterans spend hours trying to get home Veterans Karen Matthews and Ron Matthews told WPTV they had been traveling for about 10 hours after their flight from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport to Baltimore was canceled. 'Are we ever gonna get home?' Karen Matthews said. Their attempt to find another flight brought them from Fort Lauderdale to Donald J. Trump International Airport, but another cancellation awaited them. 'To have taken the shuttle bus, the train, the shuttle bus ... and then to get here and it's canceled again,' Karen Matthews said. She summed up the experience simply: 'This is really frustrating.' Traveler: 'I've been eating mints all day' Ron Matthews said the couple had not had a chance to eat during their lengthy trip. 'It's been kind of rough,' he said. 'I've been eating mints all day long just to get by.' Ron Matthews said American Airlines reissued their tickets but did not provide them with meals, transportation assistance or other accommodations. 'No accommodations, just reissuing the tickets,' he said. 'Nothing, no assistance with transportation, no upgrade of seats or anything, not a thing.' For Karen Matthews, reaching home also carried a medical concern. She said she needed to get back to medications she takes for blood pressure and acid reflux. 'I have to control my blood pressure,' she said. 'So yes, it's important.' Karen Matthews said.Their attempt to find another flight brought them from Fort Lauderdale to Donald J. Trump International Airport, but another cancellation awaited them."To have taken the shuttle bus, the train, the shuttle bus ... and then to get here and it's canceled again," Karen Matthews said.She summed up the experience simply: "This is really frustrating."Ron Matthews said the couple had not had a chance to eat during their lengthy trip."It's been kind of rough," he said. "I've been eating mints all day long just to get by."Ron Matthews said American Airlines reissued their tickets but did not provide them with meals, transportation assistance or other accommodations."No accommodations, just reissuing the tickets," he said. "Nothing, no assistance with transportation, no upgrade of seats or anything, not a thing."For Karen Matthews, reaching home also carried a medical concern. She said she needed to get back to medications she takes for blood pressure and acid reflux."I have to control my blood pressure," she said. "So yes, it's important."The nationwide ground stop began Friday afternoon after a telecommunications failure involving air traffic control infrastructure, federal officials said. The stoppage was lifted shortly after 8 p.m. Friday.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a preliminary investigation found the problem occurred while a contractor at a remote FAA facility was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber and working with a router. Travelers with upcoming flights should continue checking directly with their airline for the latest status before heading to the airport. entry.article_text: All northbound lanes were closed on Florida’s Turnpike in Martin County for an hour following a crash involving a tractor-trailer and a pickup truck. Martin County Fire Rescue states the crash happened just before 11 a.m. on Friday near the 137 mile-marker in Palm City. Two drivers involved are said to be safe with no reported injuries, but the Martin County Sheriff's Office said there were minor injuries and significant damage to both vehicles. Martin County Fire Rescue, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office, and the Florida Highway Patrol worked together to clear the debris. The closure caused a backup of nearly 10-mile on the Turnpike. entry.summary: 18-year-old dies after being struck by car in St. Lucie County; family raises concerns    cw34.com
entry.article_text: An 18-year-old man was killed after being struck by a car while walking on North Boulevard in unincorporated St. Lucie County, according to a Florida Highway Patrol crash report. Omari Linzell Williams was walking west in the westbound lane near Lee Boulevard when a Chevrolet sedan traveling west struck him with its front right corner, the report said. The crash was reported at 6:45 p.m. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach, where he was pronounced dead at 9:54 p.m., according to the report. The 30-year-old driver, who is from Vero Beach, was not injured and cooperated with law enforcement, the report said. Neighbors came outside after hearing the crash and provided aid. The Traffic Homicide Investigation is ongoing, FHP said. The report does not say whether any citations have been issued. See also: 13 state attorneys general ask Supreme Court to uphold Florida's Stop WOKE Act Williams’ family said he was walking to a store on the same road where he lived. Relatives are seeking more information about the crash and raising concerns about pedestrian safety on North Boulevard. A candlelight vigil for Williams is scheduled for 6 p.m. 13, at Lakewood Park, 5990 Emerson Ave.

entry.article_text: Somebody's hog has gone rogue, and now Indian River County deputies are trying to bring home the bacon all 250 pounds of it. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is searching for the owner of a hefty domestic boar hog found in the 5600 block of 69th Street. Weighing an estimated 200 to 250 pounds, the four-legged wanderer is currently being housed safely at the sheriff's office farm while deputies work to track down his owner. See also: Indian River County deputies tussle with alligator displaced by heavy flooding But before anyone can claim the hefty hog, they'll need to prove he's theirs. The sheriff's office is asking anyone who recognizes the animal to contact deputies with a photo or description to verify ownership. For now, the hog is safe and sound at the sheriff's office farm, presumably unaware he's the subject of a countywide search. Anyone who believes the boar belongs to them should contact the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

entry.title: 911 caller said Palm City man was chasing her with guns, newly released video shows - cw34.com
entry.summary: 911 caller said Palm City man was chasing her with guns, newly released video shows    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A woman who called 911 during a Palm City standoff told dispatchers a man was chasing her with guns and had fired them, according to the call transcript released through a public records request. Please, quickly, the woman said at the start of the call. She told the dispatcher she was running down the street and that the man was so drunk and had tried to get into a car. The call adds detail to the September standoff involving Darrel Abbey, which lasted several hours and brought Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies, SWAT team members and hostage negotiators to the home. In an earlier report, investigators said Abbey allegedly threatened his ex-girlfriend and pointed a gun at her. The woman told the dispatcher Abbey had put a gun to his head and pulled the trigger about an hour and a half earlier. She said the gun did not fire and that he was not in a good state of mind. As she ran, the caller said Abbey turned around and headed back toward the home. She stopped on the side of the road, where she said another woman had pulled over to help her. The caller also told dispatchers there were multiple guns at the property, though she was unsure whether they were inside the house, in a vehicle or in an RV. Newly released sheriff’s office video shows deputies and a tactical vehicle at the property during the response. The footage is partially obscured, and the provided clip does not clearly show Abbey or the events described in the 911 call. See also: 18-year-old dies after being struck by car in St. Lucie County; family raises concerns According to the arrest report, Abbey’s ex-girlfriend went to his home after their breakup. She told investigators he appeared intoxicated and had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts. The report says he brought the guns inside, yelled at her and pointed a gun at her several times. It also says he later tried to get into his vehicle and reached for her phone when he realized she was recording. She ran down the road and called 911. Deputies later tried to contact Abbey at the home, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, according to the arrest report. He was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. The report also identifies him as a convicted felon with a prior vehicular assault conviction in Washington state.

entry.title: High school senior helps young athletes score big by giving soccer gear to kids in need
entry.summary: Playing sports can get expensive, especially when you have to pay for all the gear. But one high school student is finding a creative way to combine her favorite sport and giving back. Ella Axtell is a senior at The Benjamin School and founded 'Gear for Goals.' WATCH: High school senior scores big by giving soccer gear to kids in need High school senior scores big by giving soccer gear to kids in need 'Gear for Goals is an organization that I go and take used and new soccer gear and equipment, and I take it to kids who are less fortunate,' Axtell said. Axtell donates the soccer gear to centers like Place of Hope, Family First and Quantum House. 'They come in there using their wheelchairs. We play soccer with them in any way that they are. We equip them and it's crazy, they love it so much. They always say how it's able to give them a place to play and give them an advantage to play,' Axtell said. She also hosts clinics to teach kids how to play. 'I love it. I honestly love it because I really do think every kid should have the chance to play and I don't want one kid not to be able to if they don't have the gear,' Axtell said. Gear for Goals is not only helping young athletes in Palm Beach County, but across the world. 'We've gone all over. I went to Costa Rica internationally with St. Mark's and I held four days in that week. I held soccer clinics and each kid got a full entire kit from shirts to cleats,' Axtell said. Axtell said when she came up with the idea for Gear for Goals, she started posting online. We have an Instagram called @ Gear_for_goals , and I send out flyers and post all the time about it. And then I started reaching out to other places that I could have boxes at. So I had one at Palm Beach Gardens Rec Center, Axtell said. I actually was able to host a soccer drive for dressing for charity at St. Mark's, and we raised money, and got a bunch of money for that. And I just spread the word, have an Amazon wish list. I'm just emailing, emailing, emailing. Donations have flooded in, with people giving new and slightly used soccer gear or buying from her online equipment wishlist. 'I just want to continue it. I want to continue it through college. I want to keep going, see how big we can grow and hopefully one day we'll be so big that we'll have clinics all over the world,' Axtell said. While helping kids score goals, Axtell says her goal is to grow the organization. She says they're always looking for donations and volunteers. To donate or learn

entry.title: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter    WPBF
entry.article_text: The parents of Jessica Clinton, a Port St. Lucie teen who died of cardiac arrest in 2003, are hosting a free heart screening event this Saturday at the St. Lucie County Health Department to raise awareness about children's heart health. Jessica Clinton's parents Ray and Cheryl Lalloo are preparing for the event, which is expected to draw about 600 children. He stressed the importance of identifying heart problems early. "You hear it all the time. Kids go to sleep, parents come in the morning, they're not awake, and it's now just infants, or SIDS, it's kids that are 10, 12, 13 years old," Ray Lalloo said. Jessica was 17 years old and at cheerleading practice at St. Lucie West Centennial High School when she went into cardiac arrest. At the time, there were no automated external defibrillators (AEDs) on campus, and Jessica died that day. Her parents said she had undergone two sports physicals in the months before her death, but no heart problem was detected. In response to their loss, Jessica's parents founded the Jessica Clinton MVP Foundation and began offering heart screenings 17 years ago. They said the screenings have helped identify previously undiagnosed heart conditions. Last year, they said about 19 children learned they had a condition that had not been detected before. "We've had a couple of kids with pretty significant diagnoses. You know, things like syndrome, the really bad ones, you know," Ray Lalloo said. Cheryl Lalloo is grateful they were able to offer free screenings. "Blessed is the word, Cheryl Lalloo said. "It makes us feel like we also have a lot more work to do. That there's still kids out there that are still diagnosed." The free screenings are available for children and young adults ages 5 to 20 and include an electrocardiogram (EKG) and a check of vital signs. A cardiologist reviews the results, and an Echocardiogram is available if needed. The Lalloos said close to 650 children have signed up for this year's event. Appointments are booked, but families can call to ask about the waiting list. Organizers said they'll try to fill openings if someone cancels or doesn't show up. Jessica's parents hope their efforts will prevent other families from experiencing a loss like theirs. "The one child could be the next president of our country. It could be the person who invents the cure for cancer. So, every life is important. Children should not die like this," Ray Lalloo said. The event will take place Saturday from 8 a.m. Lucie County Health Department, 5150 NW Milner Drive, Port St. The number to call for scheduling is 772-462-3800. entry.summary: Man dies after going 101 mph, crashing into palm trees in Fort Pierce in I-95 police chase    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 59-year-old DeLand man died when he crashed into palm trees off Interstate 95 after being pursued by Florida Highway Patrol troopers at a high rate of speed on Saturday morning in Fort Pierce. Southbound lanes of Interstate 95 at Mile Marker 128 were closed at 7:45 a.m. near Okeechobee Road, which is State Road 70. A 2020 Volvo S60 was traveling southbound three miles away at Mile Marker 141 at a high rate of speed, according to FHP. A trooper was stationary on the southbound side and clocked the vehicle at 101 miles per hour, FHP said. Troopers attempted to intercept the driver for the traffic violation, but he failed to stop and continued to travel southbound at a high rate of speed, maneuvering in and out of traffic and utilizing the paved shoulders. A trooper attempted a PIT maneuver (Precision Immobilization Technique), which was unsuccessful, north of State Road 70. The driver continued traveling south at a high rate of speed and entered the inside paved shoulder and continued into the grass median, FHP said. The vehicle struck several large palm trees with the left front/driver’s side compartment. He was ejected and was pronounced deceased at the scene, FHP said. entry.title: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new 6,000-seat soccer stadium in December
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie is getting closer to welcoming its first professional soccer team , with a groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat stadium scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12. Port St. Lucie Sports Club announced Thursday that construction will begin at Walton One, where the stadium will sit on approximately six acres. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new pro soccer stadium in December The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027, and the new stadium is expected to serve as more than just a place to watch soccer. Plans call for a year-round destination where families and community members can gather for entertainment and other events. The development group will fully fund construction of the stadium and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land. 'From day one, we knew this had to be about much more than building a soccer club,' said Gustavo Surez, founder and CEO of Port St. Lucie Sports Club. 'We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape.' The groundbreaking ceremony will begin at noon on Dec. 12, bringing together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., featuring food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages. The club says more details about the event will be announced in the coming weeks.

entry.title: Stuart Air Show celebrates 37th year at Witham Field in Martin County - WFLX
entry.summary: Stuart Air Show celebrates 37th year at Witham Field in Martin County    WFLX
entry.article_text: The Stuart Air Show is preparing to take flight at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area. The air show is celebrating its 37th year at Witham Field on Friday and this year’s event will feature the F-16 demo team along with a variety of other aircraft. The show runs through Sunday, Nov. Among those participating is Maj. Taylor Hiester, the United States Air Force F-16 Viper Demonstration Team Commander and Pilot stationed at Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter, South Carolina. “I’ve been in the Air Force for 11 years now, and it’s been a dream come true for the last three years to serve, not just as a military officer first, but fighter pilot second,” Hiester told WFLX Anchor Mike Trim. “To be the American fighter pilot that gets to connect the American people with the people that do their business around the world on their behalf, is very special.” The 37th annual air show features F-16s, large military planes, ghost riders, aerobatic planes and skydivers, along with games and food for families. “It’s for me, my last performance and for a lot of performers, it’s that it’s the close out of the year,” Hiester told WFLX. “So, it is a wonderful cocktail of emotions that come together that make a fantastic show for the people of Florida, and I think that the people are going to notice that there’s something special.” Beyond the flight demonstrations, the event also focused on education and STEM classes WFLX First Alert Weather Meteorologist Kate Wentzel spoke with students from the aerospace club from Jupiter Christian, along with students from the Parker area, the Virginia Beach area, Fort Pierce and around the Treasure Coast. “In the air show, they want to partner with all of these school groups and organizations, because really it empowers them and inspires them to go into aviation-related careers,” Wentzel said. Weather plays a critical role in aviation, and the students learned how it affects pilots. “We talked about winds, how that impacts pilots. Pilots want to take off into the wind, because the wind blowing over the wings, gives them better lift and a faster lift speed,” Wentzel said. “They also want to land into the wind, because if they have a tailwind pushing them too strong, it can make it difficult for the pilot to have a controlled landing.” Students also learned how icing can impact aircraft at high altitudes and near thunderstorms. Aircraft are supposed to stay 20 miles away from severe thunderstorms at all times, because that is where big updrafts and gusty winds develop, Wentzel said. Conditions are expected to be clear and breezy this evening, making for good viewing of the Stuart Air Show.

entry.title: Jensen Beach neighbors help families rebuild weeks after historic flooding
entry.summary: Weeks after historic flooding devastated homes in Jensen Beach, Martin County families are still cleaning up and rebuilding, with volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders joining the recovery effort. Water marks remain visible on some homes, showing how high floodwaters rose. Residents are now removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies while seeking financial assistance and answers about the area's drainage systems. Jensen Beach families rebuild as neighbors rally after historic flooding Neighbors step in to help Jensen Beach families Before-and-after video from the Jensen Beach neighborhood shows the extent of the flooding, which left several homes under feet of water. Weeks later, homeowner Lisa Marie French said cleaning up has been a major undertaking. We first told you about French's circumstances last week. 'Its a lot of work. You first have to empty the houses,' French said. 'We have to clean the houses; they're filled with mold, we have to take the drywall out.' French, whose home was impacted by the flooding, has also helped coordinate community cleanup efforts alongside Christ of Church, Family Church and other organizations. She said neighbors and other volunteers have repeatedly shown up asking what families need and then immediately gotten to work. 'People have been just coming and just hands-on,' French said. 'People are like, 'Hey, are you taking donations? What do you need?' And they get out of their cars, and they start working, and that's our neighbors. Its pretty amazing.' entry.title: Missed kicks doom Miami Dolphins in 24-22 loss to Indianapolis Colts
entry.summary: The Indianapolis Colts got the respite they needed. After losing five straight and enduring three weeks of tumult, they finally celebrated a victory. Daniel Jones threw for one score, Seth McGowan ran for another and Adetomiwa Adebawore recovered a fumble for a touchdown on Sunday as the Colts held on for a 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins to end their skid. 'It definitely feels good to win,' Jones said. 'It's hard to win in the NFL, so you have to enjoy them.' Colts fans didn't seem to enjoy this one much. Some showed up wearing bags over their heads after Indy shipped away two Pro Bowl captains and their top two receivers before the trade deadline. The Colts held onto Jones and star running back Jonathan Taylor, who said goodbye to Indy fans last week only to suit up again and finish with 103 total yards. While he helped the Colts (3-7) rush for 172 yards, Jones was booed loudly during the second half, when he had just one completion beyond the line of scrimmage. Jones was 11 of 22 for 108 yards with two interceptions. Indy was also flagged 13 times, several of which prevented the Colts from sealing the victory sooner. They wound up needing a fourth-down stop with 1:36 left and McGowan's run for a first down on the ensuing possession to close it out. The offense's struggles led to questions about a possible quarterback switch, which coach Shane Steichen quickly shut down because Indy plays Thursday night. 'Yeah, he'll be the starting quarterback this week,' Steichen said of Jones. 'I think we need to continue to get better. There are a lot of things that happen out there every day, self-inflicted wounds for sure, but we've all got to be better.' Kyle McCord had a solid starting debut for Miami (1-8), which lost its third straight. He was 17 of 32 for 209 yards, ran for a score and lost one fumble in place of Malik Willis , who went on injured reserve earlier this week with a groin injury. Ollie Gordon II had 20 carries for 76 yards. Miami missed three kicks, including a 51-yard field goal attempt in the fourth quarter that would have given the Dolphins the lead. 'We've got to make the extra point, and we've got to make the field goal,' coach Jeff Hafley said. 'It's 24-22, we miss an extra point, which forces us to go for 2, and we miss two field goals, that's seven points. We have to make those.' Indy broke a 7-7 tie when Jones found Laquon Treadwell for a 7-yard TD with 39 seconds left in the first half. It was Treadwell's first TD catch since 2021

entry.title: High school senior helps young athletes score big by giving soccer gear to kids in need
entry.summary: Playing sports can get expensive, especially when you have to pay for all the gear. But one high school student is finding a creative way to combine her favorite sport and giving back. Ella Axtell is a senior at The Benjamin School and founded 'Gear for Goals.' WATCH: High school senior scores big by giving soccer gear to kids in need High school senior scores big by giving soccer gear to kids in need 'Gear for Goals is an organization that I go and take used and new soccer gear and equipment, and I take it to kids who are less fortunate,' Axtell said. Axtell donates the soccer gear to centers like Place of Hope, Family First and Quantum House. 'They come in there using their wheelchairs. We play soccer with them in any way that they are. We equip them, and it's crazy, they love it so much. They always say how it's able to give them a place to play and give them an advantage to play,' Axtell said. She also hosts clinics to teach kids how to play. 'I love it. I honestly love it because I really do think every kid should have the chance to play, and I don't want one kid not to be able to if they don't have the gear,' Axtell said. Gear for Goals is not only helping young athletes in Palm Beach County, but across the world. 'We've gone all over. I went to Costa Rica internationally with St. Mark's and I held four days in that week. I held soccer clinics and each kid got a full entire kit from shirts to cleats,' Axtell said. Axtell said when she came up with the idea for Gear for Goals, she started posting online. We have an Instagram called @ Gear_for_goals , and I send out flyers and post all the time about it. And then I started reaching out to other places that I could have boxes at. So I had one at Palm Beach Gardens Rec Center, Axtell said. I actually was able to host a soccer drive for dressing for charity at St. Mark's, and we raised money, and got a bunch of money for that. And I just spread the word, have an Amazon wish list. I'm just emailing, emailing, emailing. Donations have flooded in, with people giving new and slightly used soccer gear or buying from her online equipment wishlist. 'I just want to continue it. I want to continue it through college. I want to keep going, see how big we can grow and hopefully one day we'll be so big that we'll have clinics all over the world,' Axtell said. So I had one at Palm Beach Gardens Rec Center,” Axtell said. “I actually was able to host a soccer drive for dressing for charity at St. Mark's, and we raised money, and got a bunch of money for that. And I just spread the word, have an Amazon wish list. I'm just emailing, emailing, emailing.”Donations have flooded in, with people giving new and slightly used soccer gear or buying from her online equipment wishlist."I just want to continue it. I want to continue it through college. I want to keep going, see how big we can grow and hopefully one day we'll be so big that we'll have clinics all over the world," Axtell said.While helping kids score goals, Axtell says her goal is to grow the organization. entry.title: 2 planes collide on the ground at Miami International Airport, minor injuries reported
entry.summary: Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries. The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said. Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle. On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft. The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days. The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said. In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries. UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened. 'We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,' UPS said in a statement. The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information.' The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people.

entry.title: Stuart Air Show celebrates 37th year at Witham Field in Martin County - WFLX
entry.summary: Stuart Air Show celebrates 37th year at Witham Field in Martin County    WFLX
entry.article_text: The Stuart Air Show is preparing to take flight at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area. The air show is celebrating its 37th year at Witham Field on Friday and this year’s event will feature the F-16 demo team along with a variety of other aircraft. The show runs through Sunday, Nov. Among those participating is Maj. Taylor Hiester, the United States Air Force F-16 Viper Demonstration Team Commander and Pilot stationed at Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter, South Carolina. “I’ve been in the Air Force for 11 years now, and it’s been a dream come true for the last three years to serve, not just as a military officer first, but fighter pilot second,” Hiester told WFLX Anchor Mike Trim. “To be the American fighter pilot that gets to connect the American people with the people that do their business around the world on their behalf, is very special.” The 37th annual air show features F-16s, large military planes, ghost riders, aerobatic planes and skydivers, along with games and food for families. “It’s for me, my last performance and for a lot of performers, it’s that it’s the close out of the year,” Hiester told WFLX. “So, it is a wonderful cocktail of emotions that come together that make a fantastic show for the people of Florida, and I think that the people are going to notice that there’s something special.” Beyond the flight demonstrations, the event also focused on education and STEM classes WFLX First Alert Weather Meteorologist Kate Wentzel spoke with students from the aerospace club from Jupiter Christian, along with students from the Parker area, the Virginia Beach area, Fort Pierce and around the Treasure Coast. “In the air show, they want to partner with all of these school groups and organizations, because really it empowers them and inspires them to go into aviation-related careers,” Wentzel said. Weather plays a critical role in aviation, and the students learned how it affects pilots. “We talked about winds, how that impacts pilots. Pilots want to take off into the wind, because the wind blowing over the wings, gives them better lift and a faster lift speed,” Wentzel said. “They also want to land into the wind, because if they have a tailwind pushing them too strong, it can make it difficult for the pilot to have a controlled landing.” Students also learned how icing can impact aircraft at high altitudes and near thunderstorms. Aircraft are supposed to stay 20 miles away from severe thunderstorms at all times, because that is where big updrafts and gusty winds develop, Wentzel said. Conditions are expected to be clear and breezy this evening, making for good viewing of the Stuart Air Show.

entry.title: 37th Stuart Air Show draws big crowds for picture-perfect weekend
entry.summary: The 37th Stuart Air Show brought aviation fans young and old together for a picture-perfect weekend filled with aircraft, family traditions, and appreciation for veterans. Organizers said the weekend got off to a strong start Friday night with a drone and fireworks show and continued with large crowds throughout the weekend. Stuart Air Show has had an amazing weekend Friday night with our drone and fireworks show. We had a great turnout, Chrissy Valvano said. Sunday, were looking at a record turnout for Veterans Appreciation Day, and this weather could not be better. For some families, attending the Stuart Air Show has become a tradition passed down through the years. The Stuart Air Show has been a part of our community for many years, Sarah Naylor said. We have many memories of coming in the past, as long as I can remember. For younger aviation fans Wyatt and Ivy Rotan, some of the biggest attractions were the military aircraft. I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly, Wyatt said. I like seeing the C-17, Ivy added. The event also gave young people a chance to learn more about aviation while honoring those who served. You get to have a lot of fun around here, just going around and seeing a bunch of planes, John Gefell said. Also because Im working on my aviation merit badge as a Boy Scout and my grandpa was a veteran, so its just real fun to come out here and just have a lot of fun. With beautiful weather and a strong turnout, the 37th Stuart Air Show once again brought the community together, giving longtime fans and a new generation of aviation enthusiasts a weekend to remember.

entry.article_text: Home Schools InnovatED Phase 2 town hall set for Monday at Sebastian River Middle by Tina Hodges Nov 15, 2026 / 12:23 PM A A A A Reset InnovatED (School District of IRC) Share on Twitter Share via Email SEBASTIAN — The School District of Indian River County will hold an InnovatED Phase 2 town hall Monday, November 16, from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m. at Sebastian River Middle School to gather public feedback on two facility proposals still under consideration. District officials have invited families, staff, and community members to hear details, ask questions, and share thoughts on the plans. The two proposals focus on a future home for Wabasso School that would add capacity and specialized learning spaces, and on creating a connected arts pathway in Sebastian. Both remain under review, with School Board consideration expected in December. Wabasso School currently serves students with specialized needs on U.S. District leaders have previously described the campus as at capacity and have discussed relocating the program to the former Glendale Elementary site in Vero Beach to allow room for growth and more tailored spaces for life skills and independent learning. The arts pathway proposal involves Sebastian Elementary School of the Arts, which officials have said could share the Sebastian River Middle School campus as a separate school while maintaining its own identity. This is the latest in a series of InnovatED community sessions. Phase 1 of the initiative, which included several school relocations, shared campuses, and boundary adjustments, took effect for the 2026-27 school year after School Board approval in December 2025. The original Sebastian River Middle School town hall for Phase 2 was postponed from Nov. Residents who cannot attend can still submit questions or comments. Share input with the planning team. entry.title: The secret to a perfect Thanksgiving turkey? Okeechobee Steakhouse says it's butter
entry.summary: If you've ever admired a perfectly golden Thanksgiving turkey and wondered how professional chefs make it look so good, Okeechobee Steakhouse co-owner Ralph Lewis has a surprisingly simple answer. 'It's butter.' And not just a little butter. During a recent Thanksgiving cooking demonstration at Okeechobee Prime Meat Market, Lewis stood beside a giant inflatable stick of butter, worked from a table piled high with butter and seasonings, and even pulled a backup rubber stick of butter from his pocket. For Lewis, butter isn't simply an ingredient. It's the foundation of a great Thanksgiving turkey. 'Are you really supposed to have a budget with butter?' Lewis joked. 'Those two words do not go together.' The Butter Trick That Makes The Difference According to Lewis, the biggest mistake many home cooks make is putting all of their butter on the outside of the bird. Instead, he recommends carefully separating the skin from the breast meat and creating pockets beneath the skin. Once those pockets are created, it's time to start adding butter. Lots of butter. 'You just want to keep working it in there,' Lewis said. 'You can't put enough. You can't put too much. That's impossible, literally impossible, and that's a chef's code.' As the turkey cooks, the butter melts beneath the skin, helping keep the meat moist while contributing to the rich color and flavor many Thanksgiving hosts are trying to achieve. After working butter beneath the skin, Lewis also coats the outside of the turkey before adding seasoning. Pro Tip: Season The Butter First One of the most useful tips Lewis shared involves seasoning the butter before it ever touches the bird. Start by taking butter out of the refrigerator and allowing it to soften to room temperature. Then combine the softened butter with herbs and seasonings such as: Kosher salt Freshly ground black pepper Thyme Rosemary Sage Mix everything together until it forms a seasoned compound butter. Then spread that butter beneath the skin and across the exterior of the turkey. By combining the herbs and seasoning directly into the butter, the flavors are distributed more evenly throughout the turkey as it cooks. Lewis says it's a simple step that can make a noticeable difference in flavor. Step-By-Step Turkey Guide1. Soften the butter Allow butter to come to room temperature. 2. entry.title: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter    WPBF
entry.article_text: The parents of Jessica Clinton, a Port St. Lucie teen who died of cardiac arrest in 2003, are hosting a free heart screening event this Saturday at the St. Lucie County Health Department to raise awareness about children's heart health. Jessica Clinton's parents Ray and Cheryl Lalloo are preparing for the event, which is expected to draw about 600 children. He stressed the importance of identifying heart problems early. "You hear it all the time. Kids go to sleep, parents come in the morning, they're not awake, and it's now just infants, or SIDS, it's kids that are 10, 12, 13 years old," Ray Lalloo said. Jessica was 17 years old and at cheerleading practice at St. Lucie West Centennial High School when she went into cardiac arrest. At the time, there were no automated external defibrillators (AEDs) on campus, and Jessica died that day. Her parents said she had undergone two sports physicals in the months before her death, but no heart problem was detected. In response to their loss, Jessica's parents founded the Jessica Clinton MVP Foundation and began offering heart screenings 17 years ago. They said the screenings have helped identify previously undiagnosed heart conditions. Last year, they said about 19 children learned they had a condition that had not been detected before. "We've had a couple of kids with pretty significant diagnoses. You know, things like syndrome, the really bad ones, you know," Ray Lalloo said. Cheryl Lalloo is grateful they were able to offer free screenings. "Blessed is the word, Cheryl Lalloo said. "It makes us feel like we also have a lot more work to do. That there's still kids out there that are still diagnosed." The free screenings are available for children and young adults ages 5 to 20 and include an electrocardiogram (EKG) and a check of vital signs. A cardiologist reviews the results, and an Echocardiogram is available if needed. The Lalloos said close to 650 children have signed up for this year's event. Appointments are booked, but families can call to ask about the waiting list. Organizers said they'll try to fill openings if someone cancels or doesn't show up. Jessica's parents hope their efforts will prevent other families from experiencing a loss like theirs. "The one child could be the next president of our country. It could be the person who invents the cure for cancer. So, every life is important. Children should not die like this," Ray Lalloo said. The event will take place Saturday from 8 a.m. Lucie County Health Department, 5150 NW Milner Drive, Port St. The number to call for scheduling is 772-462-3800. entry.title: 37th Stuart Air Show draws big crowds for picture-perfect weekend
entry.summary: The 37th Stuart Air Show brought aviation fans young and old together for a picture-perfect weekend filled with aircraft, family traditions, and appreciation for veterans. Organizers said the weekend got off to a strong start Friday night with a drone and fireworks show and continued with large crowds throughout the weekend. 'Stuart Air Show has had an amazing weekend Friday night with our drone and fireworks show. We had a great turnout,' Chrissy Valvano said. 'Sunday, we're looking at a record turnout for Veterans Appreciation Day, and this weather could not be better.' For some families, attending the Stuart Air Show has become a tradition passed down through the years. 'The Stuart Air Show has been a part of our community for many years,' Sarah Naylor said. 'We have many memories of coming in the past, as long as I can remember.' For younger aviation fans Wyatt and Ivy Rotan, some of the biggest attractions were the military aircraft. 'I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly,' Wyatt said. 'I like seeing the C-17,' Ivy added. The event also gave young people a chance to learn more about aviation while honoring those who served. 'You get to have a lot of fun around here, just going around and seeing a bunch of planes,' John Gefell said. 'Also, because I'm working on my aviation merit badge as a Boy Scout and my grandpa was a veteran, so its just real fun to come out here and just have a lot of fun.' With beautiful weather and a strong turnout, the 37th Stuart Air Show once again brought the community together, giving longtime fans and a new generation of aviation enthusiasts a weekend to remember.

entry.title: The secret to a perfect Thanksgiving turkey? Okeechobee Steakhouse says it's butter
entry.summary: If you've ever admired a perfectly golden Thanksgiving turkey and wondered how professional chefs make it look so good, Okeechobee Steakhouse co-owner Ralph Lewis has a surprisingly simple answer. 'It's butter.' And not just a little butter. Secret to a golden Thanksgiving turkey? Butter, butter and more butter During a recent Thanksgiving cooking demonstration at Okeechobee Prime Meat Market, Lewis stood beside a giant inflatable stick of butter, worked from a table piled high with butter and seasonings, and even pulled a backup rubber stick of butter from his pocket. For Lewis, butter isn't simply an ingredient. It's the foundation of a great Thanksgiving turkey. 'Are you really supposed to have a budget with butter?' Lewis joked. 'Those two words do not go together.' The Butter Trick That Makes The Difference According to Lewis, the biggest mistake many home cooks make is putting all of their butter on the outside of the bird. Instead, he recommends carefully separating the skin from the breast meat and creating pockets beneath the skin. Once those pockets are created, it's time to start adding butter. Lots of butter. 'You just want to keep working it in there,' Lewis said. 'You can't put enough. You can't put too much. That's impossible, literally impossible, and that's a chef's code.' As the turkey cooks, the butter melts beneath the skin, helping keep the meat moist while contributing to the rich color and flavor many Thanksgiving hosts are trying to achieve. After working butter beneath the skin, Lewis also coats the outside of the turkey before adding seasoning. Pro Tip: Season The Butter First One of the most useful tips Lewis shared involves seasoning the butter before it ever touches the bird. Start by taking butter out of the refrigerator and allowing it to soften to room temperature. Then combine the softened butter with herbs and seasonings such as: Kosher salt Freshly ground black pepper Thyme Rosemary Sage Mix everything together until it forms a seasoned compound butter. Then spread that butter beneath the skin and across the exterior of the turkey. By combining the herbs and seasoning directly into the butter, the flavors are distributed more evenly throughout the turkey as it cooks. entry.article_text: Everyone knows Las Vegas as Sin City, but Florida has its own share of cities on WalletHub’s list of America’s most sinful places. 6 in WalletHub’s 2026 sinful cities study, while Port St. Lucie landed near the bottom. The ranking comes as Grand Theft Auto VI brings players back to a Florida-inspired Vice City. Florida’s connection to fictional Vice City is also in the spotlight ahead of Grand Theft Auto VI, scheduled for release Nov. The game returns to a Miami-inspired setting within the fictional state of Leonida. Miami recently added a giant pink Welcome to Vice City sign atop the Kaseya Center as part of a deal with game developer Rockstar Games. County officials said the agreement is expected to bring in nearly $1 million in revenue and create marketing opportunities. WalletHub compared 182 U.S. cities using measures grouped into seven categories, including crime, gambling, drinking, charitable giving and adult entertainment. The ranking is based on selected city-level indicators, not a judgment about individual residents. entry.title: $2 million federal grant aims to ease childcare costs for Palm Beach State College parents
entry.summary: Federal dollars are coming to help local parents continue their college education while dealing with the high cost of childcare. U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel, D-Fla., announced Monday a $500,000 annual grant, funded for the next four years, designed to help student parents at Palm Beach State College. WATCH REPORT BELOW: $2M grant targets student childcare costs for Palm Beach State College parents Those accepted into the program based on income guidelines will pay on a sliding scale, anywhere from nothing to $160 a month. 'Students shouldnt have to choose between an uplifting career and taking care of their children, and this type of grant gives them the opportunity to do both,' Frankel said. Frankel says the average cost of child care in Palm Beach County is around $13,000 annually. The plan is to get 75 parents initially enrolled. Palm Beach State College President Ava Parker says 75% of the students on campus attend college part-time and need to work, so this assistance will allow the parents to find a childcare center close to their home.

entry.summary: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detectives are asking for the public's assistance in identifying a woman who was seen on video taking a bank envelope containing cash that was left on the counter at a Dollar Tree in Wellington. The incident occurred on Sept. 4 at around 12:15 p.m. at the Dollar Tree located at 10510 Forest Hill Blvd. According to PBSO, the victim made a purchase at the Dollar Tree and left a blue bank envelope containing $500 on the counter. The woman was captured on video picking up the envelope and walking out of the store with it, making no attempt to return the envelope to store employees, deputies said. The woman was wearing gray leggings and a gray T-shirt and carrying a denim handbag. Anyone with information regarding the identity of this person of interest is urged to contact Crime Stoppers at 1-800-458-TIPS (8477) or remain anonymous by downloading the PBSO app. Tips can be submitted using the 'See Something' feature. The app is available at www.pbsoapp.com.

entry.title: Heavy rain, flooding possible in West Palm Beach this week as city extends state of emergency
entry.summary: West Palm Beach residents are being urged to prepare for another round of heavy rain and possible flooding this week while parts of the city are still recovering from historic rainfall earlier this month. The city said Monday that heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding are possible from Tuesday through Thursday. According to information provided by the city from the National Weather Service, there is a 40% to 60% chance that 2 to 4 inches of rain could fall across much of South Florida's east coast, with significantly higher amounts possible in isolated locations. Additional rain could worsen flooding in areas where the ground remains saturated from the Nov. 1-2 flooding, particularly in low-lying neighborhoods. Mayor Keith James has extended West Palm Beach's local state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. 22. City officials said the extension allows West Palm Beach to continue emergency measures, coordinate resources and assist residents affected by the flooding. West Palm Beach prepares for additional flooding City crews and emergency personnel are continuing recovery work while preparing for the possibility of more flooding. According to the city, crews are monitoring affected neighborhoods and inspecting and clearing city-maintained storm drain grates. Officials are also evaluating whether garbage, recycling and yard waste collection can be accelerated in western communities hit hardest by the recent flooding to reduce the risk of additional service disruptions. The city is continuing to operate an auxiliary pumping station to lower water levels in the Apoxee Reserve. Water-control structures at Grassy Waters are also being managed to increase available storage capacity ahead of additional rainfall. City staff are meeting daily with regional partners to monitor water levels, review pumping operations and assess the capacity of the drainage system. How residents should prepare for heavy rain West Palm Beach officials are asking residents to prepare now in case flooding makes travel difficult. Residents should: Monitor weather forecasts and official city updates. Avoid driving or walking through flooded areas. Use caution around standing water and storm drains. At the time, he couldn't access his home, vehicle or the tools he depends on for work. Perez is not one of the residents represented by Garcia, but when WPTV recently returned to the neighborhood, our crew found an orange notice on his mobile home that read "UNSAFE.""Working materials are there. My screwdrivers, my drills, my saws, they're stuck there," Perez told WPTV at the time.He worried then about what the disruption would mean financially."We're not asking for nothing else but the necessary that's been lost or gonna get lost because of this, because my job wages, when rent comes down, who is gonna be, is my landlord or the people who I pay for that lot gonna say, ‘Oh, we feel sorry for you to have a discount?’ No, full payments are gonna have to be made," Perez said.Other organizations have also stepped in to address those immediate needs. The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched a fund offering $1,000 cash grants to eligible residents impacted by the crash. Other groups have provided food, shelter, supplies and services for displaced residents.But some of what these families experienced is more difficult to measure."The photos and the aerials really don't do justice to just how close these families came to being seriously hurt or killed," Garcia said.He said some of the people he's spoken with are still dealing with the emotional and psychological effects of what they experienced."It's not something you see every day, and so it definitely had an emotional or psychological impact on them," Garcia said. "Many of them are having trouble sleeping, which is a very common report when someone undergoes a very sudden, tragic and unexpected event."Garcia, who has practiced law for 32 years, is also a longtime pilot. He described himself as a commercial multi-engine instrument-rated pilot and said he previously co-owned a flight school and charter service out of Palm Beach International Airport.He said determining the impact of emotional trauma will take time."There's no formula for that, Joel. It really depends upon the degree. We rely on medical experts to make that assessment and then use our judgment based on experience," Garcia said.While representing families impacted on the ground, Garcia stressed the magnitude of the loss suffered by the families of those aboard the Learjet."My heart goes out to the victims on board the plane. They suffered a massive loss, and I think what the public needs to understand is that this had a much broader impact," Garcia said.He said his focus now is helping the families he represents move toward some sense of normalcy."It's such a massive loss, particularly to the families of the occupants of the aircraft. It's hard to put words around what those families must be going through," Garcia said. "I can't imagine what they must be going through. And so if I can do something, even just a little bit to help others who were impacted by it, then, you know, I think that's the right thing to do."WPTV has reached out to Aurora Aviation for comment and is working to hear back.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    WPEC
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: What airlines owe you after a canceled flight as FAA ground stop disruptions linger
entry.summary: Flight cancellations are dropping as airlines recover from Friday's nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop , but passengers are still dealing with delays, long layovers and an important question: What does an airline owe you when your flight is canceled? WATCH: Samantha Gutierrez's report for what passengers need to know Flight Canceled After FAA Ground Stop? Know Your Rights | WPTV Federal passenger protections provide a clear right in one key situation. If an airline cancels your flight and you decide not to travel, you are entitled to a refund, regardless of what caused the cancellation. That includes nonrefundable tickets. Hotels, meals and ground transportation are a different story. Because Friday's disruption originated with the FAA rather than an airline, carriers are not universally required to cover those additional expenses, though individual airlines may voluntarily provide assistance. Traveler: 'There's no consequence' At President Donald J. Trump International Airport, passenger Scott Danforth said the disruption left him frustrated by what he sees as an imbalance between the responsibilities of travelers and airlines. 'If we make cancellations, we get to pay a lot of money,' Danforth told WPTV. 'But they can make cancellations, and there's no consequence. That's what I don't like.' Paul Hudson of FlyersRights.org said passengers whose flights are canceled have an important decision to make. 'You can choose the offer of rebooking, or you can get a refund,' Hudson said. Under U.S. Department of Transportation rules, passengers do not have to accept airline credits or travel vouchers in place of a refund when the airline cancels their flight and they decide not to travel. What about hotels and meals? Another family WPTV met at the airport said their journey home now includes a 13-hour layover. 'Maybe they could give us, like, a hotel or something through all this chaos,' traveler Jessica Soros said. Hudson said passengers should ask their airline what assistance is available, but accommodations such as meals, hotel rooms and ground transportation aren't guaranteed when the disruption is outside the carrier's control. 'They may provide it to some passengers ... but they don't have to,' Hudson said. Travelers should still ask their carrier about meal vouchers, hotel assistance, discounted hotel rates and travel waivers. Travel insurance or benefits included with some credit cards may offer another option for qualifying expenses. '

The continued disruption stems partly from aircraft and flight crews being left out of position following the nationwide stoppage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it takes time for airlines to move crews and planes back where they need to be.The FAA has said faulty equipment led to Friday's ground stop, while officials continue investigating the precise cause. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said officials had found no evidence of anything nefarious.A preliminary investigation found that an L3Harris contractor was working at a remote FAA site to replace copper wiring with fiber and replace a router when the router began flooding other routers with data, according to Duffy. entry.summary: The chance of heavy rain this week is lingering over our five-county viewing area days after some communities in West Palm Beach dried out from a major flood event. The Hamilton Bay neighborhood in West Palm Beach was underwater last Monday, a full week after record-breaking rainfall came down. With more heavy rain in the forecast this week, neighbors tell me they're concerned. WATCH REPORT BELOW: West Palm Beach residents fear more flooding if heavy rain returns Late Monday morning, Ashley Debrowski was out strolling the sidewalks of Hamilton Bay with her children. 'A week ago today, I would still be trapped in my house,' Debrowski said. Around the corner, Tushar Bulsara was in his driveway wrapping a vehicle. 'That whole week was just unbelievable. It almost felt like a dream,' Bulsara said. Neighbors told me their community off of Jog Road was underwater for 11 days. 'Eleven days of essentially being afraid to leave the house,' Debrowski said. 'Vehicles have to be able to come in for me to do my work,' Bulsara said. 'And you know, that's business lost.' The severe, prolonged flooding impacted communities in the Hamal Community Development District, a roughly 250-acre area near Jog Road and Florida's Turnpike that includes Hamilton Bay, Briar Bay and other neighborhoods. 'It's a situation that we never thought was going to happen,' said Dwayne Barrett, the operations manager for the Hamal CDD. Barrett tells me that since then, the CDD has been working with other government entities to make sure that doesn't happen again. 'I think we're in a bigger and better place right now with additional larger pumps to what we already have already, and so that's going to help a lot to move water. It's currently in operation,' Barrett said. As those extra pumps moved water out of nearby lakes and into a canal by the turnpike, the streets in Hamilton Bay are dry. But the neighbors' minds are still flooded with worry. When I asked Bulsara if he was keeping his eye on the forecast this week, he said, 'Yes.' 'If that happens again, you know, it disrupts work, it disrupts kids going to school,' Bulsara said. 'I will say the lake behind my house definitely looks lower today, but it still makes me really nervous because you don't want to be trapped in your house. entry.title: Heavy rain, flooding possible in West Palm Beach this week as city extends state of emergency
entry.summary: West Palm Beach residents are being urged to prepare for another round of heavy rain and possible flooding this week while parts of the city are still recovering from historic rainfall earlier this month. The city said Monday that heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding are possible from Tuesday through Thursday. According to information provided by the city from the National Weather Service, there is a 40% to 60% chance that 2 to 4 inches of rain could fall across much of South Florida's east coast, with significantly higher amounts possible in isolated locations. Additional rain could worsen flooding in areas where the ground remains saturated from the Nov. 1-2 flooding, particularly in low-lying neighborhoods. Mayor Keith James has extended West Palm Beach's local state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. 22. City officials said the extension allows West Palm Beach to continue emergency measures, coordinate resources and assist residents affected by the flooding. West Palm Beach prepares for additional flooding City crews and emergency personnel are continuing recovery work while preparing for the possibility of more flooding. According to the city, crews are monitoring affected neighborhoods and inspecting and clearing city-maintained storm drain grates. Officials are also evaluating whether garbage, recycling and yard waste collection can be accelerated in western communities hit hardest by the recent flooding to reduce the risk of additional service disruptions. The city is continuing to operate an auxiliary pumping station to lower water levels in the Apoxee Reserve. Water-control structures at Grassy Waters are also being managed to increase available storage capacity ahead of additional rainfall. City staff are meeting daily with regional partners to monitor water levels, review pumping operations and assess the capacity of the drainage system. How residents should prepare for heavy rain West Palm Beach officials are asking residents to prepare now in case flooding makes travel difficult. Residents should: Monitor weather forecasts and official city updates. Avoid driving or walking through flooded areas. Use caution around standing water and storm drains. Stock up on drinking water, nonperishable food and necessary medications. Make sure they have baby supplies, pet food and other household essentials they may need if travel becomes difficult. entry.title: Palm Beach County families displaced by deadly Learjet crash seek compensation
entry.summary: Military Trail has reopened , and the crater left behind by the deadly Learjet crash has been filled, but for families who lived just feet from where the plane came down, the road to recovery is far from over. Mariano Garcia, an attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart Shipley, is representing four families from the Greenacres mobile home community whose homes, vehicles and other property were damaged by crash debris. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Much broader impact Families seek compensation after deadly Learjet crash 'The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs,' Garcia said. Those financial concerns have been a part of the aftermath since the first days following the crash. For the four families Garcia represents, the focus is now turning to financial relief for their specific losses. Family of 8 still displaced One of those families is a household of eight living in a mobile home roughly 50 feet from the impact site. entry.article_text: Military Trail has reopened, and the crater left behind by the deadly Learjet crash has been filled, but for families who lived just feet from where the plane came down, the road to recovery is far from over.Mariano Garcia, an attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart & Shipley, is representing four families from the Greenacres mobile home community whose homes, vehicles and other property were damaged by crash debris.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," Garcia said.Those financial concerns have been a part of the aftermath since the first days following the crash.For the four families Garcia represents, the focus is now turning to financial relief for their specific losses.One of those families is a household of eight living in a mobile home roughly 50 feet from the impact site. Garcia said seven members of the family were home when the crash happened, including three who were outside."Dad was on the porch holding his 1-year-old child. Mom was standing nearby when a chunk of sidewalk came busting through their porch, narrowly missing them," Garcia said.Other members of the family were inside."They all felt the explosion, the shock. They breathed all of the residue that was in the air," Garcia said. "It was a very traumatic event for them, as you can imagine."The damage to the family's home was significant."You had chunks of aircraft parts busting through the roofs, you know, allowing the water intrusion into these residences, and when you combine that with the power being out, food spoiling in refrigerators, folks being unable to return to their homes, it had a pretty significant impact on their lives," Garcia said.Power and water have since been restored to the mobile home community, according to Garcia, but the family of eight has not been able to return to its home because the residence remains unsafe. He said the family has been staying in Airbnbs provided through charity.Garcia said there is no lawsuit at this point.Instead, he is communicating with attorneys for Aurora Aviation Inc., which does business as Upper Jets and operated the Learjet, and the company's insurance carrier in an effort to secure immediate financial relief for the four families he represents.When WPTV asked whether the company has been cooperating, Garcia's response was direct."Very much so," he said. "I'm encouraged that at least the company for this charter operator, the insurance company, is responding and acknowledging that there were losses and are doing what they can to advance sums to these families and help them out."An inspector is expected to assess the affected properties as Garcia's team works to determine the extent of the losses.For now, Garcia said the immediate focus is on expenses families are already facing."The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," he said.WPTV previously spoke with Perez, a handyman whose mobile home is about 250 feet from where the Learjet crashed. At the time, he couldn't access his home, vehicle or the tools he depends on for work. Perez is not one of the residents represented by Garcia, but when WPTV recently returned to the neighborhood, our crew found an orange notice on his mobile home that read "UNSAFE.""Working materials are there. My screwdrivers, my drills, my saws, they're stuck there," Perez told WPTV at the time.He worried then about what the disruption would mean financially."We're not asking for nothing else but the necessary that's been lost or gonna get lost because of this, because my job wages, when rent comes down, who is gonna be, is my landlord or the people who I pay for that lot gonna say, ‘Oh, we feel sorry for you to have a discount?’ No, full payments are gonna have to be made," Perez said.Other organizations have also stepped in to address those immediate needs. The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched a fund offering $1,000 cash grants to eligible residents impacted by the crash. Other groups have provided food, shelter, supplies and services for displaced residents.But some of what these families experienced is more difficult to measure."The photos and the aerials really don't do justice to just how close these families came to being seriously hurt or killed," Garcia said.He said some of the people he's spoken with are still dealing with the emotional and psychological effects of what they experienced."It's not something you see every day, and so it definitely had an emotional or psychological impact on them," Garcia said. "Many of them are having trouble sleeping, which is a very common report when someone undergoes a very sudden, tragic and unexpected event."Garcia, who has practiced law for 32 years, is also a longtime pilot. He described himself as a commercial multi-engine instrument-rated pilot and said he previously co-owned a flight school and charter service out of Palm Beach International Airport.He said determining the impact of emotional trauma will take time."There's no formula for that, Joel. It really depends upon the degree. We rely on medical experts to make that assessment and then use our judgment based on experience," Garcia said.While representing families impacted on the ground, Garcia stressed the magnitude of the loss suffered by the families of those aboard the Learjet."My heart goes out to the victims on board the plane. They suffered a massive loss, and I think what the public needs to understand is that this had a much broader impact," Garcia said.He said his focus now is helping the families he represents move toward some sense of normalcy."It's such a massive loss, particularly to the families of the occupants of the aircraft. The district said it will announce any changes to Tuesday’s after-school activities and athletics based on weather conditions. Families should check the district’s official channels for updates. The district announced the following dismissal times: High schools: 12:20 p.m. Middle schools and K-8: 1 p.m. Elementary schools: 1:50 p.m. Wabasso School: 12:30 p.m. Morning arrival times will remain unchanged, and transportation will operate as normal during early dismissal. Extended Day will be available Tuesday morning but closed in the afternoon. All extracurricular activities must conclude by 2:30 p.m. The district said additional updates will be shared as information becomes available. entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.summary: Teen thrown 50 feet in Jensen Beach e-bike crash, sheriff warns parents of crackdown    WPEC
entry.article_text: Parents could face criminal charges in a crackdown on illegal e-bikes after a teen was thrown 50 feet in a crash, the Martin County sheriff warned Monday. During a news conference, the sheriff revealed that a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy suffered catastrophic injuries in Sunday's crash near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road. The teen was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center , where he is now in stable condition. According to the sheriff, the boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. See also: Kids, 6,000 fentanyl pills and stolen gun uncovered in massive Florida drug bust The first teen made it across, but the 14-year-old was struck by a northbound vehicle that had a green light. The impact sent the boy flying approximately 50 feet, while his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. "Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The crash comes amid growing concerns over e-bike safety in Martin County, where the sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders as young as 7 and as old as 80. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. I'm not anti-e-bikes, but I'm anti-illegal e-bikes being ridden irresponsibly on our streets." The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

entry.title: Jensen Beach residents concerned that forecasted heavy rainfall will cause repeat flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents concerned that forecasted heavy rainfall will cause repeat flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: As residents in Jensen Beach continue cleaning up after this month’s historic flooding, another round of heavy rainfall is heading their way. Many of the homes on Hyline Drive were flooded for eight long days, and residents are finally starting to get inside to start cleaning up. Related: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes They’re hoping the rain doesn’t ruin their progress. “Eight days of standing water. There was nothing that we could do but watch everything deteriorate and mold,” Susan Destafney said. Destafney’s home sits next to the Hyline Pond and was filled with dirty floodwater for eight days. She said they lost almost everything, and now volunteers are tearing the home down to the studs and treating it for mold. “I've cried more than I've ever cried before. It's just a lot to take in, and it should never have happened,” Destafney said. County officials have pumped water from the neighborhood and the pond, and they have set up a recovery assistance webpage for residents. But Destafney said for their day-to-day needs, they are relying on the volunteers and nonprofits to help them get by. She worries they could be knocked back to square one if the forecasted rainfall this week causes more flooding. I mean, things that I was able to save, I do have on my back porch. So, it's going to be raining. So, what's going to happen to the few things that I was able to save? It's a lot,” Destafney said. Others in the community we spoke to are also concerned about the forecast. We're trying to recover right now. My friends are trying to recover right now. All these efforts for cleanup to get us in a place to where it's dried up, the water is gone, and now they're expecting flash flooding again. So, yeah, we're nervous that this is going to be like what it was a couple of days ago all over again in a few days,” Crystal van Duyme said. WPBF 25 News reached out to the county to see what they’re doing to prep for the upcoming rainfall. The public works director was not available Monday, but we’re hoping to speak with him on Tuesday. However, residents did tell us that crews are currently draining the Hyline Pond again, likely in preparation for that rain.
