entry.summary: Port St. Lucie is getting closer to welcoming its first professional soccer team , with a groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat stadium scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12. Port St. Lucie Sports Club announced Thursday that construction will begin at Walton One, where the stadium will sit on approximately six acres. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new pro soccer stadium in December The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027, and the new stadium is expected to serve as more than just a place to watch soccer. Plans call for a year-round destination where families and community members can gather for entertainment and other events. The development group will fully fund construction of the stadium and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land. 'From day one, we knew this had to be about much more than building a soccer club,' said Gustavo Surez, founder and CEO of Port St. Lucie Sports Club. 'We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape.' The groundbreaking ceremony will begin at noon on Dec. 12, bringing together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., featuring food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages. The club says more details about the event will be announced in the coming weeks.

entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County animal shelter is urgently seeking homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency 'Empty the Shelters' adoption event on Nov. 13 and 14. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13, and Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: Treasure Coast woman loses second home in 2 years after devastating Fort Pierce flooding
entry.summary: A Treasure Coast woman who lost her home two years ago to a tornado from Hurricane Milton has lost another home to devastating flooding in Fort Pierce. 'I'm starting to feel like I'm invincible at this point,' says Terry Polk as she watched the debris pile of drywall and ruined furniture in front of her home get bigger. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Treasure Coast woman loses a second home in 2 years The water in her home was measured in feet, not inches, as the heavy rain in the first weekend of November flooded her block. 'We were actually in the house,' Polk said. 'When we were wading around, like around knee-deep water, I started getting scared.' She said they were rescued by kayaks and returned when the water receded, leaving so much damage. 'You know, to keep your focus, you just have to realize there are people out there that have it way worse. There are people out there that are so much worse, you know, and I have to be thankful that we got out with our lives,' she said. Two years ago she was living in the Spanish Lakes community of St. Lucie County when Hurricane Milton's winds created widespread tornadoes. One of the twisters, an EF3, struck the community, killing six people and destroying homes, including Terry's. 'Terry is one of the most amazing people I've met,' said friend Cindy McGee. 'She's very strong, does a lot for the community, a lot for the neighborhood.' Polk said she has flood insurance, but the damage is so extensive, she's not sure if there is enough coverage to fix everything. 'I already explained to the cats, who are looking at me like, we didn't exactly sign up for your survivor world,' she said.

entry.summary: Residents and farmers in western St. Lucie County are seeking answers and long-term drainage solutions after historic flooding left homes, farms and roads underwater last week. The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear concerns from people in the area, including farmers, residents and representatives from Save the Chimps. District members said the drainage system can handle only so much water during an extreme rainfall event and discussed engineering as part of a possible long-term plan. But residents and farmers say they want to know what can be done to reduce the risk of similar flooding during the next extreme rainfall event. entry.title: Port St. Lucie cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills, independence
entry.summary: A recent cooking class in Port St. Lucie is helping adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities learn valuable life skills and gain more independence. The participants are part of the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach Countys Guardian Advocacy Program, which provides guardianship support to people with developmental disabilities. WATCH: Cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills for independent living Cooking up confidence: Port St. Lucie program helps adults with disabilities gain independence Some of the participants are young adults who have aged out of foster care and don't have family members to rely on for support. Through a partnership with GL Homes that has lasted nearly a decade, participants are given hands-on experiences and opportunities to develop skills that can help them in everyday life. During the latest class in October, participants learned how to prepare a healthier meal, with Mediterranean chicken on the menu. From chopping vegetables and preparing ingredients to following a recipe and practicing kitchen safety, the lesson was about more than just cooking. Organizers say the goal is to give participants experiences and opportunities that are often not readily available to them while helping them become more self-sufficient. 'We wanted to give them these experiences that they just don't have and the rest of us take for granted,' said Sarah Alsofrom, Vice President of Community Relations at GL Homes. Jessica Kelson with the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County says watching participants learn new skills and take part in activities can make a meaningful difference. 'Being able to watch them learn a new skill or participate in something that's not typically offered to them is just really heartwarming and nice to see them be able to grow,' Kelson said. By the end of the class, participants had prepared their meal and sat down to enjoy what they made. For one participant, the accomplishment was something to be proud of. 'I'm proud of it,' she said. 'I am going to try this at home.' Organizers hope these experiences will give participants the confidence and practical skills to take greater control of their daily lives one meal at a time.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him, and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Alexis Hodge said. Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain,' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

entry.title: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary seeks help after historic flooding
entry.summary: Save the Chimps, a 150-acre chimpanzee sanctuary in Fort Pierce, is asking the community for help after historic flooding left parts of its property underwater, damaged equipment and disrupted normal operations. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary seeks help after historic flooding The sanctuary's more than 200 chimpanzees are safe and continue to receive food, medication, enrichment and other daily care, according to Mark Yohannan, the organization's director of facilities. But Yohannan told WPTV the sanctuary faces a long recovery after receiving 19 inches of rain. 'We've got a long way to go,' Yohannan said. He said it is the worst flooding the sanctuary has experienced in its 25 years in Fort Pierce. 'We're absolutely shut down until we get the water gone,' Yohannan said. Staff adapts to care for chimpanzees Since Tuesday, Save the Chimps staff members have had to find new ways to reach parts of the flooded sanctuary. Workers have used tractors and trailers to navigate the property and deliver supplies. Video shared with WPTV shows staff using a drone to drop food to a chimpanzee during the flooding. Despite the difficult conditions, Yohannan said the chimpanzees have continued receiving their normal care. 'They're doing great. The care staff have been on their game,' Yohannan said. 'They're getting everything they would get normally: enrichment, all their food, all their medication, blankets. They haven't missed a beat.' Yohannan said some staff members have been unable to get to work because of the flooding, but those who can reach the sanctuary have come together to keep operations moving. 'It's heavy, but it's good heavy,' Yohannan said. 'Everyone's come together.' Flooding damages vehicles and equipment The flooding has also taken a toll on equipment used for everyday operations. Yohannan said nearly 15 golf carts used to transport food, supplies and staff around the 150-acre property have broken down. 'We'd seen the water and we figured, well, no big deal, we'll drive through it, and that became impossible immediately,' he said. Yohannan said the sanctuary is looking for taller four-wheel-drive vehicles that can safely move people and supplies through the property while floodwaters remain. 'We need four-wheel-drive vehicles that are taller that can move supplies and people,' Yohannan said. He said the vehicles could be rented or donated for a short period. entry.article_text: Home Schools InnovatED Phase 2 town hall set for Monday at Sebastian River Middle by Tina Hodges Nov 15, 2026 / 12:23 PM A A A A Reset InnovatED (School District of IRC) Share on Twitter Share via Email SEBASTIAN — The School District of Indian River County will hold an InnovatED Phase 2 town hall Monday, November 16, from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m. at Sebastian River Middle School to gather public feedback on two facility proposals still under consideration. District officials have invited families, staff, and community members to hear details, ask questions, and share thoughts on the plans. The two proposals focus on a future home for Wabasso School that would add capacity and specialized learning spaces, and on creating a connected arts pathway in Sebastian. Both remain under review, with School Board consideration expected in December. Wabasso School currently serves students with specialized needs on U.S. District leaders have previously described the campus as at capacity and have discussed relocating the program to the former Glendale Elementary site in Vero Beach to allow room for growth and more tailored spaces for life skills and independent learning. The arts pathway proposal involves Sebastian Elementary School of the Arts, which officials have said could share the Sebastian River Middle School campus as a separate school while maintaining its own identity. This is the latest in a series of InnovatED community sessions. Phase 1 of the initiative, which included several school relocations, shared campuses, and boundary adjustments, took effect for the 2026-27 school year after School Board approval in December 2025. Absences caused by weather will be excused, the district said. Heavier rain is possible Wednesday through Friday and could lead to school closures. The district is monitoring conditions with the St. Lucie County Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district said it will announce any changes to Tuesday’s after-school activities and athletics based on weather conditions. Families should check the district’s official channels for updates. The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Martin County sheriff warns of illegal e-bike dangers after crash injures teen - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County sheriff warns of illegal e-bike dangers after crash injures teen    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 14-year-old boy was flown to St. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach after being injured in an illegal e-bike crash at U.S. 1 and NW Goldenrod Road in Jensen Beach over the weekend, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek expressed frustration over the incident and emphasized the risks associated with illegal e-bikes. “We’re not trying to pick on people, but there’s nothing worse than having a child laid up in a trauma center as we go into the holidays,” Budensiek said. The sheriff’s office released footage of the crash, showing two e-bikes attempting to cross U.S. While the first bike crossed safely, the second rider was struck by a vehicle that had a green light. Budensiek highlighted the importance of helmet use in preventing fatalities. “Had he not been wearing a helmet, we’d be talking about a 14-year-old dying in a fatality crash,” Budensiek said. Earlier this year, the sheriff’s office adopted a zero-tolerance policy on illegal e-bike use to address reckless riding and growing safety concerns. However, Budensiek said the message has not been effective. “So, this is serious for us. I know it’s fun for the kids, but our softer approach has not been working. We’ve had 41 e-bike crashes in Martin County this last year,” Budensiek said. Jason Moore, associate trauma medical director at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, said his hospital has treated numerous patients injured in e-bike crashes. “Yes, unfortunately we’ve seen a lot of e-bike accident patients. I’d say over the last 12 months we’ve seen hundreds of e-bike accidents,” Moore said. Moore described the severity of injuries resulting from e-bike crashes. “Unfortunately, we’ve seen pretty significant injuries, involving brain injuries, broken bones including those in the neck, the collarbone, the ribs. We see quite a few rib fractures,” Moore said. Budensiek said his office is committed to raising awareness about the dangers of illegal e-bikes and is exploring whether parents who knowingly purchase illegal e-bikes for their children could face criminal prosecution. “Parents are knowingly buying illegal e-bikes, giving them to their kids, and allowing their kids to ride them, so we are looking at criminal prosecution for parents if we can make that stick,” Budensiek said. entry.article_text: Parents could face criminal charges in a crackdown on illegal e-bikes after a teen was thrown 50 feet in a crash, the Martin County sheriff warned Monday. During a news conference, the sheriff revealed that a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy suffered catastrophic injuries in Sunday's crash near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road. The teen was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center , where he is now in stable condition. According to the sheriff, the boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. See also: Kids, 6,000 fentanyl pills and stolen gun uncovered in massive Florida drug bust The first teen made it across, but the 14-year-old was struck by a northbound vehicle that had a green light. The impact sent the boy flying approximately 50 feet, while his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. "Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The crash comes amid growing concerns over e-bike safety in Martin County, where the sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders as young as 7 and as old as 80. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. I'm not anti-e-bikes, but I'm anti-illegal e-bikes being ridden irresponsibly on our streets." The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

entry.summary: Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony. WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Veterans honored at Port St. Lucie event Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service 'It's all like my whole history. 'It's good to get the recognition that we didn't get,' Thomas said. The Port St. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they're really important to support the veterans,' Vogel told Trim. Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. Vincent Lavelle Jr. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

entry.title: Riviera Beach flood victims seek relief as city weighs $2 million aid plan
entry.summary: Riviera Beach residents demand help after historic flooding Hundreds of Riviera Beach residents packed an emergency City Council meeting seeking financial assistance after November flooding damaged homes, displaced families and left residents questioning how they will pay for repairs. The city discussed setting aside $2 million for a proposed forgivable loan or grant program for residents whose homes were damaged by the flooding. The proposed assistance would help pay for interior and exterior repairs needed to make homes safe and livable. But during the heated meeting, city Finance Director Randy Sherman said the city faces restrictions on using public money to pay for damage to private property, creating uncertainty about how the proposed relief could move forward. Riviera Beach weighs $2M flood relief plan as residents demand help Lone Pine Estates residents press city for financial relief Weeks after floodwaters inundated homes in Lone Pine Estates, residents filled the meeting room, with others standing outside, hoping city leaders would provide a path toward recovery. Keisha Hartys lives in the neighborhood and her home was impacted by the flooding. She summed up the growing frustration in the neighborhood. No help is coming. We are on our own, said Harty. Another resident challenged the city's position that public funding could not be used directly to help private homeowners, pointing to other causes the city has supported. When you say you cant use federal dollars or public funding for private citizens, I have to disagree, the resident said. Im looking for a Lone Pine relief fundraiser. Council member Shirley Lanier argued the flooding and its impact on residents should be treated as a broader public safety concern. That is a public safety issue, Lanier said. There is no way that we cannot use public money for a public concern. Residents describe the toll of the flooding Residents also used the meeting to show city leaders what recovery has looked like on the ground. One woman said firefighters rescued her from floodwaters. At the podium, she displayed basic items she said she received afterward, including a T-shirt, deodorant and socks. Why is this being given to a taxpayer on an emergency event? she asked. entry.article_text: At the podium, she displayed basic items she said she received afterward, including a T-shirt, deodorant and socks.“Why is this being given to a taxpayer on an emergency event?” she asked.The frustrations come as families continue trying to clean up and repair homes weeks after the flooding.Many residents are also concerned about additional rainfall and the possibility that already hard-hit neighborhoods could face more flooding.The Riviera Beach City Council unanimously voted to amend a motion to continue considering the $2 million emergency set-aside while seeking a legal opinion on how the money could be used.The proposal calls for establishing a forgivable loan or grant program specifically for residents whose homes were damaged by the November flooding.City leaders also considered partnerships that could provide emergency shelter, hotel or motel vouchers and temporary housing for displaced residents.Another proposal would allow the city to coordinate mutual aid with neighboring cities, counties and partner agencies for debris removal, collection and other flood recovery needs.The vote does not mean homeowners will immediately receive money. According to the sheriff, the boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. See also: Kids, 6,000 fentanyl pills and stolen gun uncovered in massive Florida drug bust The first teen made it across, but the 14-year-old was struck by a northbound vehicle that had a green light. The impact sent the boy flying approximately 50 feet, while his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. "Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The crash comes amid growing concerns over e-bike safety in Martin County, where the sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders as young as 7 and as old as 80. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. I'm not anti-e-bikes, but I'm anti-illegal e-bikes being ridden irresponsibly on our streets." The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

entry.summary: The 37th Stuart Air Show brought aviation fans young and old together for a picture-perfect weekend filled with aircraft, family traditions, and appreciation for veterans. 'I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly,' Wyatt said. 'I like seeing the C-17,' Ivy added. With beautiful weather and a strong turnout, the 37th Stuart Air Show once again brought the community together, giving longtime fans and a new generation of aviation enthusiasts a weekend to remember.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter    WPBF
entry.article_text: The parents of Jessica Clinton, a Port St. Lucie teen who died of cardiac arrest in 2003, are hosting a free heart screening event this Saturday at the St. Lucie County Health Department to raise awareness about children's heart health. Jessica Clinton's parents Ray and Cheryl Lalloo are preparing for the event, which is expected to draw about 600 children. He stressed the importance of identifying heart problems early. "You hear it all the time. Kids go to sleep, parents come in the morning, they're not awake, and it's now just infants, or SIDS, it's kids that are 10, 12, 13 years old," Ray Lalloo said. Jessica was 17 years old and at cheerleading practice at St. Lucie West Centennial High School when she went into cardiac arrest. At the time, there were no automated external defibrillators (AEDs) on campus, and Jessica died that day. Her parents said she had undergone two sports physicals in the months before her death, but no heart problem was detected. In response to their loss, Jessica's parents founded the Jessica Clinton MVP Foundation and began offering heart screenings 17 years ago. They said the screenings have helped identify previously undiagnosed heart conditions. Last year, they said about 19 children learned they had a condition that had not been detected before. "We've had a couple of kids with pretty significant diagnoses. You know, things like syndrome, the really bad ones, you know," Ray Lalloo said. Cheryl Lalloo is grateful they were able to offer free screenings. "Blessed is the word, Cheryl Lalloo said. "It makes us feel like we also have a lot more work to do. That there's still kids out there that are still diagnosed." The free screenings are available for children and young adults ages 5 to 20 and include an electrocardiogram (EKG) and a check of vital signs. A cardiologist reviews the results, and an Echocardiogram is available if needed. The Lalloos said close to 650 children have signed up for this year's event. Appointments are booked, but families can call to ask about the waiting list. Organizers said they'll try to fill openings if someone cancels or doesn't show up. Jessica's parents hope their efforts will prevent other families from experiencing a loss like theirs. "The one child could be the next president of our country. It could be the person who invents the cure for cancer. So, every life is important. Children should not die like this," Ray Lalloo said. The event will take place Saturday from 8 a.m. Lucie County Health Department, 5150 NW Milner Drive, Port St. The number to call for scheduling is 772-462-3800. entry.title: Jensen Beach neighbors help families rebuild weeks after historic flooding - WFLX
entry.summary: Jensen Beach neighbors help families rebuild weeks after historic flooding    WFLX
entry.article_text: Weeks after historic flooding devastated homes in Jensen Beach, Martin County families are still cleaning up and rebuilding, with volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders joining the recovery effort. Water marks remain visible on some homes, showing how high floodwaters rose. Residents are now removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies while seeking financial assistance and answers about the area's drainage systems. Neighbors step in to help Jensen Beach families Before-and-after video from the Jensen Beach neighborhood shows the extent of the flooding, which left several homes under feet of water. Weeks later, homeowner Lisa Marie French said cleaning up has been a major undertaking. We first told you about French's circumstances last week. You first have to empty the houses," French said. "We have to clean the houses; they're filled with mold, we have to take the drywall out." French, whose home was impacted by the flooding, has also helped coordinate community cleanup efforts alongside Christ of Church, Family Church and other organizations. She said neighbors and other volunteers have repeatedly shown up asking what families need and then immediately gotten to work. "People have been just coming and just hands-on," French said. "People are like, 'Hey, are you taking donations? What do you need?' And they get out of their cars, and they start working, and that's our neighbors. It’s pretty amazing." Residents seek answers about flooding and drainage As cleanup continues, residents say they also want answers about what contributed to the severe flooding. Some are questioning how much pumping from Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce into the Savannas Preserve may have contributed to flooding in their neighborhood. Stephen Leighton, chief of staff for U.S. Brian Mast, R-Fla., told WPTV that questions remain as officials work through the recovery process. "There's a lot of answers that these residents need, and hopefully we can do that," Leighton said. Leighton also said the state had taken steps toward an emergency declaration and reached out to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Families look for financial assistance For some homeowners, rebuilding also brings financial uncertainty. French said her home is not in a flood zone and she does not have flood insurance, leaving her family dependent on whatever assistance, donated materials and volunteer help becomes available. "We're trying to get any type of help. We don't have flood insurance here," French said. "We're way above sea level; we are not a flood zone. So it's just whatever volunteers and help and materials we can get is what we get." Community calls for more volunteers Residents say more hands are still needed as families work to make their homes livable again. Leighton said a question-and-answer town meeting with residents and county, state and federal officials is planned this week as the community seeks clarity about the flooding and available assistance. For volunteers, Leighton said even small acts can make a difference for families trying to put their lives back together. "To help somebody take that picture off the wall and put it in a box, so they can move on, is a big deal," he said. With Thanksgiving approaching, he said the need for community support remains urgent. "We're two weeks out from Thanksgiving, and we really need the community to come together and help," Leighton said. entry.title: FAU researchers find the best treatment for Childhood Apraxia of Speech could come down to timing
entry.summary: For families with children who have an acute speech disorder known as Child Apraxia of Speech, it's always a race against the clock to find the most optimal therapy. Researchers at Florida Atlantic University may have recently discovered that helping to connect the dots between a child's brain and their speech could come down to the time of day of their therapy. WATCH: The best treatment for complex speech disorder could come down to timing Study: Time of day could make speech therapy more effective Sara Tutoni's daughter was too young to participate in the study, but the family does seek treatment at FAU for CAS. Tutoni says she realized something wasn't right around age 2. 'She could make every sound an animal makes, every sound a car makes, but no words,' Tutoni said. In the study, published in the journal Clinical Linguistics Phonetics , FAU researchers shared a striking difference in how speech-motor learning unfolded for participants with and without CAS. Their findings suggest that the time of day may influence speech-motor learning differently in young people with CAS and could eventually help clinicians identify ways to make therapy more effective without simply adding more hours of treatment. The study consisted of 82 adolescents and young adults ages 12 to 21 with and without CAS. Researchers found that participants with typical speech showed a slight benefit from evening training, while those with CAS performed better after morning training. Dr. Anne van Zelst, one of the lead researchers, says further study is needed, but believes this starting point could be critical to helping families and other stakeholders save time and money on expensive therapies. '(It could save) parents, school districts and insurance companies. It's very demanding on families,' van Zelst said. Tutoni said she wishes she would've had tools like this early on and sees it as a game changer for other families navigating CAS. Her focus is on her daughter and giving her the best chance at success.

entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Heavy rain and gusty winds are forecast in Indian River County from Tuesday, Nov. Solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents: If water covers the road, turn around. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage to the road. If your usual route home is flooded, take another route or wait somewhere safe. Never drive around a barricade. Stay out of flooded areas and avoid driving to see how high the water is. Keeping roads clear gives deputies and rescue crews room to reach people who need help. Martin County Fire Rescue advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods. Residents should also have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and unsecured recovery materials. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Lucie County asks that the survey be completed by November 30, https://arcg.is/05f4b13 .

entry.title: Trump's Presidential Library foundation amasses $57.6 million
entry.summary: The foundation overseeing President Donald Trumps future presidential library amassed $57.6 million by the end of last year, new tax filings show, as the president turned legal battles with major media and tech companies into an unusual source of funding for the project. The filings do not identify the donors or reveal how much of the money came from controversial settlements. But the documents, provided to CNN by the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation, confirm the organization has a sizable head start on his unconventional vision for a presidential library a towering Miami skyscraper that he has suggested could also serve as a hotel. RELATED STORY | Eric Trump shares renderings of a proposed Trump presidential library and museum The foundation reported spending just $349,000 during its first seven months. Much of that was paid to Bermello Ajamil Partners, the architecture firm that produced renderings of the proposed 47-story library. It previously told the Internal Revenue Service that it expected to raise about $50 million by the end of 2025. But it anticipated fundraising would accelerate considerably: The organization estimated it will bring in nearly $1 billion by the end of 2027. Its unclear whether the organization remains on track toward reaching that goal. Recently, two of Trumps top political operatives, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, donated to the foundation amid revelations they left the country ahead of the midterms to provide counsel for Republika Srpska, a pro-Russia Balkan government. In the months since Trump circulated renderings for his proposed library including a gilded entranceway and an Air Force One on display he has announced other expensive legacy construction projects, including a White House ballroom that has attracted seven- and eight-figure checks from large companies and political allies. A pro-Trump super PAC, MAGA Inc., closely connected to the president has also brought in hundreds of millions of dollars. Trumps planned library was designated to receive sizable sums from settlements with companies he sued during the presidential campaign and after his first term. ABC News agreed in December 2024 to pay $15 million toward the library, and Meta earmarked $22 million for the library in a January 2025 settlement. entry.title: Teen arrested in hit-and-run crash that critically injured 24-year-old woman in Port St. Lucie
entry.summary: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after a hit-and-run crash critically injured a 24-year-old woman on an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie, police said. The incident happened Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace, Port St. Lucie police said. According to investigators, the victim was riding an electric scooter westbound on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard. As the woman on the scooter entered the crosswalk, she was struck by the 18-year-old driver of a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the driver fled the scene and failed to stop to render aid to the woman. The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer and located the vehicle through its investigation. entry.article_text: Families across the Treasure Coast are watching the forecast closely after historic flooding overwhelmed parts of Port St. Just as many neighborhoods are drying out, forecasters are warning another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days, raising concerns about renewed flooding in areas still recovering from the record rainfall. The flooding two weeks ago left cars stranded, some families trapped in their homes and others wading through deep water. "It was horrible," said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. "Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods." Among those caught off guard was freshman Noah Julian. 2, Noah stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson quickly spread on social media, showing the teenager swimming through floodwaters just to reach his driveway. "When I see the video, I'm like, what?" said Noah's father, Romeo Julian. We got alligators here, snakes, sharp objects could have cut him up. A thousand things could've happened to him." With another round of heavy rain in the forecast, residents say they aren't taking any chances." "Today I'm going to get stuff before flood comes," Perez said. See also: From banks to flights, outages leave south Floridians frustrated St. Lucie Public Schools is also preparing ahead of the storm. The district announced a two-hour early release Tuesday in an effort to avoid a repeat of the flooding issues that affected students taking the bus home earlier this month. "But why it always takes one thing to make them wake up." Meanwhile, county crews have been inspecting and clearing canals and drainage systems ahead of the expected rainfall. Officials warn that because the ground is still saturated from recent storms, it will take far less rain than usual to cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and be prepared for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.

entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.summary: Rough surf and rip currents create dangerous conditions along Treasure Coast    WPBF
entry.article_text: Strong winds and high surf are creating dangerous conditions along the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with red flag warnings and a high risk of rip currents keeping most beachgoers out of the water. At Stuart Beach, the wind is whipping through the area, churning up rough water conditions. The beach is nearly empty, with no one in the water and only a few people on the sand. "Take advantage of this; it may not be great weather, but there's not a lot of people. So, you got quiet time to yourself. It's beautiful," said Jon Ciffolillo, a beachgoer. Despite the roaring wind, some are still venturing out to enjoy the morning before another round of heavy rain is expected to move through the area. "It's a beautiful day out here. The wind and the surf is just a different view of nature's beauty," said Frank Harvey, who was walking on the beach with his wife, Joan. Joan Harvey added, "A lot of time in your condo is not always ideal. So, you got to take it when it's not raining." Beachgoers are being urged to take caution, as conditions in the water remain dangerous. A high surf advisory is in effect along the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast, along with a high risk for rip currents. Red flag warnings are also in place along Martin County's beaches, signaling that even experienced swimmers can be pulled away from shore. Martin County Ocean Rescue advises beachgoers to check with lifeguards about water conditions and to swim in guarded areas when conditions improve. The high surf advisory and high risk for rip currents are expected to last through Thursday. You can check the latest beach conditions across Martin County on their Safe Beach Day website. entry.title: Student ACES helping build the next generation of leaders in Palm Beach County
entry.summary: For more than a decade, Student ACES has been working with student-athletes across Palm Beach County, using sports as a starting point to teach lessons that extend far beyond the field. The nonprofit focuses on character and leadership development through interactive programs, including team building, role-playing exercises and real-world case studies. WATCH: Student ACES helping build the next generation of leaders in Palm Beach County WPTV SEASON OF HOPE STUDENT ACES We teach character and leadership to student athletes. We go through team-building, role-play exercises, and case studies. Its very, very interactive, said Krissy Webb, executive director of Student ACES. Webb said the organization has worked with about 60,000 students since it was founded in 2013. Student ACES offers five different programs aimed at helping young people develop leadership skills and prepare for their futures. One of those programs is based at the Student ACES Center in Belle Glade, which serves high school students from Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay throughout the year. Students receive mentoring and support in areas including academics, college preparation, career readiness, mental health, health and wellness, entrepreneurship, and character and leadership. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with student athletes who say the program is also helping them build confidence and think about what comes after high school. The five Student ACES programs are offered at no cost to students, helping remove a potential barrier for families who want their children to participate. The Student ACES Center (The SAC) in Belle Glade provides year-round afterschool and summer programming for high school students from Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay. Students receive mentoring and individualized support focused on academics, college and career preparation, leadership, health and wellness, mental health and entrepreneurship. The ACE Flagship Program brings together high school juniors from across Palm Beach County for character and leadership development. Students take part in mentoring, team-building activities, real-world case studies and leadership challenges. Captains Summits are one-day experiences for team captains and other influential student-athletes. The program focuses on communication, accountability, teamwork and learning how to lead by example. Leadership Workshops bring customized mentoring and leadership programs directly to athletic teams, schools and student groups

entry.title: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: Martin County families still recovering from this month’s flooding are bracing for more rain, and on Tuesday, many of them asked county commissioners not to wait on federal help before opening an emergency shelter. Speaker after speaker told commissioners during public comment that water was already back in their streets. Some said their homes took on water earlier this month. Their main request was a public shelter, open before the next round of rain, for both unhoused residents and families who lost their homes in the flooding. Commissioners are discussing funding options at both the local and federal level. Florida has asked President Donald Trump for a major disaster declaration for the flooding, and as of Tuesday, it had not been signed. Once a disaster receives a federal declaration, FEMA must cover 75 percent of state and local response and recovery costs, according to the Florida Policy Institute. Without one, counties pay those costs on their own. Several speakers argued the county does not need to wait for that approval to act. Commissioner, you do not need FEMA’s blessing to open a school. Neighboring counties didn’t wait. Churches didn’t wait, one speaker said. Yamila Rollan Escalona, founder and executive director of Yaya Por Vida, a grassroots harm reduction organization, said she emailed her comments Tuesday morning as water rose in her neighborhood again, then came to speak in person. She said her group has been asking commissioners for emergency shelter for most of the year. See also: Palm Beach County braces for more flooding as cities offer sandbags, prepare for storm Please give us emergency shelter now. It’s no longer about just individuals that are unhoused. It’s also about individuals that just became unhoused because of this tragedy, Rollan Escalona told CBS12 News after the meeting. Rollan Escalona said unhoused residents have nowhere to go, pointing to a 2024 state law that bans sleeping on public property. She said some people are still staying in campsites surrounded by standing water, and some residents have not been accounted for. With drains and the ground already saturated, she said there is no time to wait. She also warned the damage won’t end when the water goes down. Rollan Escalona said mental health services on the Treasure Coast are already hard to access, and she worries the stress and hopelessness of losing everything could lead to more overdoses and people returning to substance use. Other speakers looked further ahead, linking the flooding to development in the county, including a proposed hyperscale data center. They asked commissioners to consider runoff and drainage before approving large projects. Take the 30,000-foot view the next time you look at a large project. How does it affect your neighbors? Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite previously told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes. Residents whose homes were damaged can report it and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Ahead of the rain, Martin County is handing out sand and sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park, 8303 SW Lost River Road. Distribution runs from noon to 6 p.m. Each household can take up to 25 sandbags, and residents will be asked for their name and address. The county asks residents to check its map for the exact pickup spot inside the park. CBS12 News will update this story with what commissioners decide on funding and a possible shelter.

entry.title: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district is asking families to monitor its official channels for updates as weather conditions change. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.article_text: An 18-year-old is under arrest after police say he was playing a game of ding, dong, ditch with some friends and then hit a woman on an e-scooter and drove away. Police have identified the driver as Tristan Ray Sanchez-Chasmer, 18, of Port St. "Pranks especially at somebody's front door, especially at late hours of the night, early hours of the morning can be very dangerous," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. Lucie Police say the crash happened Monday, November 16, at about 5:10 am near the intersection of SW Gatlin Blvd. and SW Feather Terrace in Port St. Police say a 24 year old woman on an e-scooter was hit by a vehicle that did not stop. The victim was on her way to a Wendy's where she works and she was in the crosswalk on SW Feather Terrace when she was hit. "I think for somebody to just leave another human being on the side of the road who was possibly injured, to not stop and check on them, it's truly heartbreaking that somebody would make that decision," said Katie Santana, a Port St. Lucie resident who lives near the intersection where the accident happened. We spoke with a high school student who rides an e-scooter in the area where the crash occurred. "I get a little bit fearful sometimes, 'cause I'll see some people going through red lights, not paying attention when they're turning and I've almost been hit a couple times," said John Rogalewski, age 15. See also: Bodycam footage shows deputy fatally shoot armed Florida mother, army veteran outside bar Police say a good Samaritan got the license plate number of the hit and run vehicle and stopped to help the victim. With that information, police determined a Chevy Tahoe struck the woman, and they determined the driver was an 18-year-old. Sanchez-Chasmer is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Police say the victim was rushed to a hospital and, at last report, she was hospitalized in critical condition. Police say she is in a coma. If she does not survive, the State Attorney's Office would decide if Sanchez-Chasmer could face a more serious charge. Police say two other individuals who were in the Chevy Tahoe with Sanchez-Chasmer have not been charged.

entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
