entry.article_text: Palm Beach County homeowners hoping for new financial help after this month's devastating flooding will have to wait a little longer.County commissioners voted 7-0 Tuesday to postpone consideration of a proposed $2 million Flood Disaster Assistance Program, choosing to spend more time working through questions about eligibility, insurance, contractors, temporary housing and how to stretch a limited amount of money among residents who need help.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The proposal is now expected to return to commissioners Dec. 1."We here at the Palm Beach County Commission wanna make sure that we get this right," Commissioner Bobby Powell Jr. told WPTV reporter Joel Lopez after the meeting. "Also, we need to hear from residents. 1 is when we'll have that meeting, and I would look forward to having residents come to that meeting. But also residents should call our offices, talk to us, and let's walk through this and work through it together."The proposed program comes roughly two weeks after extraordinary rainfall left neighborhoods underwater across Palm Beach County.In a previous meeting, county officials said parts of West Palm Beach received more than 22 inches of rain, causing roads to become waterways, leaving vehicles stranded and some residents unable to leave their neighborhoods. In Century Village near West Palm Beach, firefighters responded to more than seventy 911 calls in one night, with nearly 100 residents trapped in stranded vehicles as floodwaters rapidly rose. In Riviera Beach, the county's Swiftwater Response Team evacuated 71 people, conducted two medical rescues and evacuated nine pets.Powell, who represents District 7, was among those rescued during the flooding."Fire Rescue came to get me this morning, so I'm one of the people they had to rescue," Powell told commissioners during the meeting held earlier this month.Now, the county is trying to determine how to help residents recover.County staff proposed using $2 million from the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program to help income-qualified homeowners whose homesteaded properties suffered flood damage.SHIP is a state program funded through documentary stamp taxes that provides money to counties and qualifying municipalities for affordable housing programs.Under the proposal presented Tuesday, eligible homeowners could receive up to $50,000. The money could be used for uninsured structural damage that threatens health or safety, interim repairs to prevent additional damage, insurance deductibles and temporary relocation assistance."It's up to $50,000," Powell said. "Some homeowners may need less, some may need more, but this is a start. What we would like to do is analyze what the needs of the individuals who are requesting funding are so that we can better fulfill their needs."County officials said roughly 80 homes have reported damage so far, although officials noted that number depends on homeowners and municipalities reporting damage.They said they've been communicating with City of Riviera Beach officials who reported closer to 300 homes.The relatively small pool of money compared with the potential need quickly became a major part of Tuesday's discussion.If households received close to the proposed $50,000 maximum, commissioners noted the $2 million could help roughly 40 to 50 households. Some commissioners questioned whether that maximum should be lowered so the county could reach more families.They also raised concerns about whether assistance should simply be distributed on a first-come, first-qualified basis or whether the county should prioritize residents with the greatest need, including seniors and people whose homes are no longer habitable.Powell said what he has seen in some of the hardest-hit communities is difficult to describe."People have worked their entire lives to own a home. Or to get to where they have been in a safe and secure place, people have been put in a position where they no longer feel safe, comfortable, and protected," Powell said. "And able to thrive because their worldly possessions are sitting on the street corner because their house was damaged to an extent that they can no longer inhabit it by an event that they had not anticipated."Commissioners also spent considerable time questioning how the county would handle homeowners with insurance, people without flood insurance, contractor selection and residents who may also qualify for assistance offered by their cities.Temporary housing was another concern.The proposal included up to $10,000 of the $50,000 maximum for temporary relocation assistance for displaced residents for up to six months. Commissioners questioned whether those rules should be flexible enough to allow residents to stay with family members under certain circumstances, particularly given the cost and availability of short-term rentals in Palm Beach County.There were also questions about how the county should coordinate with municipalities such as Riviera Beach, which is exploring its own assistance for flood victims, while making sure residents are not reimbursed twice for the same expense."We have to work together. We have to resolve these issues together. It can be done," Powell said. "We need to work with the citizens, with the cities, the city of Riviera Beach, the city of West Palm Beach, and the county to come up with solutions that actually help people. There's no way around this."Powell acknowledged the frustration facing residents who have been seeking help since the flooding."This has been a problem since Nov. People have been reaching out asking for help, and now we're getting there; we're working on it, but we have to get it right," he said.County administrators originally hoped that, with commission approval Tuesday, applications could begin as soon as Wednesday. Instead, after more than an hour of discussion, commissioners agreed to give staff additional time to refine the proposal and bring it back Dec. 1.The county's efforts come as local leaders continue dealing with the aftermath of a flooding event that prompted Gov. Ron DeSantis to add Palm Beach County to Florida's state of emergency. The declaration provided additional authority and resources for response, recovery and mitigation efforts.For residents still waiting for help, Powell encouraged them to stay involved as county officials rework the program."We will get it right. We'll make sure we get assistance for people, and we'll keep working on it. Keep, keep showing up, keep knocking on doors. I know you're frustrated," Powell said. Do not stop."Powell also encouraged residents affected by the flooding to contact commissioners and participate when the proposal returns Dec. 1."It's our job and those who've been impacted to tell the stories and to show people so that we can make sure that you get the help that is needed and necessary," Powell said.With more rain possible, Powell urged residents to prepare for the possibility of additional flooding."Let's be proactive now we know the rain is coming. Let's do our best to be prepared," Powell said.He also called on government agencies to make sure drainage systems are ready."Let's make sure that every opportunity to drain water is working today so that we're not facing the same thing we saw last time."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Another flooding threat tests St. Lucie County as leaders brace for Amendment 3 budget cuts
entry.summary: As the threat of another round of November rain and flooding takes aim at Florida's east coast, many local governments are once again preparing for what may be ahead. 'I think everybody is well aware now that this storm drain system was not designed for the flooding we're getting nowadays,' St. Lucie County spokesman Erick Gill said. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flooding and Budget Worries on Treasure Coast He said crews are being deployed across the county as they were two weeks ago. 'There were probably 50 to 100 staff members out there, including crews in public works, out in the field working during the storm. That's unbudgeted overtime,' Gill said. This week, the county offered free sand , donated by Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials, for residents to bag. Other services cost money, and Gill said budgeting is already on the minds of county leaders now that the Amendment 3 tax cuts are coming. What is uncertain is how the loss of revenue will affect things like storm preparation and response. 'We still don't know what the total impacts will be for, you know, with Amendment 3 with the additional homestead exemption,' Gill said. 'We're looking at the early estimates in this next upcoming fiscal year to be about a $60 million shortfall and then about $120 million once the exemption goes up.'

entry.title: Lake Worth Beach prepares for more rain as residents continue recovering from historic flooding
entry.summary: With more heavy rain possible this week , the City of Lake Worth Beach is taking steps to prepare as some residents continue recovering from last week's historic flooding. The city says it is closely monitoring weather conditions and working to maintain critical infrastructure in an effort to minimize additional flooding. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Lake Worth Beach prepares for more rain as residents continue recovering from historic flooding As part of those preparations, residents can pick up sandbags Tuesday from 12:30 p.m. to 7 p.m. and Wednesday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Osborne Community Center, located at 1699 Wingfield St. The pickup is self-service, supplies are available while they last, and residents must provide proof of Lake Worth Beach residency. City crews are also working to address drainage concerns in areas vulnerable to flooding. Water Utilities crews are clearing storm drains along 18th Avenue South and in other flood-prone areas, including Bryant Park. Sewer collections crews are monitoring water levels along 7th Avenue North and South Lakeside Drive to help ensure the system is prepared for additional rainfall. During an interview with WPTV, Vice Mayor Mimi May said the city is working to get ahead of future storms. 'They are cleaning out the storm drains, they are making sure that there's no debris there, they are cleaning out the pump house that's in Bryant Park,' May said. May said the city is also pursuing grants to strengthen its drainage infrastructure over the long term, while prioritizing maintenance and clearing existing systems in the immediate future. In the South Palm neighborhood, city leaders say crews recently removed nearly 23 yards of sediment from the sewer system, clearing an estimated 75% of a blockage. Although the neighborhood still experienced flooding, city leaders say removing the blockage weeks earlier helped prevent conditions from becoming significantly worse and helped keep raw sewage out of homes. Residents can contact Solid Waste at 561-533-7344 or solidwasteinfo@lakeworthbeachfl.gov to ask about scheduling a pickup.Residents who need repairs following flood damage can also contact the city's Building Division to request an expedited building permit at 561-586-1786 or BldgDiv@lakeworthbeachfl.gov.The Lake Worth Drainage District (LWDD) says its canals in southeastern Palm Beach County are prepared for a potentially heavy rainfall event.However, the district emphasizes that neighborhood drainage systems are also the responsibility of individual communities, homeowners associations and property managers.Residents are encouraged to safely clear debris from storm drains around their homes and report blocked internal drainage systems to the appropriate HOA or municipality.The district also reminds residents that emergency operable flood-control structures are not authorized to be opened at this time.As another round of rain approaches, officials are urging residents to avoid driving or walking through standing water and to use alternate routes when encountering flooded roadways.

Known as the 'Father of the Vero Beach Art Village,' Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. entry.title: St. Lucie schools closed Wednesday as more flooding threatens Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie schools closed Wednesday as more flooding threatens Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: Just two weeks after historic flooding forced schools to close for three straight days, St. Lucie County students are getting another day off as more heavy rain threatens the area. Lucie Public Schools announced Tuesday that all schools and district offices will be closed Wednesday due to the threat of significant rainfall and localized flooding. The announcement comes after the district dismissed students two hours early Tuesday as worsening weather conditions raised concerns about flooding. It's the latest disruption for the district, which was forced to close schools for three consecutive days Nov. 4, 5 and 6 after historic flooding left roads underwater and communities struggling to recover. entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district announced Tuesday afternoon that schools and offices will be closed Wednesday as a precaution. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.title: Port St. Lucie e-scooter rider critically injured in hit-and-run; 18-year-old arrested - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie e-scooter rider critically injured in hit-and-run; 18-year-old arrested    cw34.com
entry.article_text: An 18-year-old is under arrest after police say he was playing a game of ding, dong, ditch with some friends and then hit a woman on an e-scooter and drove away. Police have identified the driver as Tristan Ray Sanchez-Chasmer, 18, of Port St. "Pranks especially at somebody's front door, especially at late hours of the night, early hours of the morning can be very dangerous," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. Lucie Police say the crash happened Monday, November 16, at about 5:10 am near the intersection of SW Gatlin Blvd. and SW Feather Terrace in Port St. Police say a 24 year old woman on an e-scooter was hit by a vehicle that did not stop. The victim was on her way to a Wendy's where she works and she was in the crosswalk on SW Feather Terrace when she was hit. "I think for somebody to just leave another human being on the side of the road who was possibly injured, to not stop and check on them, it's truly heartbreaking that somebody would make that decision," said Katie Santana, a Port St. Lucie resident who lives near the intersection where the accident happened. We spoke with a high school student who rides an e-scooter in the area where the crash occurred. "I get a little bit fearful sometimes, 'cause I'll see some people going through red lights, not paying attention when they're turning and I've almost been hit a couple times," said John Rogalewski, age 15. See also: Bodycam footage shows deputy fatally shoot armed Florida mother, army veteran outside bar Police say a good Samaritan got the license plate number of the hit and run vehicle and stopped to help the victim. With that information, police determined a Chevy Tahoe struck the woman, and they determined the driver was an 18-year-old. Sanchez-Chasmer is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Police say the victim was rushed to a hospital and, at last report, she was hospitalized in critical condition. Police say she is in a coma. If she does not survive, the State Attorney's Office would decide if Sanchez-Chasmer could face a more serious charge. Police say two other individuals who were in the Chevy Tahoe with Sanchez-Chasmer have not been charged.

entry.title: Jensen Beach Festival of Giving brings together more than 50 local nonprofits
entry.summary: More than 50 local nonprofits are coming together for the third annual Festival of Giving at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, filling the Jensen Beach museum with holiday displays while allowing community organizations to share the work they do throughout the region. Christina McIntosh, community outreach and events coordinator for the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, said participating nonprofits come from communities stretching from Palm Beach County north through the Treasure Coast. 'Those are the five counties that our education department here at the museum works with and works with the schools,' McIntosh said. More than Christmas decorations The Festival of Giving uses decorated Christmas trees and holiday displays to introduce visitors to nonprofit organizations serving South Florida and the Treasure Coast. For the organizations involved, the gathering also provides a chance to learn more about one another. Treasure Coast Community Singers is among the nonprofits participating. 'The really great thing about this event is that we get to know other nonprofits,' Sharon Savageaux of Treasure Coast Community Singers said. We get to understand what they do. And we can help spread their word.' The singers also performed at the museum during a festival breakfast event. A Grinch-themed tree with a community mission The GFWC Hobe Sound Womans Club is also participating, decorating its display with a Grinch theme. Sandy Vucik, who represented the organization at the festival, said the money it raises supports several community organizations, including Family Promise, CareBag and Real Life Childrens Ranch in Okeechobee. Vucik said the club is currently helping 19 children at the ranch. 'We're really hoping to give them a nice Christmas,' Vucik said. The holiday setting gives visitors a chance to discover organizations they may not otherwise encounter while allowing nonprofits themselves to make new community connections. Family Night brings Santa, cookies and hot chocolate to Jensen Beach. The festival includes several special events beyond its nonprofit displays. McIntosh said Family Night will include a visit from Santa along with hot chocolate, cookie decorating, and craft activities. 'Santa's coming into town,' McIntosh said. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners approve emergency funding for flood victims - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners approve emergency funding for flood victims    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County officials announced their plans to support flood victims as they begin the long road to recovery. County commissioners fielded hours of public comment at their meeting Tuesday. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The county has set up a sandbag distribution site at Halpatiokee Regional Park where folks can fill up to 25 sandbags per household. That is just one part of what they’re doing to prepare for more storms and help residents. “The county needs to help us. Somebody needs to come forward. There's got to be an emergency fund. I can't understand how Martin County, one of the richest counties in Florida, does not have one,” Mary Berner, who lost her home on Hyline Drive in the flood, said. One by one, residents stepped to the podium at the meeting airing their frustrations at the flood disaster response. “We sat there for eight days and didn't have any response until we had a, you know, a meeting and made several phone calls to our commissioner and got no response from her. So, it's hard to not be heard,” Berner said. Commissioners made sure those pleas were heard Tuesday. They approved an increase of an up to $25,000 in grant funding for each eligible household from the county’s SHIP Disaster Assistance fund. Eligibility is determined by household income based on HUD guidelines. “These funds come through the state through something called the Sadowski funds. These funds are captured for each county when there's a real estate transaction, and then the state delivers to each county a certain amount each year to allocate for not only disaster, but things like rehabilitation of your home,” Michelle Miller, Martin County Human Services director, said. The county currently has $900,000 in that fund. “There are certain eligibility uses for that disaster funding, which, again, are expenses to weatherproof your house, rental assistance ... also, emergency hotel vouchers,” Miller said. As far as preps go, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that right now, crews are pumping several lakes and ponds to create more space for any excess water to go. He said they’re especially focusing on the Hyline Drive area where Berner’s home is and was destroyed. “There's no way to rebuild if you have nothing. And I mean, literally nothing is left. And then, of course, long-term goals, they need to figure out this problem; they need to stop developing in wetlands,” Berner said. To apply for the SHIP emergency funding, applicants should go to the county’s human services office or call 772-320-3169. As for the sandbags, residents can grab them Wednesday from 7 a.m. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast - cw34.com
entry.summary: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Martin County families still recovering from this month’s flooding are bracing for more rain, and on Tuesday, many of them asked county commissioners not to wait on federal help before opening an emergency shelter. Speaker after speaker told commissioners during public comment that water was already back in their streets. Some said their homes took on water earlier this month. Their main request was a public shelter, open before the next round of rain, for both unhoused residents and families who lost their homes in the flooding. Commissioners are discussing funding options at both the local and federal level. Florida has asked President Donald Trump for a major disaster declaration for the flooding, and as of Tuesday, it had not been signed. Once a disaster receives a federal declaration, FEMA must cover 75 percent of state and local response and recovery costs, according to the Florida Policy Institute. Without one, counties pay those costs on their own. Several speakers argued the county does not need to wait for that approval to act. Commissioner, you do not need FEMA’s blessing to open a school. Neighboring counties didn’t wait. Churches didn’t wait, one speaker said. Yamila Rollan Escalona, founder and executive director of Yaya Por Vida, a grassroots harm reduction organization, said she emailed her comments Tuesday morning as water rose in her neighborhood again, then came to speak in person. She said her group has been asking commissioners for emergency shelter for most of the year. See also: Palm Beach County braces for more flooding as cities offer sandbags, prepare for storm Please give us emergency shelter now. It’s no longer about just individuals that are unhoused. It’s also about individuals that just became unhoused because of this tragedy, Rollan Escalona told CBS12 News after the meeting. Rollan Escalona said unhoused residents have nowhere to go, pointing to a 2024 state law that bans sleeping on public property. She said some people are still staying in campsites surrounded by standing water, and some residents have not been accounted for. With drains and the ground already saturated, she said there is no time to wait. She also warned the damage won’t end when the water goes down. Rollan Escalona said mental health services on the Treasure Coast are already hard to access, and she worries the stress and hopelessness of losing everything could lead to more overdoses and people returning to substance use. Other speakers looked further ahead, linking the flooding to development in the county, including a proposed hyperscale data center. They asked commissioners to consider runoff and drainage before approving large projects. Take the 30,000-foot view the next time you look at a large project. How does it affect your neighbors? Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite previously told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes. Residents whose homes were damaged can report it and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Ahead of the rain, Martin County is handing out sand and sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park, 8303 SW Lost River Road. Distribution runs from noon to 6 p.m. Each household can take up to 25 sandbags, and residents will be asked for their name and address. The county asks residents to check its map for the exact pickup spot inside the park. CBS12 News will update this story with what commissioners decide on funding and a possible shelter.

entry.article_text: More than 50 local nonprofits are coming together for the third annual Festival of Giving at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast, filling the Jensen Beach museum with holiday displays while allowing community organizations to share the work they do throughout the region. Christina McIntosh, community outreach and events coordinator for the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast, said participating nonprofits come from communities stretching from Palm Beach County north through the Treasure Coast. “Those are the five counties that our education department here at the museum works with and works with the schools,” McIntosh said. More than Christmas decorations The Festival of Giving uses decorated Christmas trees and holiday displays to introduce visitors to nonprofit organizations serving South Florida and the Treasure Coast. For the organizations involved, the gathering also provides a chance to learn more about one another. Treasure Coast Community Singers is among the nonprofits participating. “The really great thing about this event is that we get to know other nonprofits,” Sharon Savageaux of Treasure Coast Community Singers said. “We get to understand what they do. And we can help spread their word.” The singers also performed at the museum during a festival breakfast event. A Grinch-themed tree with a community mission The GFWC Hobe Sound Woman’s Club is also participating, decorating its display with a Grinch theme. Sandy Vucik, who represented the organization at the festival, said the money it raises supports several community organizations, including Family Promise, CareBag and Real Life Children’s Ranch in Okeechobee. Vucik said the club is currently helping 19 children at the ranch. “We’re really hoping to give them a nice Christmas,” Vucik said. The holiday setting gives visitors a chance to discover organizations they may not otherwise encounter while allowing nonprofits themselves to make new community connections. The festival includes several special events beyond its nonprofit displays. “Santa’s coming into town,” McIntosh said. “He loves this event, so the kids will be able to visit with him.” Family Night is scheduled for Tuesday evening on Nov. 17, at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast. An adult holiday pajama party follows Friday The celebration takes a turn for the grown-ups Friday with an adult holiday pajama party. “We will be a museum full of adults dressed in their holiday pajamas because who doesn’t want to go to a party and go home and go right to bed,” McIntosh said. The festival continues through Saturday, Nov. 21, at 2 p.m., according to McIntosh. The Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast is located at 1707 NE Indian River Drive in Jensen Beach. entry.summary: 'Overwhelming': St. Lucie County residents prepare for heavy rainfall with sandbag stations    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County residents are preparing for heavy rainfall this week, with officials offering free self-serve sandbag stations and working to clear drainage systems to address potential flooding. Dreamland Park in Fort Pierce, residents were seen filling sandbags to protect their homes. Resident Lisa Powell is concerned. "My ditches are full from the last storm, they haven't gone down, so this could be very bad. The water is just still standing there, up to the yard." Another resident shared their concerns, saying, "My crawlspace got a foot of water in there, so trying to get all these bags to try and cover up the opening, you know." Public works crews in St. Lucie County are actively checking and clearing swales and drainage systems as the area braces for more severe weather. Recent flooding left parts of the county submerged, with residents in the Creekside development trapped inside, some using kayaks to navigate flooded streets while others waded through the water. Fredrick Reeves, a resident whose home was previously flooded, is preparing for the upcoming rain by using sandbags and mulch to block water from entering his house. "It was pretty bad, and the house itself, once it started coming in, I thought maybe we would be alright. I threw down all my clothes trying to soak it up, but that didn't do anything. The next thing you knew, it was in the house," Reeves said. He described the situation as "overwhelming." The City of Fort Pierce is offering free self-serve sandbag stations at Martin Luther King Jr. Dreamland Park and Jaycee Park. Residents are advised to bring their own bags and shovels. Both parks are open daily from dawn to dusk. Lucie County has also set up self-service sandbag distribution points at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds West Parking Lot and Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot, thanks to donations of sand from Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials. Residents must bring their own supplies and fill their own bags. For updates about the precautions residents should take, please visit St. Lucie County’s emergency management portal at: www.readystlucie.org. For more information, residents can contact the Public Works Department or visit the county’s emergency management portal. entry.summary: St. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district announced Tuesday afternoon that schools and offices will be closed Wednesday as a precaution. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.title: From unrecruited walk-on to NFL hopeful: FAU's Easton Messer eyes becoming NFL draft pick
entry.summary: After back-to-back 1,000-yard receiving seasons, FAU wide receiver Easton Messer is on several NFL Draft boards and looks to be the Owls' first draft pick in six years. I sat down with the FAU Owls standout for a one-on-one conversation about his journey one that spanned multiple countries before leading him to South Florida. WATCH REPORT BELOW: FAU's Easton Messer aims to become Owls' first NFL Draft pick since 2020 Messer moved around a lot over the years. 'My first place was Costa Rica, then I moved back to Louisville, then Panama, and lastly Malaysia,' Messer said. Growing up, he played both soccer and American football a combination he credits with shaping his footwork and technique. 'I really haven't thought about the fact that soccer helped out my feet and helped me play receiver, but soccer is big pretty much everywhere but the U.S. Just being over in those places and trying to get integrated into the culture,' Messer said. Football, though, was always his sport. 'Growing up, that was my sport. I played football, basketball and a little bit of baseball, but football was my favorite one. I went to high school at Christian Academy in Louisville,' Messer said. In high school, Messer was a standout receiver but felt he was under-recruited. 'It was pretty short; it wasn't a ton of recruiting with me being undersized and not passing the eye test. I had a couple offers, and I wasn't sure if they were commitable, and I ended up having to walk on at Western Kentucky,' Messer said. After standing out over three years at Western Kentucky, Messer entered the transfer portal and ultimately arrived at FAU. 'My transfer portal recruitment wasn't really popping either; not a lot of people reached out,' Messer said. Since 2020, no Owls player has heard their name called in the NFL Draft. Messer could change that in a few months. 'Personally, for me, going from a walk-on and not really getting recruited to possibly getting my name called on draft night, it doesn't even feel real at this point, but we got some other guys too,' Messer said. entry.article_text: Just two weeks after historic flooding forced schools to close for three straight days, St. Lucie County students are getting another day off as more heavy rain threatens the area. Lucie Public Schools announced Tuesday that all schools and district offices will be closed Wednesday due to the threat of significant rainfall and localized flooding. The announcement comes after the district dismissed students two hours early Tuesday as worsening weather conditions raised concerns about flooding. It's the latest disruption for the district, which was forced to close schools for three consecutive days Nov. 4, 5 and 6 after historic flooding left roads underwater and communities struggling to recover. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding Now, with the ground already saturated, district leaders say they aren't taking any chances. According to the district, forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall, although uncertainty remains about exactly when and where the heaviest rain will fall. "Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," district officials said in a statement. John Carroll High School also announced it will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 18, due to the threat of heavy rainfall and flooding across the region. The decision follows an early dismissal Tuesday and a review of weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials said all Wednesday activities, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs and other events, have been canceled. John Carroll anticipates reopening Thursday, pending weather and road conditions. Administrators will continue monitoring forecasts and coordinating with local authorities before making further decisions. Updates will be shared through the school's official communication channels. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday have also been canceled. District officials said they will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and access to schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision on whether schools will reopen Thursday is expected Wednesday evening. Families are encouraged to monitor the district's official website and social media channels for updates.

entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie e-scooter rider critically injured in hit-and-run; 18-year-old arrested - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie e-scooter rider critically injured in hit-and-run; 18-year-old arrested    cw34.com
entry.article_text: An 18-year-old is under arrest after police say he was playing a game of ding, dong, ditch with some friends and then hit a woman on an e-scooter and drove away. Police have identified the driver as Tristan Ray Sanchez-Chasmer, 18, of Port St. "Pranks especially at somebody's front door, especially at late hours of the night, early hours of the morning can be very dangerous," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. Lucie Police say the crash happened Monday, November 16, at about 5:10 am near the intersection of SW Gatlin Blvd. and SW Feather Terrace in Port St. Police say a 24 year old woman on an e-scooter was hit by a vehicle that did not stop. The victim was on her way to a Wendy's where she works and she was in the crosswalk on SW Feather Terrace when she was hit. "I think for somebody to just leave another human being on the side of the road who was possibly injured, to not stop and check on them, it's truly heartbreaking that somebody would make that decision," said Katie Santana, a Port St. Lucie resident who lives near the intersection where the accident happened. We spoke with a high school student who rides an e-scooter in the area where the crash occurred. "I get a little bit fearful sometimes, 'cause I'll see some people going through red lights, not paying attention when they're turning and I've almost been hit a couple times," said John Rogalewski, age 15. See also: Bodycam footage shows deputy fatally shoot armed Florida mother, army veteran outside bar Police say a good Samaritan got the license plate number of the hit and run vehicle and stopped to help the victim. With that information, police determined a Chevy Tahoe struck the woman, and they determined the driver was an 18-year-old. Sanchez-Chasmer is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Police say the victim was rushed to a hospital and, at last report, she was hospitalized in critical condition. Police say she is in a coma. If she does not survive, the State Attorney's Office would decide if Sanchez-Chasmer could face a more serious charge. Police say two other individuals who were in the Chevy Tahoe with Sanchez-Chasmer have not been charged.

entry.summary: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after a hit-and-run crash critically injured a 24-year-old woman on an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie, police said. WATCH: Update from Chief Leo Niemczyk Port St. Lucie police give update on hit-and-run crash The incident happened Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace, Port St. Lucie police said. According to investigators, the victim was riding an electric scooter westbound on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard. As the woman on the scooter entered the crosswalk, she was struck by the 18-year-old driver of a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the driver fled the scene and failed to stop to render aid to the woman. The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer and located the vehicle through its investigation. Investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing 'ding dong ditch' just before the crash. He was arrested on a charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, police said.

entry.title: St. Lucie County superintendent of schools promises review of district policies after historic flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County superintendent of schools promises review of district policies after historic flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince apologized to the district Tuesday night and promised a review of all decisions and actions from the historic flooding on Nov. "It was very stressful for our families, and I certainly apologize for the stress that they went through on that day," Prince said. A video from that day shows a boy getting off a school bus on SW Coleman Avenue in Port St. Lucie and walking through flood waters that reach as high as his chest. Critics have pointed to that video and questioned the actions of the school district. In an exclusive interview, Prince expressed regret over the events of Nov. 2, stating that decisions were made based on the information available at the time. He emphasized that the flooding was unexpected. "The bottom line is I don't know of anything that could have predicted what transpired as the day progressed," Prince said. Prince assured that every decision made that day is being analyzed. "We are going to review all our procedures, our policies to make sure that if there's anything that we could have done differently, that moving forward we will," he said. With heavy rain in the forecast, St. Lucie County Schools decided to cancel classes for Wednesday. Prince said he hopes the decision is an overreaction. At the same time, though, he does not want to take any chances. "The ground is so saturated, but if the conditions worsen tomorrow, we don't want a repeat of what happened November 2," Prince said. Prince said the district will monitor the weather Wednesday and decide late Wednesday afternoon if classes should be canceled again Thursday. He said they'll follow that model until they are sure it's safe for students to return to class. entry.title: Riviera Beach residents brace for more rain weeks after homes flooded
entry.summary: Residents in Riviera Beach are preparing for another round of rain weeks after floodwaters damaged or destroyed hundreds of homes, including properties in Lone Pine Estates. With families still recovering, residents lined up for sandbags Tuesday as city leaders worked to identify financial assistance for homeowners. For families who recently watched water enter their homes, the possibility of more rain is bringing back fears of another flood. WATCH: Riviera Beach residents brace for more rain after devastating floods Riviera Beach residents brace for more rain after devastating floods Residents prepare for more rain WPTV saw a line of cars as residents waited to pick up sandbags, with neighbors shoveling sand and loading bags into their vehicles. Keeping my fingers crossed, said Keisha Harty while preparing for the rain. WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache reconnected with the Harty family, who were waiting in line for sandbags while still recovering from the previous flooding. We need sandbags to put in front, just in case, Harty said. I dont want another flood. Not another one again. Lone Pine Estates was among the Riviera Beach communities hit by the recent flooding, which left hundreds of homes damaged or destroyed. Homeowner Guy Volel said his house flooded on consecutive days. Last week my house got flooded both days, Volel said. All the stuff inside my house is falling apart. Riviera Beach considers $2 million relief proposal The preparations come after an emergency meeting Monday night as residents continued pressing city leaders for help. Riviera Beach Mayor Douglas Lawson told WPTV that city officials are looking for ways to get financial assistance to affected homeowners. Residents are hurting and were trying to find every vehicle to help them to get the resources they need to rebuild their homes, Lawson said. City leaders are considering a $2 million relief proposal for residents affected by the flooding. Lawson said officials directed staff to move quickly and hoped to have more information before the Thanksgiving break. We demanded that staff comes back as quickly as possible, Lawson said. So hopefully by next week, prior to the Thanksgiving break, well have some answers for our residents to be able to disseminate some of this money weve allocated for them. City hopes for federal disaster assistance Lawson said the city is also hoping for a major disaster declaration from the president that could make federal disaster assistance available to reside

entry.title: Mary Peltola projected to flip Alaska Senate seat, giving Democrats 56-44 majority
entry.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to the Associated Press, delivering a significant pickup for Democrats. Peltola's victory marks the first time since 2008 that a Democrat has won a U.S. Senate election in Alaska, and gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate though two lawmakers identify as Independents and simply caucus with the Democrats. 'As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,' Peltola said in a statement. 'As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaskas working families. Thank you Alaska. Lets get to work. Peltola, who made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, focused her Senate campaign on lowering the cost of living and addressing economic challenges facing everyday Alaskans. She previously served in the U.S. House of Representatives, where she became known for emphasizing issues important to Alaska, including the state's fishing industry and economic development. The race drew national attention as Republicans fought to defend their Senate majority. Sullivan, a military veteran seeking a third term, received support from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Sullivan aligned his campaign with the Trump administration's tax and spending priorities and advocated for expanding fossil fuel production. The race in Alaska was complicated by the presence of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, ran as a long shot Democratic candidate for Senate. Both Dan Sullivans running prompted a legal fight early in the campaign, and President Donald Trump later called the former teacher's campaign 'fake' and 'a hoax by the Democrats.'

entry.title: Some Treasure Coast schools close Wednesday due to heavy rainfall concerns; Indian River, Martin open - WPBF
entry.summary: Some Treasure Coast schools close Wednesday due to heavy rainfall concerns; Indian River, Martin open    WPBF
entry.article_text: Due to anticipated rainfall, at least one public-school district and a private school on the Treasure Coast will close. LUCIE COUNTY A spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Public Schools announced on Tuesday, Nov. 17, that the school district will be closed to students and employees on Wednesday, Nov. “While there remains some uncertainty regarding the exact timing, location, and amount of rainfall, current forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees,” the school district spokesperson said in a statement. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. All afterschool activities, after-care programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday were canceled. The spokesperson added that school district officials will continue to monitor rainfall, flooding, road closures and the accessibility of schools, bus stops and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. A decision about school reopening on Thursday will be announced on Wednesday evening. The school district said it will provide updates on its website and social media platforms. John Carroll High School: The private school in Fort Pierce announced it will be closed on Wednesday because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding throughout the region. "The decision follows today’s early dismissal and a review of current weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials determined that closing campus is the best course of action to ensure the safety of students, faculty, staff, and families," the school said in a statement to WPBF 25 News on Tuesday evening. "All school-sponsored activities scheduled for Wednesday, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs, and other events, have been canceled." The school added it anticipates resuming normal operations on Thursday, Nov. 19, pending weather and road conditions. "Administrators will continue to monitor forecasts and remain in communication with local authorities before making any further decisions regarding school operations," the schools said. "Updates will be shared through the school’s official communication channels as conditions warrant." Boys Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County: All after-school programs and Clubhouse locations will be closed on Wednesday, November 18. MARTIN COUNTY The Martin County School District said that school and Extended Day will be open to students on Wednesday, but all other after-school activities, athletic practices and events are canceled for Wednesday. Officials in Martin County will monitor weather conditions. Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County: All Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County locations will reopen on Wednesday, November 18, and resume normal operating hours. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY The School District of Indian River County announced on Tuesday afternoon that there will be a regular school schedule for students and employees, including Extended Day and extracurricular activities, on Wednesday, Nov. "District teams found no standing water affecting safe routes to bus stops. Families are encouraged to make the best decision for their circumstances," a spokesperson for the school district said in a statement on Tuesday. "Weather-related absences will follow standard attendance procedures and will not be excused solely due to weather."
