entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.title: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: Martin County families still recovering from this month’s flooding are bracing for more rain, and on Tuesday, many of them asked county commissioners not to wait on federal help before opening an emergency shelter. Speaker after speaker told commissioners during public comment that water was already back in their streets. Some said their homes took on water earlier this month. Their main request was a public shelter, open before the next round of rain, for both unhoused residents and families who lost their homes in the flooding. Commissioners are discussing funding options at both the local and federal level. Florida has asked President Donald Trump for a major disaster declaration for the flooding, and as of Tuesday, it had not been signed. Once a disaster receives a federal declaration, FEMA must cover 75 percent of state and local response and recovery costs, according to the Florida Policy Institute. Without one, counties pay those costs on their own. Several speakers argued the county does not need to wait for that approval to act. Commissioner, you do not need FEMA’s blessing to open a school. Neighboring counties didn’t wait. Churches didn’t wait, one speaker said. Yamila Rollan Escalona, founder and executive director of Yaya Por Vida, a grassroots harm reduction organization, said she emailed her comments Tuesday morning as water rose in her neighborhood again, then came to speak in person. She said her group has been asking commissioners for emergency shelter for most of the year. See also: Palm Beach County braces for more flooding as cities offer sandbags, prepare for storm Please give us emergency shelter now. It’s no longer about just individuals that are unhoused. It’s also about individuals that just became unhoused because of this tragedy, Rollan Escalona told CBS12 News after the meeting. entry.article_text: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after Port St. Lucie Police Department investigators say he struck a 24-year-old woman riding an electric scooter to work and left the scene, leaving her critically injured. Police say the driver had been playing a "ding-dong-ditch" prank with friends shortly before Monday morning's crash. WATCH: E-Scooter Hit-and-Run in Port St. Lucie Police identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested on a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, according to the department. The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when she was hit by a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Tuesday the woman remained unconscious and in critical condition. "We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said. Police said a witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and was able to get the SUV's license plate information. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and the driver. Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing "ding-dong-ditch" shortly before the crash. "They were specifically playing, I'll call it ring and run, ding-dong-ditch, at a house that belonged to a friend of theirs, and apparently the mother came to the door and they fled the scene," Niemczyk told WPTV. Niemczyk said investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred. "They're aware that they hit something. According to Niemczyk, Sanchez-Chasmer and the two passengers did not call 911. Niemczyk said the decision to leave the scene was key to the criminal investigation. "Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome," Niemczyk said. "There probably wouldn't have been criminal charges at that point." Sanchez-Chasmer was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. According to published reports citing law enforcement records, he was being held on a $5,000 bond. Police have not announced charges against the two passengers. WPTV returned to the intersection after the crash and spoke with 15-year-old John Rogalewski, who said he rides an e-scooter to school and is sometimes on the road early in the morning. "I'm looking at my surroundings almost the whole time," Rogalewski said. "I'm making sure every time I have to cross the street that there's not a car coming up, and that it is my sign to go, no matter how long I have to wait to cross." Police said the 24-year-old woman was wearing a helmet when she was struck. The investigation remains active, according to police, and toxicology results are still pending. entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Some Treasure Coast schools close Wednesday due to heavy rainfall concerns; Indian River, Martin open - WPBF
entry.summary: Some Treasure Coast schools close Wednesday due to heavy rainfall concerns; Indian River, Martin open    WPBF
entry.article_text: Due to anticipated rainfall, at least one public-school district and a private school on the Treasure Coast will close. LUCIE COUNTY A spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Public Schools announced that the school district will be closed to students and employees on Wednesday, Nov. "While there remains some uncertainty regarding the exact timing, location, and amount of rainfall, current forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," the school district spokesperson said in a statement. All after-school activities, after-care programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday were canceled. The spokesperson added that school district officials will continue to monitor rainfall, flooding, road closures and the accessibility of schools, bus stops and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision about school reopening on Thursday will be announced on Wednesday evening. The school district said it will provide updates on its website and social media platforms. John Carroll High School: The private school in Fort Pierce announced it will be closed on Wednesday because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding throughout the region. "The decision follows today's early dismissal and a review of current weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials determined that closing campus is the best course of action to ensure the safety of students, faculty, staff, and families," the school said in a statement to WPBF 25 News on Tuesday evening. "All school-sponsored activities scheduled for Wednesday, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs, and other events, have been canceled." The school added it anticipates resuming normal operations on Thursday, Nov. 19, pending weather and road conditions. "Administrators will continue to monitor forecasts and remain in communication with local authorities before making any further decisions regarding school operations," the school said. "Updates will be shared through the school’s official communication channels as conditions warrant." Boys Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County: All after-school programs and Clubhouse locations will be closed on Wednesday, Nov. MARTIN COUNTY The Martin County School District said that school and Extended Day will be open to students on Wednesday, but all other after-school activities, athletic practices and events are canceled for Wednesday. Officials in Martin County will monitor weather conditions. Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County: All Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County locations will reopen on Wednesday, Nov. 18, and resume normal operating hours. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY The School District of Indian River County announced on Tuesday afternoon that there will be a regular school schedule for students and employees, including Extended Day and extracurricular activities, on Wednesday, Nov. "District teams found no standing water affecting safe routes to bus stops. Families are encouraged to make the best decision for their circumstances," a spokesperson for the school district said in a statement on Tuesday. "Weather-related absences will follow standard attendance procedures and will not be excused solely due to weather." entry.title: St. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district announced Tuesday afternoon that schools and offices will be closed Wednesday as a precaution. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.title: Martin County Teacher of the Year Richard Acosta celebrates educators who inspire students - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County Teacher of the Year Richard Acosta celebrates educators who inspire students    WPTV
entry.article_text: Pinewood Elementary School science teacher Richard Acosta has been named the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year, earning the opportunity to represent the county in the Florida Department of Education’s statewide Teacher of the Year competition.The Education Foundation of Martin County announced Acosta as the overall winner during its Teacher of the Year Award Celebration on Nov. 6 at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center in Port St. Lucie.Acosta was also named Elementary Teacher of the Year.“This is phenomenal,” Acosta said after the honor was revealed. “I feel incredibly invigorated and inspired to go to the next level and represent Martin County at the state competition.”Acosta was among three educators recognized with top honors.Miriam Hernández, an intensive reading teacher at Indiantown Middle School, was named Middle School Teacher of the Year.Marc Turull, who teaches International Baccalaureate physics and chemistry at South Fork High School, was named High School Teacher of the Year.Turull said the award also represents the people he works alongside.“It’s such an honor,” Turull said. “I teach physics, and I work with amazing people, so to represent them and be Teacher of the Year makes me so grateful.”Hernández described the recognition as both a privilege and an honor.During the celebration, the three teachers emphasized the importance of educators at every stage of a student's education.“The fact is that it takes all three of us for excellence in Martin County schools,” Acosta said. “We start with the foundation in elementary school. We move on to middle school intensive reading, and then we finish at the high school at South Fork. So we, we feel very blessed to be working together.”The Education Foundation said Acosta’s 35-year career in education can be traced partly to his own experience as a teenager.According to the Education Foundation of Martin County, at 16, Acosta was struggling with confidence and direction when he entered teacher John Lynskey’s American history class. According to the foundation, Lynskey’s storytelling and encouragement helped Acosta develop a love of learning.Acosta still keeps two history books Lynskey gave him.His path toward teaching became clearer when Acosta later tutored a younger student after school and watched the child's confidence and enthusiasm for learning grow, according to the foundation.Today, Acosta teaches science to students from prekindergarten through fifth grade at Pinewood Elementary.“I love what I do, and I love energizing the classroom and engaging them to the greatest possibility,” Acosta said.His lessons include hands-on investigations tied to the natural environment around Martin County. The Education Foundation said students have examined sea turtle skull models, shells and other materials connected to the Indian River Lagoon while studying how adaptations help turtles survive.Acosta also helped develop a “Birds of the Everglades” curriculum with environmental partners and has been involved with schoolwide science initiatives and family STEAM events.For Acosta, the recognition provides another opportunity beyond representing Martin County at the state level.“I feel very blessed to be in this position because I get to mentor other teachers from other schools,” Acosta said.Acosta also receives a one-year vehicle lease provided through Audi Stuart and Infiniti Stuart.“That is amazing and spectacular,” Acosta said. “I cannot wait to pick out a car on Saturday.”The celebration recognized 24 school-level Teachers of the Year who were selected by their peers. According to the Education Foundation, nominees submitted application portfolios and participated in interviews before a panel of judges.Felix A. Williams Elementary School also won the Spirit Award for its enthusiasm, interpretation of the event's theme, and props.The recognition comes as Martin County educators continue the everyday work behind the awards: helping children learn, building their confidence and creating connections that can influence students long after they leave the classroom.For Acosta, that circle is especially meaningful. A teacher once helped him see greater possibilities for his own future. Decades later, he is working to create those possibilities for another generation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline in Florida already getting results just hours after its launch
entry.summary: A new 24/7 animal cruelty hotline in Florida is already getting results just hours after its launch was announced. Big Dog Ranch Rescue CEO and founder Lauree Simmons said the hotline went live Monday, and the organization received more than 30 calls. It also led to the rescue of an abandoned and neglected dog in Bay County. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Big Dog Ranch applauds Florida's new animal cruelty hotline The hotline gives people a place to report suspected animal abuse, including cruelty, abandonment and dog fighting. The reports are then turned over to law enforcement, animal control or a government agency for possible investigation. 'These animals can't call you can. You see an animal being neglected, starved, call and report it,' Simmons said. The Florida Statewide Animal Cruelty Hotline is operated by Big Dog Ranch Rescue, located in Loxahatchee Groves, and funded through the state. The hotline number is 844-4-SOSPET (844-476-7738). People can report anonymously, and it's available 24/7.

entry.title: Woman dies after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run; police say driver was playing 'ding dong ditch' beforehand
entry.summary: A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie , police said Wednesday. The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Teen Charged in Port St. Lucie E-Scooter Hit-and-Run | WPTV The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement. The department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police. Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing 'ding dong ditch' with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman. Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said. Following the woman's death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney's Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation. Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday's news release.

"He loves this event, so the kids will be able to visit with him."Family Night is scheduled for Tuesday evening on Nov. 17, at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast.An adult holiday pajama party follows FridayThe celebration takes a turn for the grown-ups Friday with an adult holiday pajama party."We will be a museum full of adults dressed in their holiday pajamas because who doesn’t want to go to a party and go home and go right to bed," McIntosh said.The festival continues through Saturday, Nov. 21, at 2 p.m., according to McIntosh. entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: South Florida Water Management District authorizes emergency pumping as flooding threat continues
entry.summary: The South Florida Water Management District has issued an emergency order allowing certain pumping and water-management measures as communities contend with saturated ground and the threat of additional heavy rainfall. The emergency final order, signed by Executive Director Drew Bartlett, is intended to help address flooding caused by the heavy rainfall that has hit portions of Florida beginning Oct. 31. The district said some impacted areas received more than 10 inches of rain in 36 hours, causing widespread flooding and leaving standing water and saturated ground. WATCH BELOW: Flood victims worried as Martin County braces for more rain Flood victims worried as Martin County braces for more rain The order comes as additional localized heavy rain threatens areas already hit hard by flooding. The district said those conditions create an 'imminent threat' of additional significant flooding and damage to life and property. The emergency action stems from state-of-emergency declarations issued by Gov. Ron DeSantis on Nov. 2 and Nov. 4 in response to the flooding. Under the order, water can be moved from flooded portions of a property, including roadways, parking lots and swales, to ponds, lakes or other areas on the same property without notifying the district, as long as the water is not being discharged off-site. Moving floodwater off-site requires more oversight. The district must approve such discharges after a field inspection, and the flooding must pose an immediate threat to public health, safety or welfare. The order specifically says minor flooding, such as standing water in roads, swales or yards, does not qualify as an immediate threat. entry.title: Boca Raton opens its first climate-controlled indoor pickleball and padel club with 25 courts
entry.summary: A massive indoor pickleball facility is opening its doors in Boca Raton. Boca Paddle by City Pickle is officially welcoming players to 25 brand-new courts. It's the city's first fully climate-controlled indoor pickleball and padel club. Day passes cost $40, with Boca Raton residents getting $5 off. The center also features a restaurant and bar, a shop, and fitness and recovery spaces like a sauna and cold plunge. One of its co-founders says Boca Paddle is unlike anything else in the city. Boca Raton's mayor says the city is the right fit for this type of facility. The area that we're in right now, here in North Park, is in need of revitalization. And this facility, by itself, takes a huge step in that direction to help revitalize this part of the city,' Boca Raton Mayor Andy Thomson said. The facility will also be the home of a new professional team. 'I'm excited that we're a home for the Palm Beach Royals , which is major league pickleball's newest franchise. They paid $16 million last year. They're going to be based here,' Boca Paddle Co-Founder Brian Levine said. By the numbers, the facility spans 100,000 square feet and cost around $20 million to build. It has 14 indoor pickleball courts and nine outdoor courts, along with two padel courts. entry.article_text: Due to anticipated rainfall, at least one public-school district and a private school on the Treasure Coast will close. LUCIE COUNTY A spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Public Schools announced that the school district will be closed to students and employees on Wednesday, Nov. "While there remains some uncertainty regarding the exact timing, location, and amount of rainfall, current forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," the school district spokesperson said in a statement. All after-school activities, after-care programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday were canceled. The spokesperson added that school district officials will continue to monitor rainfall, flooding, road closures and the accessibility of schools, bus stops and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision about school reopening on Thursday will be announced on Wednesday evening. The school district said it will provide updates on its website and social media platforms. John Carroll High School: The private school in Fort Pierce announced it will be closed on Wednesday because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding throughout the region. "The decision follows today's early dismissal and a review of current weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials determined that closing campus is the best course of action to ensure the safety of students, faculty, staff, and families," the school said in a statement to WPBF 25 News on Tuesday evening. "All school-sponsored activities scheduled for Wednesday, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs, and other events, have been canceled." The school added it anticipates resuming normal operations on Thursday, Nov. 19, pending weather and road conditions. "Administrators will continue to monitor forecasts and remain in communication with local authorities before making any further decisions regarding school operations," the school said. "Updates will be shared through the school’s official communication channels as conditions warrant." Boys Girls Club of Palm Beach County: All Boys Girls Club school sites in Palm Beach County are closed November 18 due to weather concerns, while other club sites remain open. Lucie County: All after-school programs and Clubhouse locations will be closed on Wednesday, Nov. MARTIN COUNTY The Martin County School District said that school and Extended Day will be open to students on Wednesday, but all other after-school activities, athletic practices and events are canceled for Wednesday. Officials in Martin County will monitor weather conditions. Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County: All Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County locations will reopen on Wednesday, Nov. 18, and resume normal operating hours. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY The School District of Indian River County announced on Tuesday afternoon that there will be a regular school schedule for students and employees, including Extended Day and extracurricular activities, on Wednesday, Nov. "District teams found no standing water affecting safe routes to bus stops. Families are encouraged to make the best decision for their circumstances," a spokesperson for the school district said in a statement on Tuesday. "Weather-related absences will follow standard attendance procedures and will not be excused solely due to weather." entry.title: Mary Peltola projected to flip Alaska Senate seat, giving Democrats 56-44 majority
entry.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to the Associated Press, delivering a significant pickup for Democrats. ANALYSIS | The significance of Peltola's election win The significance of Peltola's election win Peltola's victory marks the first time since 2008 that a Democrat has won a U.S. Senate election in Alaska, and gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate though two lawmakers identify as Independents and simply caucus with the Democrats. 'As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,' Peltola said in a statement. 'As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaskas working families. Thank you Alaska. Lets get to work. Peltola, who made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, focused her Senate campaign on lowering the cost of living and addressing economic challenges facing everyday Alaskans. She previously served in the U.S. House of Representatives, where she became known for emphasizing issues important to Alaska, including the state's fishing industry and economic development. The race drew national attention as Republicans fought to defend their Senate majority. Sullivan, a military veteran seeking a third term, received support from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Sullivan aligned his campaign with the Trump administration's tax and spending priorities and advocated for expanding fossil fuel production. The race in Alaska was complicated by the presence of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, ran as a long shot Democratic candidate for Senate. Both Dan Sullivans running prompted a legal fight early in the campaign, and President Donald Trump later called the former teacher's campaign 'fake' and 'a hoax by the Democrats.'

entry.title: Another flooding threat tests St. Lucie County as leaders brace for Amendment 3 budget cuts
entry.summary: As the threat of another round of November rain and flooding takes aim at Florida's east coast, many local governments are once again preparing for what may be ahead. 'I think everybody is well aware now that this storm drain system was not designed for the flooding we're getting nowadays,' St. Lucie County spokesman Erick Gill said. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flooding and Budget Worries on Treasure Coast He said crews are being deployed across the county as they were two weeks ago. 'There were probably 50 to 100 staff members out there, including crews in public works, out in the field working during the storm. That's unbudgeted overtime,' Gill said. This week, the county offered free sand , donated by Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials, for residents to bag. Other services cost money, and Gill said budgeting is already on the minds of county leaders now that the Amendment 3 tax cuts are coming. What is uncertain is how the loss of revenue will affect things like storm preparation and response. 'We still don't know what the total impacts will be for, you know, with Amendment 3 with the additional homestead exemption,' Gill said. "I think everybody is well aware now that this storm drain system was not designed for the flooding we're getting nowadays," St. Lucie County spokesman Erick Gill said.WATCH REPORT BELOW: He said crews are being deployed across the county as they were two weeks ago. "There were probably 50 to 100 staff members out there, including crews in public works, out in the field working during the storm. That's unbudgeted overtime," Gill said. This week, the county offered free sand, donated by Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials, for residents to bag. Other services cost money, and Gill said budgeting is already on the minds of county leaders now that the Amendment 3 tax cuts are coming. What is uncertain is how the loss of revenue will affect things like storm preparation and response. "We still don't know what the total impacts will be for, you know, with Amendment 3 with the additional homestead exemption," Gill said. "We're looking at the early estimates in this next upcoming fiscal year to be about a $60 million shortfall and then about $120 million once the exemption goes up."

entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: Martin County families still recovering from this month’s flooding are bracing for more rain, and on Tuesday, many of them asked county commissioners not to wait on federal help before opening an emergency shelter. Speaker after speaker told commissioners during public comment that water was already back in their streets. Some said their homes took on water earlier this month. Their main request was a public shelter, open before the next round of rain, for both unhoused residents and families who lost their homes in the flooding. Commissioners are discussing funding options at both the local and federal level. Florida has asked President Donald Trump for a major disaster declaration for the flooding, and as of Tuesday, it had not been signed. Once a disaster receives a federal declaration, FEMA must cover 75 percent of state and local response and recovery costs, according to the Florida Policy Institute. Without one, counties pay those costs on their own. Several speakers argued the county does not need to wait for that approval to act. Commissioner, you do not need FEMA’s blessing to open a school. Neighboring counties didn’t wait. Churches didn’t wait, one speaker said. Yamila Rollan Escalona, founder and executive director of Yaya Por Vida, a grassroots harm reduction organization, said she emailed her comments Tuesday morning as water rose in her neighborhood again, then came to speak in person. She said her group has been asking commissioners for emergency shelter for most of the year. See also: Palm Beach County braces for more flooding as cities offer sandbags, prepare for storm Please give us emergency shelter now. It’s no longer about just individuals that are unhoused. It’s also about individuals that just became unhoused because of this tragedy, Rollan Escalona told CBS12 News after the meeting. Rollan Escalona said unhoused residents have nowhere to go, pointing to a 2024 state law that bans sleeping on public property. She said some people are still staying in campsites surrounded by standing water, and some residents have not been accounted for. With drains and the ground already saturated, she said there is no time to wait. She also warned the damage won’t end when the water goes down. Rollan Escalona said mental health services on the Treasure Coast are already hard to access, and she worries the stress and hopelessness of losing everything could lead to more overdoses and people returning to substance use. Other speakers looked further ahead, linking the flooding to development in the county, including a proposed hyperscale data center. They asked commissioners to consider runoff and drainage before approving large projects. Take the 30,000-foot view the next time you look at a large project. How does it affect your neighbors? Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite previously told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes. Residents whose homes were damaged can report it and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Ahead of the rain, Martin County is handing out sand and sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park, 8303 SW Lost River Road. Distribution runs from noon to 6 p.m. Each household can take up to 25 sandbags, and residents will be asked for their name and address. The county asks residents to check its map for the exact pickup spot inside the park. CBS12 News will update this story with what commissioners decide on funding and a possible shelter.

entry.article_text: A 24-year-old woman who was critically injured in a hit-and-run crash while riding an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie has died, according to police. The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. 16 near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace, according to the Port St. Officers said the victim was struck by a vehicle whose driver fled the scene without stopping to provide aid or contact law enforcement. Investigators with the department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle involved as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a residence in Port St. Police identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer, 18. According to investigators, Sanchez-Chasmer had been participating in a game of "ding dong ditch" with friends shortly before the crash. Police said he struck the scooter rider while leaving a residence where the group had been carrying out the prank and then left the scene. Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony under Florida law. The victim died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Following her death, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said it expects the State Attorney's Office to pursue enhanced and/or additional charges as the investigation continues. In a news release issued Wednesday morning, police extended condolences to the victim's family and loved ones, describing the death as a tragic loss for the community Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates

entry.title: Inside PBSO's training simulator: How deputies prepare for split-second decisions
entry.summary: After five Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office deputy-involved shootings since August, WPTV is taking a closer look at how the agency trains deputies for critical encounters where decisions can be made in a matter of seconds. Hoffman participated in the training firsthand, experiencing how quickly a situation can develop and how deputies are expected to decide whether to escalate, de-escalate or rely on communication alone. entry.article_text: After five Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office deputy-involved shootings since August, WPTV is taking a closer look at how the agency trains deputies for critical encounters where decisions can be made in a matter of seconds.The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office invited WPTV's Michael Hoffman inside its immersive training simulator, which puts deputies through scenarios ranging from active shooters and potentially deadly encounters to situations where no lethal force is necessary.Hoffman participated in the training firsthand, experiencing how quickly a situation can develop and how deputies are expected to decide whether to escalate, de-escalate or rely on communication alone.The training comes at a time following five deputy-involved shootings involving the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office in recent months.Those incidents happened in:West Palm Beach on Aug. 6South Palm Beach on Sept. 10Each incident carries its own circumstances, but collectively they raise questions about how deputies prepare for encounters in which rapidly changing conditions can force them to make consequential decisions.To better understand that training, Hoffman went through it.Inside the simulator, deputies face a wide range of scenarios."We go from active shooter, and we have ones that are just completely, there's going to be no lethal force," Cpl. Capobianco, a PBSO training deputy, said.The training isn't necessarily limited to a predetermined outcome.According to Capobianco, trainers can change how a scenario develops depending on how the deputy interacts with the person on screen."We're able to choose different, how should I say, different like categories to select from to escalate, de-escalate the situation, all based off of how the deputy's communicating to the screen and how the scenario is reacting from there," Capobianco said.That means a deputy's words and actions can influence what happens next.Before Hoffman entered the simulator, trainers sat him down in a classroom and explained what he could expect.Deputies then walked him through the equipment available during training."We have every weapon platform that we have here," Capobianco said.The options include handguns, shotguns and rifles, along with Tasers and other less-lethal devices.Then, it was Hoffman's turn.He went through multiple simulated encounters designed to test how he would respond under pressure.But the scenario that stood out most did not require him to use a weapon at all.The scenario involved a man standing on a highway overpass and threatening to throw a baby.Hoffman's primary tools were his voice and his ability to de-escalate the situation."Has this gone too far already, or is there a way out?" the simulated man asked."You're not too late," Hoffman responded. "Let's just take a breath and slow this down a little bit, OK?"After the scenario ended, trainers immediately began breaking down what happened and why."You controlled the situation, right? You verbally made sure that he was making contact with you," one trainer told Hoffman.The trainer pointed specifically to Hoffman's decision not to immediately introduce a weapon into the encounter."You took the time to de-escalate the situation without having to escalate things even further by the mere presence of drawing your weapon," the trainer said.That debrief is part of the training.Rather than simply running deputies through a scenario, trainers can walk through the decisions made during an encounter and examine how communication or tactical choices affected its direction.For Hoffman, the experience showed how quickly emotion can become part of a critical encounter."I'm sure that everyone's been in a situation where they're really emotional and they're not seeing rational thought, and they have the thought to do something crazy," Hoffman said after the exercise. "But it just takes someone to take an extra second, be like, 'Hey, life is still going on. Just slow down, man.'"The scenario was simulated. The adrenaline and stress were not.And following five deputy-involved shootings in recent months, the exercise offered a firsthand look at one way PBSO trains deputies for situations in which they may have only seconds to determine what happens next.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Loxahatchee Groves nursery recovers from flooding, prepares for more rain
entry.summary: Two weeks after floodwaters covered Gardino Nursery in Loxahatchee Groves, conditions are improving, but the cleanup is far from over as the business prepares for the possibility of more rain. WPTV reporter Christy Waite first visited Gardino Nursery two weeks ago, when parts of the property were covered in water up to her shins, and fish could be seen swimming through the floodwater. WATCH REPORT BELOW: FLOOD-HIT NURSERY BRACES FOR RAIN Waite returned to the nursery this week to see how conditions have changed and how the business is preparing for more wet weather. The water has since receded, but signs of the flooding remain. Thick mud still covers parts of the property, making it difficult for employees to move around as they continue cleaning up. Owner Sid Gardino said conditions have been improving enough for workers to once again reach some areas of the property by golf cart. But another round of rain brought three-quarters of an inch of water to the area. Now, his attention is turning to the weather ahead. 'I don't know what's going to happen. They are forecasting a lot more rain,' Gardino said. Gardino Nursery is an appointment-only plant nursery in Loxahatchee Groves. Unfortunately, this year's weather has forced them to close business to visitors since October. Gardino said being closed for so long because of the recent flooding is setting them back thousands of dollars in revenue. For Gardino, it's not his first rodeo with Florida weather. Just this year, his business survived the freeze earlier this year, the drought over the summer, recent flooding, and now the potential for even more rain. After weeks of bad weather, he's hoping for dry and sunny weather ahead.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie restores water service, but boil water notice remains
entry.summary: Water service has been fully restored to the Tradition and western Port St. Lucie areas following a major water main break Tuesday, but a precautionary boil water notice remains in effect. The break happened Nov. 17 near Glades Cut Off Road when a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged a 36-inch water main, according to city officials. Crews completed repairs Tuesday evening and began flushing the water main shortly afterward. The city initially recommended a 48-hour precautionary boil water notice Tuesday at noon for the Tradition area, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, west of Interstate 95 to Becker Road. The notice also covers communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano. City officials said water quality testing began Wednesday. Because of the number of customers affected, a significant number of samples must be collected and tested before the notice can be lifted. Residents should continue boiling water until the city confirms it is safe to use without boiling. Restored water service does not mean the boil water notice has ended. The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible. Updates will be posted at CityofPSL.com .

entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.summary: Woman dies after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run; police say driver was playing 'ding dong ditch' beforehand    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie , police said Wednesday. The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement. The department’s Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police. Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing “ding dong ditch” with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman. Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said. Following the woman’s death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney’s Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation. Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday’s news release.

entry.summary: 18-year-old charged in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured woman riding e-scooter    WPTV
entry.article_text: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after Port St. Lucie Police Department investigators say he struck a 24-year-old woman riding an electric scooter to work and left the scene, leaving her critically injured. Police say the driver had been playing a "ding-dong-ditch" prank with friends shortly before Monday morning's crash.WATCH: E-Scooter Hit-and-Run in Port St. LuciePolice identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested on a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, according to the department.The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when she was hit by a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace.Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Tuesday the woman remained unconscious and in critical condition."We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said.Police said a witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and was able to get the SUV's license plate information. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and the driver. Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing "ding-dong-ditch" shortly before the crash. "They were specifically playing, I'll call it ring and run, ding-dong-ditch, at a house that belonged to a friend of theirs, and apparently the mother came to the door and they fled the scene," Niemczyk told WPTV.Niemczyk said investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred."They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that," he said.According to Niemczyk, Sanchez-Chasmer and the two passengers did not call 911.Niemczyk said the decision to leave the scene was key to the criminal investigation."Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome," Niemczyk said. "There probably wouldn't have been criminal charges at that point."Sanchez-Chasmer was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. According to published reports citing law enforcement records, he was being held on a $5,000 bond. Police have not announced charges against the two passengers. WPTV returned to the intersection after the crash and spoke with 15-year-old John Rogalewski, who said he rides an e-scooter to school and is sometimes on the road early in the morning."I'm looking at my surroundings almost the whole time," Rogalewski said. "I'm making sure every time I have to cross the street that there's not a car coming up, and that it is my sign to go, no matter how long I have to wait to cross."Police said the 24-year-old woman was wearing a helmet when she was struck.The investigation remains active, according to police, and toxicology results are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Power says more galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are in the works, bringing new opportunities for artists, residents and visitors.A historic Vero Beach neighborhood becomes a canvasUnder the shade of a century-old lychee tree, Power reads from a poem dedicated to the tree as a dancer performs beneath its branches."A place where you and me can become we," Power said.For the longtime sculptor, the tree represents something bigger: a gathering place where art can bring people together.That vision is unfolding in Edgewood, a neighborhood established in 1916 that was once home to Vero Beach's first public school and first motel, according to the Vero Beach Art Village organization.Over the years, parts of the neighborhood fell into disrepair. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential."It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that," Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood.Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami.Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas.Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of artOne of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art."I'm taking the alleys which are the ugliest part of the neighborhood and turning them into mural opportunities where the alleys are going to be like unbelievable for people to come and visit," Power said."There's a lack of buildings but there's not a lack of fences."Power sees those fences, walls and underused spaces as opportunities to showcase local artists and create an outdoor art experience.But the effort goes beyond beautifying back streets.Special zoning allows artists to live and work in the villageThe city of Vero Beach has established Cultural Arts Village zoning districts designed to encourage artistic businesses while preserving Edgewood's historic residential character.According to the city and the Vero Beach Art Village organization, the zoning creates opportunities for art galleries, studios, live-work spaces and other businesses, depending on the property's classification and applicable approvals.The goal is to create a walkable neighborhood where historic homes can become studios and galleries, and artists can collaborate with their neighbors.“I’ve been working on a bunch of different paintings. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. It's to create a community where artists can thrive together and residents can take pride in their neighborhood."If you want to eat great food, hear great music, see great things, meet great artists, this is the place," Power said.And beneath the sprawling branches of that century-old lychee tree, Power hopes the community he's helping cultivate will continue to grow.Where is the Vero Beach Art Village?The Vero Beach Art Village is located in the historic Edgewood neighborhood, just west of downtown Vero Beach.The neighborhood generally stretches between 14th and 20th avenues and 18th and 20th streets.The Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village nonprofit encourages residents and visitors to support the effort through volunteering, donations and participation in community art projects.Click here for more information about the village, its projects and opportunities to get involved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
